Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Use the SI laboratory chart and source conventions: $\rho:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ has units $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-3}$ and $J:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ has units $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Let $a,c,\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, and let $\rho,J$ be jointly $C^\infty$, vanish for $|y|>a$, and satisfy $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_yJ=0$. Let $K=[u_-,u_+]\subset\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate compact interval, $u_-<u_+$, and put $K^\sharp=[u_--2a/c,u_++2a/c]$. For $j=0,1,2$, define

$$M_{\rho,j}:=\sup_{\overline B_a\times K^\sharp}|\partial_t^j\rho|,\qquad M_{J,j}:=\sup_{\overline B_a\times K^\sharp}|\partial_t^jJ|.$$

For $n\in S^2$ and $u\in K$, define the retarded current moment and its derivative by

$$I(n,u):=\int_{B_a}J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy,\qquad V(n,u):=\partial_u I(n,u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy.$$

Let $E,B$ be the selected retarded fields of the preceding theorem, set $S=E\times B/\mu_0$, and define

$$\Gamma_E:=\frac{\mu_0\lambda_3(B_a)}{4\pi}\left(4c^2M_{\rho,0}+13caM_{\rho,1}+a^2M_{\rho,2}+3aM_{J,1}+\frac{a^2}{c}M_{J,2}\right),$$

$$\Gamma_B:=\frac{\mu_0\lambda_3(B_a)}{4\pi}\left(4M_{J,0}+\frac{13a}{c}M_{J,1}+\frac{a^2}{c^2}M_{J,2}\right).$$

Then for every $n\in S^2$, $u\in K$ and $r\ge2a$, with $E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times V(n,u))$,

$$\left|E(rn,u+r/c)-E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)\right|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2},\qquad \left|B(rn,u+r/c)-\frac{n\times E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)}{c}\right|\le\frac{\Gamma_B}{r^2}.$$

Consequently the radiation data of the preceding definition exist uniformly on $S^2\times K$ and equal

$$E_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}n\times(n\times V(n,u)),\qquad B_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u)=\frac{n\times E_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u)}{c}.$$

For each fixed retarded time $u$, the outward retarded-time flux has the exact limit

$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot S(rn,u+r/c)\,d\Omega(n)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}|n\times V(n,u)|^2\,d\Omega(n).$$

citations.quote:
Fix a named positively oriented inertial laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$, spatial domain $\mathbb R^3$, and time domain $\mathbb R$. Adopt SI
units, a vacuum speed $c>0$, an angular frequency $\omega>0$, and
$k_0:=\omega/c$ (so $[k_0]=\mathrm{m}^{-1}$). Let
$\mathbf x_\perp:=(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$. Use the unitary two-dimensional
Fourier transform $\mathcal F_2$ whose Schwartz-space convention is
$$\widehat f(\boldsymbol\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(\mathbf x_\perp) e^{-2\pi i\mathbf x_\perp\cdot\boldsymbol\xi}\,d^2\mathbf x_\perp,$$
and whose inverse is its unitary $L^2$ extension. The variable
$\boldsymbol\xi$ is in cycles per metre; its associated angular spatial
wavevector is $\mathbf q:=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, with
$|\mathbf q|^2:=q_x^2+q_y^2$.

Choose $0<\delta<1$ and $u_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ with
$\mathcal F_2u_0$ supported, up to null sets, in
$D_\delta:=\{\boldsymbol\xi:|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|\le\delta k_0\}$.
For $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$ put
$$k_z(\boldsymbol\xi):=\sqrt{k_0^2-|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2},$$
which is real and strictly positive there. For each $z\in\mathbb R$, define the
exact multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=\begin{cases}e^{izk_z(\boldsymbol\xi)},&\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta,\\0,&\boldsymbol\xi\notin D_\delta,\end{cases}$$
and define the paraxial multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=e^{ik_0z}e^{-iz|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/(2k_0)}.$$
The exact scalar and paraxial scalar propagators are the $L^2$ equivalence
classes
$$u_{\mathrm{exact}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right],\qquad u_{\mathrm{par}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right].$$
The associated real scalar fields are the real parts of these phasors multiplied
by $e^{-i\omega t}$. If $u_0$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, both propagated
fields carry the same unit. “Exact” here names the exact positive axial
dispersion multiplier inside this scalar model; it does not assert exact
Maxwell validity. Forward propagation is $z\ge0$; the formulas also define the
mathematical continuation to negative $z$.

At a fixed $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$, write
$\mathbf K(\boldsymbol\xi):=(2\pi\xi_x,2\pi\xi_y,k_z(\boldsymbol\xi))$.
A candidate monochromatic vector plane-wave mode at frequency $\omega$ has
complex amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$ in the real-field
encoding $e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot(x,y,z)-\omega t)}$. It is called an exact
source-free vacuum mode only when its associated real fields satisfy the
adopted source-free vacuum Maxwell equations. The longitudinal electric
coefficient is $e_z$, and
$\mathbf e_\perp:=(e_x,e_y)$ has norm
$|\mathbf e_\perp|^2:=|e_x|^2+|e_y|^2$. No scalar/vector polarization
factorization is part of this definition.

Let $k_0>0$, $0<\delta<1$, $z\in\mathbb R$, and $s\in[0,\delta^2]$. Define

$$R(s):=1-\frac{s}{2}-\sqrt{1-s}.$$

Then

$$R(s)=\frac{s^2}{4\left(1-\frac{s}{2}+\sqrt{1-s}\right)},\qquad 0\le R(s)\le\frac{s^2}{8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},$$

and

$$\left|e^{izk_0\sqrt{1-s}}-e^{izk_0(1-s/2)}\right| \le \frac{|z|k_0s^2}{8(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}}.$$

More generally, for all real $a,b$,
$$|e^{ia}-e^{ib}|\le|a-b|.$$

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define

The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. statement.

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Set $\delta_n:=1/(n+2)$ and $R_n:=\delta_n k_0/(2\pi)$. Let $\Xi_n:=[R_n(1-\delta_n/4),R_n(1-\delta_n/8)] \times[0,R_n\delta_n/8]$. Its side lengths are both $R_n\delta_n/8>0$, so [F4] gives $0<|\Xi_n|=R_n^2\delta_n^2/64<\infty$. Define $\widehat u_{0,n}:=A_\star|\Xi_n|^{-1/2}\mathbf 1_{\Xi_n}$; then $\|\widehat u_{0,n}\|_2=A_\star$. For $\mathbf q=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$ with $\boldsymbol\xi\in\Xi_n$, $q_x\ge\delta_n k_0(1-\delta_n/4)>\delta_n k_0(1-\delta_n)$ and $|\mathbf q|^2\le\delta_n^2k_0^2[(1-\delta_n/8)^2+(\delta_n/8)^2] \le\delta_n^2k_0^2$; hence this nonzero spectrum lies in the angular cone and concentrates near its outer radius.

Let $u_{0,n}:=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\widehat u_{0,n}$ and $z_n:=8\pi/(k_0\delta_n^4)>0$. This fixes the scale in [F6] at $8\pi$. By [F3], $\|u_{0,n}\|_2=A_\star$, so each input is nonzero and admissible for the refuted statement.

For $\boldsymbol\xi\in\Xi_n$, put $s_n:=|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/k_0^2$. Step 1.1 gives $(1-\delta_n/4)^2\le s_n/\delta_n^2\le1$, so this ratio tends to $1$ uniformly on $\Xi_n$. Also $0\le s_n\le\delta_n^2$, and $|1-\sqrt{1-s_n}|=s_n/(1+\sqrt{1-s_n})\le s_n$, so $1-s_n/2+\sqrt{1-s_n}\to2$ uniformly. By [F2], the relative phase difference is $\Delta_n:=z_nk_0R(s_n) =2\pi(s_n/\delta_n^2)^2/(1-s_n/2+\sqrt{1-s_n})$, which tends uniformly to $\pi$.

The actual exact-minus-paraxial phase is $-\Delta_n$, so [F5] makes the modulus of the multiplier difference $|e^{i\Delta_n}-1|$. Put $u=e^{i\Delta_n}-1$ and $v=e^{i\pi}-1$. By [F7], $\bigl||u|-|v|\bigr|\le|u-v|$; [F5] gives $|v|=2$, and [F2] gives $|u-v|=|e^{i\Delta_n}-e^{i\pi}|\le|\Delta_n-\pi|\to0$ uniformly on $\Xi_n$. Thus the multiplier-difference modulus tends uniformly to $2$.

By [F3], the squared relative $L^2$ error is the average of $|e^{i\Delta_n}-1|^2$ over $\Xi_n$ with respect to normalized Lebesgue measure. Since step 3.1 gives uniform convergence of that modulus to $2$, the averages of its square tend to $4$; the relative errors are nonnegative, so they tend to $2$, not $0$. This contradicts the Statement refuted and proves the claimed counterexample.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a named positively oriented inertial laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$, spatial domain $\mathbb R^3$, and time domain $\mathbb R$. Adopt SI
units, a vacuum speed $c>0$, an angular frequency $\omega>0$, and
$k_0:=\omega/c$ (so $[k_0]=\mathrm{m}^{-1}$). Let
$\mathbf x_\perp:=(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$. Use the unitary two-dimensional
Fourier transform $\mathcal F_2$ whose Schwartz-space convention is
$$\widehat f(\boldsymbol\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(\mathbf x_\perp) e^{-2\pi i\mathbf x_\perp\cdot\boldsymbol\xi}\,d^2\mathbf x_\perp,$$
and whose inverse is its unitary $L^2$ extension. The variable
$\boldsymbol\xi$ is in cycles per metre; its associated angular spatial
wavevector is $\mathbf q:=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, with
$|\mathbf q|^2:=q_x^2+q_y^2$.

Choose $0<\delta<1$ and $u_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ with
$\mathcal F_2u_0$ supported, up to null sets, in
$D_\delta:=\{\boldsymbol\xi:|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|\le\delta k_0\}$.
For $z\in\mathbb R$ put
$$k_z(\boldsymbol\xi):=\sqrt{k_0^2-|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2},$$
which is real and strictly positive on $D_\delta$, and define the exact scalar
and paraxial scalar propagators as the $L^2$ equivalence classes
$$u_{\mathrm{exact}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[ e^{izk_z(\boldsymbol\xi)}\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right],\qquad u_{\mathrm{par}}(z):=e^{ik_0z}\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[ e^{-iz|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/(2k_0)}\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right].$$
The associated real scalar fields are the real parts of these phasors multiplied
by $e^{-i\omega t}$. If $u_0$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, both propagated
fields carry the same unit. “Exact” here names the exact positive axial
dispersion multiplier inside this scalar model; it does not assert exact
Maxwell validity. Forward propagation is $z\ge0$; the formulas also define the
mathematical continuation to negative $z$.

At a fixed $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$, write
$\mathbf K(\boldsymbol\xi):=(2\pi\xi_x,2\pi\xi_y,k_z(\boldsymbol\xi))$.
A candidate monochromatic vector plane-wave mode at frequency $\omega$ has
complex amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$ in the real-field
encoding $e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot(x,y,z)-\omega t)}$. It is called an exact
source-free vacuum mode only when its associated real fields satisfy the
adopted source-free vacuum Maxwell equations. The longitudinal electric
coefficient is $e_z$, and
$\mathbf e_\perp:=(e_x,e_y)$ has norm
$|\mathbf e_\perp|^2:=|e_x|^2+|e_y|^2$. No scalar/vector polarization
factorization is part of this definition.

citations.quote:
Fix a named, positively oriented SI laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$ and angular frequency $\omega>0$. Adopt the SI constants and
coordinate units of the laboratory convention: $c>0$ is in m s$^{-1}$,
$k_0:=\omega/c$ is in m$^{-1}$, and electric-field components are in V
m$^{-1}$. Let
$\Pi=\{(x,y,z_0):(x,y)\in D\}$ be a specified reference plane, where
$z_0\in\mathbb R$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a specified nonempty region.
Its oriented orthonormal transverse basis is $(e_x,e_y)$ and its normal is
$e_z$.

For the paraxial context, adopt $c>0$, $k_0=\omega/c$, and
$0<\delta<1$. The angular-spectrum variable $\xi\in\mathbb R^2$ is measured
in cycles per metre, $q=2\pi\xi$ is in m$^{-1}$, and the forward propagating
cone is $D_\delta=\{\xi:|q|\le\delta k_0\}$ with
$k_z(\xi)=\sqrt{k_0^2-|q|^2}>0$. The matrix below is defined pointwise for the
two-component projection; it does not assert that an arbitrary random
superposition is an exact Maxwell field or that the individual-mode
longitudinal bound extends to an ensemble without additional hypotheses.

Let $(\Xi,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a specified probability space. At each
fixed $\rho\in D$, let $Z_\rho:\Xi\to\mathbb C^2$ be measurable, with four real
coordinates
$X_\rho=(\operatorname{Re}Z_x,\operatorname{Im}Z_x,
\operatorname{Re}Z_y,\operatorname{Im}Z_y)$ forming a square-integrable
$\mathbb R^4$ random vector and
$\mathbb E[|Z_x(\rho)|^2+|Z_y(\rho)|^2]<\infty$. For $\sigma\in\Xi$, the
associated transverse real-field model is
$E_\perp(\rho,\sigma,t)=\operatorname{Re}(Z_\rho(\sigma)e^{-i\omega t})$.
Expectation is taken over this declared classical ensemble and is applied
componentwise to complex integrable variables. Define
$$\Gamma(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_\rho Z_\rho^\dagger],\qquad \Gamma_{ij}(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_i(\rho)\overline{Z_j(\rho)}]\quad(i,j\in\{1,2\}).$$
Thus $\Gamma$ is the uncentered second-moment matrix of the two selected
components; no zero-mean assumption is made. The degree of polarization is
defined only when $S_0>0$ by
$$S_0:=\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22},\quad S_1:=\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22},\quad S_2:=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_{12},\quad S_3:=-2\operatorname{Im}\Gamma_{12},\qquad \mathcal P:=\frac{\sqrt{S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2}}{S_0}.$$
The minus sign in $S_3$ is fixed by the stated phasor convention and the
ordered basis $(e_x,e_y)$. In this two-component model, a positive-intensity
state is called unpolarized when $\Gamma=(S_0/2)I_2$; this label concerns
second moments and does not say that any realization is a quantum state.
The $S_j$ have units (V m$^{-1}$)$^2$; $S_0$ is a mean-square field coordinate,
not an absolutely calibrated irradiance.

The construction applies to any ordered pair of square-integrable classical
complex amplitudes. When the pair labels transverse electric components,
$S_j$ have the polarization interpretation just defined. When it labels two
beam channels, the same matrix entries are channel correlations; they are not
polarization components.

Let $Z=(Z_1,Z_2)^{\mathsf T}$ be a measurable square-integrable complex
two-component vector on a probability space and define
$\Gamma:=\mathbb E[ZZ^\dagger]$, with
$\Gamma_{ij}:=\mathbb E[Z_i\overline{Z_j}]$. Put
$S_0:=\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22}$,
$S_1:=\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22}$,
$S_2:=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_{12}$, and
$S_3:=-2\operatorname{Im}\Gamma_{12}$; when $S_0>0$, put
$\mathcal P:=\sqrt{S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2}/S_0$. Then $\Gamma$ is positive
semidefinite, meaning
$v^\dagger\Gamma v\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb C^2$; its rank is the complex
dimension of its image. The Stokes coordinates satisfy
$$S_0\ge0,\qquad S_0^2\ge S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2.$$
Equality in the second relation holds exactly when $\Gamma=0$ or $\Gamma$ has
rank one. Consequently $\mathcal P\in[0,1]$ when $S_0>0$, and it is undefined
when $S_0=0$. If a fixed deterministic dimensionless complex-linear map
$M:\mathbb C^2\to\mathbb C^2$ (a Jones matrix in this model) sends each
realization $Z$ to $MZ$, then
$\Gamma$ transforms to $M\Gamma M^\dagger$.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

derivations.claim:
Expanding the squared modulus in [A1] gives
$|A_\zeta|^2=|A_2|^2+|A_1|^2+
\zeta A_1\overline{A_2}+\overline\zeta A_2\overline{A_1}$.
Taking expectations, using [F1] and [F3], yields
$I(\zeta)=I_1+I_2+2\operatorname{Re}(\zeta\Gamma_{12})$.

Put $S=I_1+I_2$ and $c=\Gamma_{12}$. Write
$\zeta=a+ib$ and $c=u+iv$. Since $\zeta\in\mathbb T$,
$a^2+b^2=1$. By [F4], $|c|^2=u^2+v^2$ and
$\operatorname{Re}(\zeta c)=au-bv$. Therefore
$$|c|^2-\bigl(\operatorname{Re}(\zeta c)\bigr)^2=(a^2+b^2)(u^2+v^2)-(au-bv)^2=(av+bu)^2\ge0,$$
so each $\operatorname{Re}(\zeta c)$ lies in $[-|c|,|c|]$. If $c\ne0$,
set $r:=|c|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}>0$ and $\zeta_0:=(u-iv)/r$. Then
$|\zeta_0|^2=(u^2+v^2)/r^2=1$, so $\zeta_0\in\mathbb T$, and direct
multiplication gives $\zeta_0c=r$ while $(-\zeta_0)c=-r$. Both endpoints
are therefore attained. If $c=0$, the cross term is identically zero. Hence
$I_{\max}=S+2|c|$ and $I_{\min}=S-2|c|$.

By [F2],
$S^2-4|c|^2=(I_1-I_2)^2+4(I_1I_2-|c|^2)\ge0$; since $S\ge0$, this gives
$2|c|\le S$. Under the given $S>0$ condition,
$I_{\max}+I_{\min}=2S>0$, so substitution of step 2.1 into the visibility
definition gives $V=2|c|/S\le1$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a named, positively oriented SI laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$ and angular frequency $\omega>0$. Adopt the SI constants and
coordinate units of the laboratory convention: $c>0$ is in m s$^{-1}$,
$k_0:=\omega/c$ is in m$^{-1}$, and electric-field components are in V
m$^{-1}$. Let
$\Pi=\{(x,y,z_0):(x,y)\in D\}$ be a specified reference plane, where
$z_0\in\mathbb R$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a specified nonempty region.
Its oriented orthonormal transverse basis is $(e_x,e_y)$ and its normal is
$e_z$.

For the paraxial context, adopt $c>0$, $k_0=\omega/c$, and
$0<\delta<1$. The angular-spectrum variable $\xi\in\mathbb R^2$ is measured
in cycles per metre, $q=2\pi\xi$ is in m$^{-1}$, and the forward propagating
cone is $D_\delta=\{\xi:|q|\le\delta k_0\}$ with
$k_z(\xi)=\sqrt{k_0^2-|q|^2}>0$. The matrix below is defined pointwise for the
two-component projection; it does not assert that an arbitrary random
superposition is an exact Maxwell field or that the individual-mode
longitudinal bound extends to an ensemble without additional hypotheses.

Let $(\Xi,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a specified probability space. At each
fixed $\rho\in D$, let $Z_\rho:\Xi\to\mathbb C^2$ be measurable, with four real
coordinates
$X_\rho=(\operatorname{Re}Z_x,\operatorname{Im}Z_x,
\operatorname{Re}Z_y,\operatorname{Im}Z_y)$ forming a square-integrable
$\mathbb R^4$ random vector and
$\mathbb E[|Z_x(\rho)|^2+|Z_y(\rho)|^2]<\infty$. For $\sigma\in\Xi$, the
associated transverse real-field model is
$E_\perp(\rho,\sigma,t)=\operatorname{Re}(Z_\rho(\sigma)e^{-i\omega t})$.
Expectation is taken over this declared classical ensemble and is applied
componentwise to complex integrable variables. Define
$$\Gamma(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_\rho Z_\rho^\dagger],\qquad \Gamma_{ij}(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_i(\rho)\overline{Z_j(\rho)}]\quad(i,j\in\{1,2\}).$$
Thus $\Gamma$ is the uncentered second-moment matrix of the two selected
components; no zero-mean assumption is made. The degree of polarization is
defined only when $S_0>0$ by
$$S_0:=\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22},\quad S_1:=\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22},\quad S_2:=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_{12},\quad S_3:=-2\operatorname{Im}\Gamma_{12},\qquad \mathcal P:=\frac{\sqrt{S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2}}{S_0}.$$
The minus sign in $S_3$ is fixed by the stated phasor convention and the
ordered basis $(e_x,e_y)$. In this two-component model, a positive-intensity
state is called unpolarized when $\Gamma=(S_0/2)I_2$; this label concerns
second moments and does not say that any realization is a quantum state.
The $S_j$ have units (V m$^{-1}$)$^2$; $S_0$ is a mean-square field coordinate,
not an absolutely calibrated irradiance.

The construction applies to any ordered pair of square-integrable classical
complex amplitudes. When the pair labels transverse electric components,
$S_j$ have the polarization interpretation just defined. When it labels two
beam channels, the same matrix entries are channel correlations; they are not
polarization components.

Let $Z=(Z_1,Z_2)^{\mathsf T}$ be a measurable square-integrable complex
two-component vector on a probability space and define
$\Gamma:=\mathbb E[ZZ^\dagger]$, with
$\Gamma_{ij}:=\mathbb E[Z_i\overline{Z_j}]$. Put
$S_0:=\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22}$,
$S_1:=\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22}$,
$S_2:=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_{12}$, and
$S_3:=-2\operatorname{Im}\Gamma_{12}$; when $S_0>0$, put
$\mathcal P:=\sqrt{S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2}/S_0$. Then $\Gamma$ is positive
semidefinite, meaning
$v^\dagger\Gamma v\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb C^2$; its rank is the complex
dimension of its image. The Stokes coordinates satisfy
$$S_0\ge0,\qquad S_0^2\ge S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2.$$
Equality in the second relation holds exactly when $\Gamma=0$ or $\Gamma$ has
rank one. Consequently $\mathcal P\in[0,1]$ when $S_0>0$, and it is undefined
when $S_0=0$. If a fixed deterministic dimensionless complex-linear map
$M:\mathbb C^2\to\mathbb C^2$ (a Jones matrix in this model) sends each
realization $Z$ to $MZ$, then
$\Gamma$ transforms to $M\Gamma M^\dagger$.

An exact spherical Einstein–Maxwell–$\Lambda$ datum consists of the orbit
geometry specified above, a smooth rotationally invariant real two-form
$\mathcal F$, a constant $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, and
the equations
$$d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}(g)_{ab}=\Lambda g_{ab}+2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F),$$
where
$$Q_{ab}(\mathcal F):=\mathcal F_{ac}\mathcal F_b{}^c -\frac14g_{ab}\mathcal F_{cd}\mathcal F^{cd}.$$
This is a mathematical system of equations, not a physical postulate. For
$\Lambda=0$ it uses exactly the curvature, Hodge, and Maxwell normalization of
the previously defined geometric electrovac equations. For $\Lambda\ne0$ the extra constant
term is part of this local mathematical definition; it is not supplied by
that zero-$\Lambda$ item.

By the preceding Maxwell reduction lemma, the field has unique constant
flux parameters $q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ and
$$\mathcal F=\frac{q_e}{r^2}\epsilon_2+q_m\omega_{S^2},\qquad Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2.$$
In geometric units, coordinates have length, $r,q_e,q_m$ have length, the
metric components are dimensionless, and $\Lambda$ has units of inverse
length squared. Define
$$z:=q^{-1}(dr,dr),\qquad \varpi:=\frac r2(1-z)+\frac{Q^2}{2r}-\frac{\Lambda r^3}{6}.$$
Thus $z$ is dimensionless and $\varpi$ has length. The scalar $\varpi$ is
called the charged spherical mass function; this definition does not assert
that it is constant. The field equations are local on $U\times S^2$ and
impose no global potential, bundle, horizon, asymptotic, completeness, or
extension condition.

The geometric-electrovacuum flux convention inherits only $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
through the supplied geometric electrovac definition. No full axiom of choice is used
by this definition or by the subsequent local algebra.

For an exact spherical Einstein–Maxwell–$\Lambda$ datum, let
$z=q^{-1}(dr,dr)$ and
$\Delta_qr:=q^{AB}(\nabla^q_A dr)_B$. The warped metric
$g=q+r^2\gamma_{S^2}$ has
$$\operatorname{Ric}(g)_{AB} =\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{AB}-2r^{-1}(\nabla^q_A dr)_B,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}(g)_{ij}=(1-z-r\Delta_qr)\gamma_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}(g)_{Ai}=0.$$
Its Maxwell tensor satisfies
$$Q_{AB}(\mathcal F)=-\frac{Q^2}{2r^4}q_{AB},\qquad Q_{ij}(\mathcal F)=\frac{Q^2}{2r^4}g_{ij},\qquad Q_{Ai}(\mathcal F)=0.$$
Consequently the Einstein–Maxwell–$\Lambda$ equations imply
$$\nabla^q_A dr_B=\frac12(\Delta_qr)q_{AB},\qquad \Delta_qr=\frac{1-z}{r}-\Lambda r-\frac{Q^2}{r^3},\qquad d\varpi=0.$$

Let $(U,q,\epsilon_2)$ be a connected, oriented, time-oriented smooth
two-dimensional Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+)$ with
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.
In local coordinates $y^0,y^1$, define
$$\Gamma^A{}_{BC}:=\frac12q^{AD} (\partial_Bq_{DC}+\partial_Cq_{BD}-\partial_Dq_{BC}),$$
and use the resulting metric-selected derivative $\nabla^q$ and the
curvature convention
$$R^A{}_{BCD}:=\partial_C\Gamma^A{}_{DB}-\partial_D\Gamma^A{}_{CB} +\Gamma^A{}_{CE}\Gamma^E{}_{DB}-\Gamma^A{}_{DE}\Gamma^E{}_{CB}.$$
Let $\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}:=q^{AC}q_{AE}R^E{}_{BCD}$ and
$S_q:=q^{BD}\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}$. Then
$$\nabla^q\epsilon_2=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}(q)=\frac12S_q\,q.$$
The only inherited choice assumption is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ from the
four-dimensional Levi-Civita supplier used below; no full axiom of choice is
used.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ and let $p\in M$. Then there exist
$h>0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a smooth map

$$ \Phi:(-h,h)\times U\to M $$

such that for every $q\in U$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,q)$ is the unique
integral curve of $X$ on $(-h,h)$ with initial value $\Phi(0,q)=q$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
(The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$), let $F$ be its integral function
(The integral function $F(x) := \int_a^x f$ of an integrable $f$), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters and put
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$. Let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and require
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\ne0\qquad(r\in J).$$
On the smooth product $\mathcal M_J:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J_r\times S^2$,
use $S^2=\{(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb R^3:X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\}$ with its subspace
topology ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). Specify the smooth
structure by the sphere atlas of [[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]],
Definition (b): for $\varepsilon=\pm1$, delete $p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$
and use $\sigma_\varepsilon(X,Y,Z)=(X,Y)/(1-\varepsilon Z)$.
For $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $h=u_1^2+u_2^2$, its inverse is
$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=(2u_1,2u_2,\varepsilon(h-1))/(1+h)$;
the transition is $u\mapsto u/h$ on $h>0$. These rational maps are smooth
on their domains. The product atlas consists of
$(x^0,r,p)\mapsto(x^0,r,\sigma_\varepsilon(p))$ on
$\mathbb R\times J\times(S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\})$;
its transitions leave $x^0,r$ fixed and apply the displayed sphere transition.
The product is Hausdorff and second countable by the subspace topology from
$\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^3$, whose rational balls give a countable basis.
These charts specify its maximal smooth atlas, including when $J$ is empty.
The inclusion of $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$ is smooth with injective differential
in these parametrizations; its induced unit round metric is $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]).
Orient $S^2$ by its outward unit normal: for $p\in S^2$ and
$u,v\in T_pS^2$, define
$$ (\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v):=\det(p,u,v). $$
Thus $\omega_{S^2}$ is the positive area form of $\gamma_{S^2}$, and in the
polar chart $X=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $Y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$,
$Z=\cos\theta$ it is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. The **dyonic RN
datum** is
$$g=-f(r)\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+f(r)^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}, \qquad \mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dx^0\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
Here $x^0$ and $r$ have units of metres, angles on $S^2$ are dimensionless,
and $M,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres. The metric components are dimensionless
in length coordinates; the nonzero coordinate components of $\mathcal F$ have
units inherited from their coordinate Jacobians. Use the orientation
$dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$.

The set $J$ may have several connected components. On $\{f>0\}$ choose the
time orientation $\partial_{x^0}$; on $\{f<0\}$ choose $\partial_r$. These
are smooth timelike fields on their respective open subsets because
$g(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})=-f<0$ when $f>0$ and
$g(\partial_r,\partial_r)=f^{-1}<0$ when $f<0$. Since $f$ has no zero on
$\mathcal M_J$, this defines a smooth time orientation on the whole product.
The sphere area form and the displayed two-form are global on $S^2$.

Let $N,S$ denote the north and south poles. On
$U_N:=S^2\setminus\{S\}$ and $U_S:=S^2\setminus\{N\}$, respectively,
local potential one-forms are
$$\mathcal A_N=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0+q_m(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad \mathcal A_S=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0-q_m(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi.$$
Each displayed potential extends smoothly over its named included pole:
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $N$ and
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $S$. Direct differentiation gives
$d\mathcal A_N=d\mathcal A_S=\mathcal F$ on the respective patches. Their
overlap difference is $2q_m\,d\phi$; it is local potential data, not a global
real gauge function on the entire sphere. The definition assumes no $U(1)$
bundle or charge quantization. To verify pole smoothness, use local coordinates
$u=X,v=Y$ near each pole. There
$d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(u^2+v^2)$. Near $N$,
$1-\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1+Z)$, so
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1+Z)$ is smooth. Near $S$,
$1+\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1-Z)$, so
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1-Z)$ is smooth. The denominators are
nonzero on the respective named patches.

Let $U$ be a nonempty, connected, simply connected, second-countable smooth
two-manifold without boundary. Let $q$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on $U$ such that $q_y$ is nondegenerate of signature $(-,+)$
for every $y\in U$. Choose a smooth vector field $N$ on $U$ with
$q(N,N)<0$ everywhere; the **time orientation** is the choice of the
connected component containing $N_y$ in each timelike cone
$\{v\in T_yU:q_y(v,v)<0\}$. Choose an orientation of $U$, and let
$\epsilon_2$ be its metric volume form, characterized by
$\epsilon_2(e_0,e_1)=1$ on every positively oriented $q$-orthonormal frame
with $q(e_0,e_0)=-1$ and $q(e_1,e_1)=1$. Let $r:U\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth.
Take $S^2=\{p\in\mathbb R^3:p\cdot p=1\}$ with the smooth structure and
induced round metric fixed by the earlier dyonic Reissner–Nordström data
definition cited below. Its tangent plane is
$T_pS^2=\{u\in\mathbb R^3:p\cdot u=0\}$, its metric is
$\gamma_{S^2,p}(u,v)=u\cdot v$, and its outward area form is
$(\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v)=\det(p,u,v)$. Write $\wedge$ for the exterior
product of alternating forms. In polar coordinates
$\omega_{S^2}=\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. Put
$\mathcal M:=U\times S^2$ and define its projections by
$\pi_U(y,p):=y$ and $\pi_S(y,p):=p$. For a smooth map $F:X\to Y$ and a
smooth covariant $2$-tensor field $h$ on $Y$, define its pullback by
$$(F^*h)_x(v,w):=h_{F(x)}(dF_xv,dF_xw),$$
where $x\in X$, $v,w\in T_xX$, and $dF_x:T_xX\to T_{F(x)}Y$ is the
derivative. This formula also defines pullback of a covariant $2$-form.
Define
$$g:=\pi_U^*q+(r\circ\pi_U)^2\pi_S^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$
It has Lorentzian signature $(-,+,+,+)$.
The fibre over $y\in U$ is $S^2_y:=\pi_U^{-1}(\{y\})=\{y\}\times S^2$.
Its induced Riemannian metric is $r(y)^2\gamma_{S^2}$ and its area form is
$r(y)^2\omega_{S^2}$; in polar angles $0<\theta<\pi$ and
$0\le\phi<2\pi$, its area is
$\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi r(y)^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi r(y)^2$.
Thus $r(y)>0$ is the areal radius of this orbit sphere.
Choose the four-dimensional orientation so that its metric volume form is
$$\mathrm{vol}_g=-(r\circ\pi_U)^2\,\pi_U^*\epsilon_2\wedge\pi_S^*\omega_{S^2}.$$
In any chart $(x^0,r)$ for which $\epsilon_2=-dx^0\wedge dr$, this gives
$\mathrm{vol}_g=dx^0\wedge dr\wedge r^2\omega_{S^2}$.

Define
$$SO(3):=\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3,\ \det R=1\}.$$
Each $R\in SO(3)$ acts on $S^2$ by $p\mapsto Rp$ and defines the smooth
diffeomorphism $\rho_R:\mathcal M\to\mathcal M$,
$\rho_R(y,p)=(y,Rp)$, whose inverse is $\rho_{R^{\mathsf T}}$.
For nonnegative integers $a,b$, a smooth tensor field of type $(a,b)$ on
$\mathcal M$ is a smooth section of
$$T^a_b\mathcal M:=(T\mathcal M)^{\otimes a}\otimes(T^*\mathcal M)^{\otimes b};$$
at each $x\in\mathcal M$ its value is multilinear on $a$ covectors in
$T_x^*\mathcal M$ and $b$ vectors in $T_x\mathcal M$, where
$T_x^*\mathcal M:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(T_x\mathcal M,\mathbb R)$.
Smoothness means that the components of the section in every smooth product
chart are $C^\infty$. For such a field $T$, define its pullback by the
diffeomorphism $\rho_R$ by
$$(\rho_R^*T)_x(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_a;v_1,\ldots,v_b)=T_{\rho_R(x)}(\alpha_1\circ(d\rho_R)_x^{-1},\ldots,\alpha_a\circ(d\rho_R)_x^{-1};(d\rho_R)_xv_1,\ldots,(d\rho_R)_xv_b)$$
where $\alpha_i\in T_x^*\mathcal M$, $v_j\in T_x\mathcal M$, and
$(d\rho_R)_x:T_x\mathcal M\to T_{\rho_R(x)}\mathcal M$ is the derivative
of $\rho_R$ at $x$.
A real two-form is a smooth alternating tensor field of type $(0,2)$.
The field $T$ is **rotationally invariant** if $\rho_R^*T=T$ for every
$R\in SO(3)$; a two-form $\mathcal F$ is rotationally invariant in exactly
this sense. This definition specifies a local warped-product model and a
group action. It asserts no global quotient, global potential, maximal
extension, or field equation.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be smooth vector fields on $M$. Their **Lie bracket** is the
operator on smooth functions defined by

$$ [X,Y]f:=X(Yf)-Y(Xf). $$

The next results show that this commutator is again induced by a smooth vector
field on $M$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $d\varpi=0$. Any two points in a connected smooth manifold can be joined by a piecewise smooth path: the set reachable from a point by such paths and its complement are both unions of coordinate-ball neighborhoods, so connectedness makes the reachable set the whole patch. Along each smooth path segment $\sigma$, $(\varpi\circ\sigma)'=d\varpi(\sigma')=0$, so the one-variable mean-value theorem makes $\varpi$ constant along the segment. Thus $\varpi=m$ on the patch.

e0$ because $dr
e0$. Antisymmetry gives $X(r)=0$. In an oriented orthonormal frame with $\epsilon_2=-e^0\wedge e^1$, direct contraction gives $q(X,X)=-(r_0)^2+(r_1)^2=-z$. By [F2] the Hessian is $
abla^q dr=	frac12(\Delta_qr)q$, and [F3] gives $
abla^q\epsilon_2=0$. Hence $
abla_A X_B=	frac12(\Delta_qr)\epsilon_{BA}$, which is antisymmetric in $A,B$. In local coordinates, [F9] and the Lie-derivative definition give $(\mathcal L_Xq)_{AB}=X^C\partial_Cq_{AB}+q_{CB}\partial_AX^C+q_{AC}\partial_BX^C$. Expanding $
abla^q_A X_B+
abla^q_B X_A$ with $X_B=q_{BC}X^C$ and the Christoffel formula for $
abla^q$ in [F3] gives the same expression: the coefficient of $X^C$ reduces to $\partial_Cq_{AB}$ by $2\Gamma^D{}_{AB}q_{DC}=\partial_Aq_{BC}+\partial_Bq_{AC}-\partial_Cq_{AB}$. Applying the defining Lie-derivative formula to the warped metric yields $\mathcal L_{\widehat X}g=\pi_U^*(\mathcal L_Xq)+2(r\circ\pi_U)(Xr)\pi_S^*\gamma_{S^2}=0$. Thus the lifted vector field is Killing for the full four-dimensional metric, and in the constructed coordinates it is the lift $K$ of $\partial_t$.

The smooth local flow theorem [F4] gives a local flow $\Phi_t$ of the nonvanishing field $X$. To construct a transverse curve, choose a chart $(y^0,y^1)$ with $\partial_{y^0}r\ne0$ at the point; the map $(y^0,y^1)\mapsto(r(y^0,y^1),y^1)$ has invertible differential there. The inverse function theorem [F5], after restricting the chart, therefore gives a smooth curve $\sigma(s)$ through the point with $r(\sigma(s))=s$. Define $\Psi(t,s):=\Phi_t(\sigma(s))$ on a sufficiently small product neighborhood. The identity $X(r)=0$ gives $r(\Psi(t,s))=s$. At the initial point the two derivatives of $\Psi$ are $X$ and $\sigma'(s)$; they are independent because $dr(X)=0$ and $dr(\sigma')=1$. Thus $d\Psi$ is invertible, and [F5] makes $(t,r)$ valid local coordinates with $X=\partial_t$.

Since $X=\partial_t$ and $\mathcal L_Xq=0$, each coordinate coefficient is independent of $t$, so $q=A(r)dt^2+2B(r)\,dt\,dr+C(r)dr^2$. From step 1.2, $A=q(X,X)=-z\ne0$. Fix real parameters $m>0$ and $q_e,q_m$ with $q_e^2+q_m^2=m^2$, and use the selected ingoing dyonic Reissner–Nordström metric on $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\times S^2$ with signature $(-,+,+,+)$:

$$g=-D(r)\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad D(r)=\left(1-\frac mr\right)^2.$$

Here $\gamma_{S^2}$ is the metric induced on the unit sphere $S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$ by the Euclidean metric, and $\omega_{S^2}$ is its outward area form. The coordinates $v,r$ and parameters $m,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres; angular coordinates are dimensionless. The displayed Maxwell two-form uses the supplied geometric normalization, with no additional SI normalization: its $vr$ coordinate component has units $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and its angular components have units $\mathrm m$. In the supplied ingoing RN background with mass parameter $M=m$, the fixed Maxwell two-form is

$$\mathcal F_{\mathrm{in}}=-q_e r^{-2}\,dv\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$

Use the unique torsion-free, $g$-compatible connection; in every smooth chart its coefficients are $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc})$ and are smooth. For the horizon-data result, set $M=m$, $Q^2=q_e^2+q_m^2=M^2$ and $f(r):=1-2M/r+Q^2/r^2=D(r)$. It states that $\xi=\partial_v$ obeys $\mathcal L_\xi g=0$ and is normalized by $g(\xi,\xi)\to-1$ as $r\to\infty$; at $r=M$, $g^{-1}(dr,dr)=f(M)=0$, $\xi^\flat=dr$, and $\xi$ is tangent to the level. Thus $r=m$ is the local Killing horizon generated by $\xi$, with signed surface gravity fixed by $d(g(\xi,\xi))=-2\kappa_H\xi^\flat$ and equal to $\kappa_H=f'(M)/2=0$ (units $\mathrm m^{-1}$). No maximal-extension or global event-horizon assertion is included. The metric and displayed Maxwell field are fixed. A neutral test scalar has no electromagnetic gauge coupling or scalar coupling to that field, and does not source either background.

A reduced spherical scalar profile is a real function $\psi:\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\to\mathbb R$ whose coordinate partial derivatives through total order three are continuous. Its full scalar on $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the spherical lift $\widetilde\psi(v,r,\omega):=\psi(v,r)$; in radial formulas we use $\psi(v,r)$ for the reduced profile, and the notation $\Box_g\psi=0$ means $\Box_g\widetilde\psi=0$. For a $C^3$ scalar lift, define the extension of the smooth-scalar wave operator by the trace of its $C^1$ scalar Hessian,

$$\Box_g\widetilde\psi:=g^{ab}\bigl(\partial_a\partial_b\widetilde\psi-\Gamma^c{}_{ab}\partial_c\widetilde\psi\bigr).$$

The second-order chain rule and the connection-coefficient transformation law make these components a covariant $2$-tensor, so the trace is chart independent and $C^1$. This agrees with the supplied smooth-scalar definition when the lift is smooth. In every smooth chart, with $w=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}$, metric compatibility and the density formula give

$$\Box_g\widetilde\psi=\frac1w\partial_a\bigl(wg^{ab}\partial_b\widetilde\psi\bigr).$$

For the spherical lift in an angular chart, $w=r^2\sqrt{\det(\gamma_{AB})}$ and this becomes

$$\Box_g\widetilde\psi=\frac1{r^2}\left[\partial_v(r^2\partial_r\psi)+\partial_r\!\left(r^2(\partial_v\psi+D\partial_r\psi)\right)\right].$$

The density identity used here is stated for smooth vector fields, but its coordinate proof uses only first derivatives of their components and the product rule; it therefore holds for $C^1$ vector fields as well. Here $g^{ab}\partial_b\widetilde\psi$ is $C^2$, so the formula is defined and $\Box_g\widetilde\psi$ is $C^1$. In particular the wave equation can be differentiated once in $r$ for a $C^3$ profile. Set $\phi(v,r)=r\psi(v,r)$ and take every $\partial_r$ derivative in this regular ingoing chart. If $[\psi]$ denotes the arbitrary scalar-field unit, then $[\phi]=[\psi]\,\mathrm m$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), let $(U,x)$ be a
smooth chart, and define the local **metric density** by
$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}$ on $U$, using the matrix of metric components
in this chart. This definition requires no orientation or volume form. Write
$g^{ab}$ for the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]) and
$\Gamma^{a}{}_{bc}$ for the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in the chart.

**(a) Derivative of the density.** At every point of $U$,

$$\partial_a w=\tfrac12\,w\,g^{bc}\,\partial_a g_{bc}.$$

**(b) Trace of the Christoffel symbols.** At every point of $U$,

$$\Gamma^{b}{}_{ba}=w^{-1}\partial_a w .$$

**(c) Divergence formula.** For every smooth vector field $J$ on $M$, at every
point of $U$,

$$\nabla_aJ^a=\partial_aJ^a+\Gamma^{a}{}_{ab}J^b=w^{-1}\partial_a\bigl(w\,J^a\bigr),$$

where $\nabla_aJ^a=g^{ab}\nabla_bJ_a$ is the divergence of $J$ contracted with
the metric and $J^a$ are the components of $J$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).

The identity of (c) is a chart formula for a chart-independent scalar: the
right-hand side is independent of the chart, as the left-hand side is.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
(Interior, closure, boundary and exterior of a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In a local sphere chart with angular metric components $\gamma_{AB}$, the ingoing $(v,r)$ metric block and its inverse are
$$\begin{pmatrix}-D&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&D\end{pmatrix}.$$
The first block has determinant $-1$, so the full metric density is $w=r^2\sqrt{\det(\gamma_{AB})}$. Put $J^a:=g^{ab}\partial_b\widetilde\psi$. The spherical lift gives $J^v=\psi_r$, $J^r=\psi_v+D\psi_r$, and $J^A=0$; this vector field is $C^2$, so [F2] applies. By [F1], [F3] and metric compatibility, $\Box_g\widetilde\psi=\nabla_aJ^a$. Applying the density formula and cancelling the angular density, which is independent of $v,r$, gives
$$0=\Box_g\widetilde\psi=\frac1{r^2}\left[\partial_v(r^2\psi_r)+\partial_r\!\left(r^2(\psi_v+D\psi_r)\right)\right].$$
Expanding the derivatives and using equality of the continuous mixed partials yields
$$2r^2\psi_{vr}+2r\psi_v+\partial_r(r^2D\psi_r)=0.$$

Since $\phi=r\psi$, one has $2r^2\psi_{vr}+2r\psi_v=2r\phi_{vr}$ and $r^2D\psi_r=D(r\phi_r-\phi)$. Differentiating the latter expression gives $\partial_r(r^2D\psi_r)=rD\phi_{rr}+rD'\phi_r-D'\phi$. Divide the equation of step 1.1 by $r>0$ to obtain
$$2\phi_{vr}+D\phi_{rr}+D'\phi_r-\frac{D'}r\phi=0.$$

From $D=(1-m/r)^2$ it follows by direct differentiation that $D(m)=D'(m)=0$. Substituting $r=m$ into step 2.1 leaves $2\phi_{vr}(v,m)=0$. The assumed $C^3$ regularity makes $H_\psi(v)=\phi_r(v,m)$ continuous and differentiable with $H_\psi'(v)=\phi_{rv}(v,m)=\phi_{vr}(v,m)=0$.

The real line is an order-convex interval, so [F4] applied to $H_\psi$ and step 3.1 shows that $H_\psi(v)=H_\psi(v_0)$ for every pair $v,v_0\in\mathbb R$. If this common value is nonzero, the defining equality $\partial_r\phi(v,m)=H_\psi(v)$ shows that the ingoing transverse derivative is the same nonzero number for every $v$ and therefore cannot tend to zero.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), let $(U,x)$ be a
smooth chart, and define the local **metric density** by
$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}$ on $U$, using the matrix of metric components
in this chart. This definition requires no orientation or volume form. Write
$g^{ab}$ for the inverse-metric components
([[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]) and
$\Gamma^{a}{}_{bc}$ for the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in the chart.

**(a) Derivative of the density.** At every point of $U$,

$$\partial_a w=\tfrac12\,w\,g^{bc}\,\partial_a g_{bc}.$$

**(b) Trace of the Christoffel symbols.** At every point of $U$,

$$\Gamma^{b}{}_{ba}=w^{-1}\partial_a w .$$

**(c) Divergence formula.** For every smooth vector field $J$ on $M$, at every
point of $U$,

$$\nabla_aJ^a=\partial_aJ^a+\Gamma^{a}{}_{ab}J^b=w^{-1}\partial_a\bigl(w\,J^a\bigr),$$

where $\nabla_aJ^a=g^{ab}\nabla_bJ_a$ is the divergence of $J$ contracted with
the metric and $J^a$ are the components of $J$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).

The identity of (c) is a chart formula for a chart-independent scalar: the
right-hand side is independent of the chart, as the left-hand side is.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Assume Countable Choice for the smooth tangent-bundle and time-orientation conventions of the Lorentzian suppliers. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$. A **closed spacelike two-surface** is a nonempty smooth embedded two-manifold $S\subset M$ that is compact without boundary. Let $\iota:S\hookrightarrow M$ be the inclusion and let its induced metric be $q:=\iota^*g$; require $q$ to be positive definite. Its normal bundle is $\mathcal NS=(TS)^\perp$. Work on an open set $U\subseteq S$ carrying a smooth ordered pair of future null normal fields $\ell,k$ with $g(\ell,\ell)=g(k,k)=0$ and $g(\ell,k)=-2$; such pairs exist locally by the preceding lemma. No global pair is part of the definition unless one is explicitly supplied.

For tangent fields $X,Y$ on $U$, define the null second fundamental form, expansion and shear by
$$\chi_\ell(X,Y):=g(\nabla_X\ell,Y),\qquad \theta_\ell:=\operatorname{tr}_q\chi_\ell,\qquad \sigma_\ell:=\chi_\ell-\frac{\theta_\ell}{2}q.$$
Here $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection; its derivative of a section along $S$ means the pullback connection, equivalently the derivative of any smooth ambient extension along tangent directions. The preceding lemma establishes extension independence, symmetry of $\chi_\ell$, and positive definiteness of the screen metric. A **normal-frame boost** is the change $\ell\mapsto e^f\ell$, $k\mapsto e^{-f}k$ for a smooth real function $f$ on $U$. It leaves $q$ fixed; $\chi_\ell,\theta_\ell,\sigma_\ell$ scale by $e^f$.

A **null geodesic hypersurface congruence from $U$** along the chosen initial normal field $\ell$ is a smooth map $F:U\times J\to M$, where $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval containing $0$, such that $F(p,0)=p$ and $\partial_\lambda F(p,0)=\ell_p$ for every $p\in U$, each curve $\gamma_p(\lambda):=F(p,\lambda)$ is future-directed and null, and its tangent $\ell:=\partial_\lambda F$ obeys the affine geodesic equation
$$D_\lambda\ell=0$$
along every curve $\gamma_p$; here $D_\lambda$ is the covariant derivative along a curve from [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]. For each $p\in U$, let $J_{\mathrm{reg}}(p)$ be the connected component containing $0$ of the parameter values for which $d(F_\lambda)_p:T_pU\to T_{F(p,\lambda)}M$ is injective and the pullback form $(X,Y)\mapsto g(d(F_\lambda)_pX,d(F_\lambda)_pY)$ is positive definite on $T_pU$. Require, for every $\lambda\in J$, that its variation directions satisfy
$$g_{F(p,\lambda)}\bigl(\ell(p,\lambda),dF_{(p,\lambda)}(X,0)\bigr)=0\qquad(X\in T_pU).$$
Thus its variation directions are orthogonal to $\ell$. For $\lambda\in J_{\mathrm{reg}}(p)$, the map $F$ has rank three locally near $(p,\lambda)$: its two section directions are spacelike and orthogonal to the nonzero null vector $\ell$. Its local image is a null hypersurface, with tangent space $\ell^\perp$ and induced radical $\mathbb R\ell$, as in [[lem-gr-fx-null-normal-plane-and-screen]]. The parameter $\lambda$ is affine. On each section in $J_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the **screen** is $\mathscr S=\ell^\perp/\mathbb R\ell$ with metric $\bar q([X],[Y])=g(X,Y)$; it is the positive two-dimensional quotient, identified isometrically with the tangent plane of that section by projection. The induced form on the full null hypersurface has radical $\mathbb R\ell$ and has no inverse. All traces and inverses in this definition are taken on the screen.

All screen bundles associated with this congruence are understood as bundles over the parameter domain $U\times J$: the notation $\mathscr S_{F(p,\lambda)}$ denotes the branch determined by $(p,\lambda)$, so self-intersections do not identify distinct screen fibers. For each $\lambda\in J$, the screen Jacobi map $A_\lambda:T_pS\to\mathscr S_{F(p,\lambda)}$ sends $X$ to the screen class of the variation field $J_X(\lambda):=dF_{(p,\lambda)}(X,0)$; it is invertible for $\lambda\in J_{\mathrm{reg}}(p)$. A **focal instant** is a positive parameter in $J$ where $A_\lambda$ loses rank; the **first focal instant**, if it exists, is the least such parameter after $0$. Along an affine generator the screen derivative is $\mathcal D_\ell[X]:=[D_\ell X]$; it is independent of the representative, by the preceding lemma. On $J_{\mathrm{reg}}$, the derivative $A_\lambda'$ is taken using $\mathcal D_\ell$, and the **optical endomorphism** is $B_\lambda:=A_\lambda'A_\lambda^{-1}$. Its **optical expansion** is $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}B$, and its **optical shear** is $\sigma:=B-\frac12\theta\,\mathrm{id}_{\mathscr S}$. Since the congruence is normal to a null hypersurface, $B$ is self-adjoint. Its antisymmetric part $\omega:=(B-B^*)/2$, called the twist, therefore vanishes. At $\lambda=0$, $B$ is the endomorphism $q^{-1}\chi_\ell$ and these optical quantities agree with $\theta_\ell,\sigma_\ell$.

No orientation of $M$, $S$, or the screen is required for these constructions. Indeed, if two orthonormal screen frames are related by a real $2\times2$ matrix $O$ with $O^{\mathsf T}O=I_2$, then the endomorphism matrices obey $\widehat B=O^{-1}BO$ and $\widehat\sigma=O^{-1}\sigma O$. Cyclicity of the matrix trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\widehat B=\operatorname{tr}B$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\widehat\sigma^2)=\operatorname{tr}(\sigma^2)=|\sigma|_{\bar q}^2$; the last equality follows by summing the squared entries of the symmetric shear matrix in an orthonormal frame. This includes $\det O=-1$. The screen inner products and the rank of $A_\lambda$ are likewise invariant under changes of frame, so neither the index-form contractions nor the focal condition uses a signed screen area form. The preceding lemma constructs normal pairs using the supplied time orientation and only a local spacelike complement; changing the complement's sign interchanges the two future null rays. No global ordered pair follows. If an orientation is additionally supplied, the same formulas apply on that oriented subclass.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lorentzian supplier conventions. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, let $S$ be a smooth spacelike two-surface, and let $F:U\times J\to M$ be a smooth null geodesic hypersurface congruence from an open section $U\subseteq S$, as defined in [[def-gr-fx-null-screen-geometry]]. Write $\ell=\partial_\lambda F$ and fix $p\in U$. Before the first focal instant let $A_\lambda:T_pS\to\mathscr S_{F(p,\lambda)}$ be the screen Jacobi map, $B=A'A^{-1}$ the optical endomorphism, $\theta=\operatorname{tr}B$ its expansion, and $\sigma=B-\frac12\theta\,\mathrm{id}$ its shear. Let $\operatorname{Ric}$ be the Ricci tensor in [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Then, along the generator $\gamma(\lambda)=F(p,\lambda)$ and before the first focal instant,
$$\frac{d\theta}{d\lambda}=-\frac{\theta^2}{2}-|\sigma|_{\bar q}^2-\operatorname{Ric}(\ell,\ell).$$
If $\operatorname{Ric}(\ell,\ell)\ge0$ along the generator and $\theta(0)<0$, then a first focal instant occurs by affine parameter
$$\lambda_*=\frac{2}{|\theta(0)|},$$
provided the smooth congruence and generator are defined through $\lambda_*$. Here a focal instant means that the screen Jacobi map loses rank; the conclusion is local along this generator and asserts no curvature singularity.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, as required by the supplied
causal-curve and push-up results. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold. Let $S$ be a smooth embedded two-manifold without
boundary whose induced metric $q:=g|_{TS}$ is positive definite, and let
$p\in S$. Choose an open neighborhood $U\subseteq S$ of $p$ and a smooth
future null normal field $\ell$ along $U$, so
$g(\ell_q,Y)=0$ for every $q\in U$ and $Y\in T_qS$.
Let $\gamma:[0,L_1]\to M$ be smooth up to its endpoints, with
$$\gamma(0)=p,\qquad \dot\gamma(0)=\ell_p,\qquad g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=0,\qquad g(\dot\gamma,N)<0,\qquad D_\lambda\dot\gamma=0.$$
Here $D_\lambda$ is covariant differentiation along the curve. Put
$\chi_\ell(X,Y):=g(\nabla_X\ell,Y)$ as in
[[def-gr-fx-null-screen-geometry]], and set $B_0:T_pS\to T_pS$ by
$q(B_0X,Y)=\chi_\ell(X,Y)$ for all $X,Y\in T_pS$.
The screen along $\gamma$ is
$$\mathscr S_\lambda:=\dot\gamma(\lambda)^\perp/\mathbb R\dot\gamma(\lambda),$$
with its positive metric and screen derivative $\mathcal D_\lambda$ from
[[def-gr-fx-null-screen-geometry]]. Define
$$\mathcal R_\lambda[X]:=[R(X,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma].$$
A **normal screen Jacobi field** is a smooth section $J$ of $\mathscr S$ that
satisfies $\mathcal D_\lambda^2J+\mathcal R_\lambda J=0$ and the initial
conditions $J(0)=[X]$, $\mathcal D_\lambda J(0)=B_0X$ for some
$X\in T_pS$. A **focal instant** $\lambda_0\in(0,L_1]$ is a parameter at
which such a field with $X\ne0$ has $J(\lambda_0)=0$.

Put $I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p)$,
$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p)$, and
$E^+(S):=J^+(S)\setminus I^+(S)$, using the causal-reachability conventions
of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]].

If $\lambda_0$ is a focal instant, there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that
$$\gamma(\lambda)\in I^+(S)\qquad (\lambda_0<\lambda<\lambda_0+\varepsilon).$$
Consequently, no point on this portion of the generator belongs to
$E^+(S)$. The conclusion is local along the generator and does not assert
geodesic incompleteness or curvature blow-up. In an SI interpretation take
$x^0=ct$ and $\lambda$ in metres; the proof itself is independent of units.

derivations.claim:
On $S$, $q=R^2d\Omega^2$. For tangent $X,Y$, flat-space differentiation
gives $\nabla_X\partial_r=X/R$ and $\nabla_X\partial_t=0$. Therefore
$\chi_\ell=q/R$ and $\chi_k=-q/R$, and since the screen dimension is two,
$\theta_\ell=2/R$ and $\theta_k=-2/R$. Direct inner products give
$g(\ell,\ell)=g(k,k)=0$ and $g(\ell,k)=-1-1=-2$; both fields are future
because their $t$ components are $1$.

In Cartesian coordinates the inward geodesic is
$\gamma_\omega(\lambda)=(\lambda,(R-\lambda)\omega)$. Varying $\omega$ in a
tangent direction $X\in T_{R\omega}(R\mathbb S^2)$ gives the Jacobi field
$J_X(\lambda)=(1-\lambda/R)X$. Its screen map is therefore
$A_\lambda=(1-\lambda/R)\operatorname{id}$ for $0\le\lambda<R$, with first
rank loss at $R$. Hence $B=-\operatorname{id}/(R-\lambda)$,
$\theta=-2/(R-\lambda)$, $\sigma=0$, and $\operatorname{Ric}=0$. Differentiating
$\theta$ verifies the equation in [F2], and
$2/|\theta(0)|=2/(2/R)=R$, so the comparison bound is sharp.

Fix $R<\lambda<3R$. The point $p_-= (0,-R\omega)\in S$ and
$q_\lambda=\gamma_\omega(\lambda)$ have time separation $\lambda$ and spatial
separation
$$|(R-\lambda)\omega-(-R\omega)|=|2R-\lambda|<\lambda.$$
The straight segment from $p_-$ to $q_\lambda$ is future timelike because
its time component is positive and its squared interval is
$-\lambda^2+(2R-\lambda)^2<0$. Thus $q_\lambda\in I^+(S)$. This agrees with
[F3] for parameters sufficiently close to $R$; the displayed segment proves
the stronger stated range $R<\lambda<3R$ directly.

The induced form on the full null hypersurface has radical $\mathbb R\ell$ and has no inverse. All traces and inverses in this definition are taken on the screen.

Before the first **focal instant**, the screen Jacobi map $A_\lambda:T_pS\to\mathscr S_{F(p,\lambda)}$ sends $X$ to the screen class of the variation field $J_X(\lambda):=dF_{(p,\lambda)}(X,0)$ and is invertible. The first focal instant is the first positive $\lambda$ at which $A_\lambda$ loses rank. Along an affine generator the screen derivative is $\mathcal D_\ell[X]:=[D_\ell X]$; it is independent of the representative, by the preceding lemma. The derivative $A_\lambda'$ is taken using $\mathcal D_\ell$. The **optical endomorphism** is $B_\lambda:=A_\lambda'A_\lambda^{-1}$, the **optical expansion** is $\theta:=\operatorname{tr}B$, and the **optical shear** is $\sigma:=B-\frac12\theta\,\mathrm{id}_{\mathscr S}$. Since the congruence is normal to a null hypersurface, $B$ is self-adjoint; equivalently its twist vanishes. At $\lambda=0$, $B$ is the endomorphism $q^{-1}\chi_\ell$ and these optical quantities agree with $\theta_\ell,\sigma_\ell$.

Let $\operatorname{Ric}$ be the Ricci tensor in [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Then, along the generator $\gamma(\lambda)=F(p,\lambda)$ and before the first focal instant,
$$\frac{d\theta}{d\lambda}=-\frac{\theta^2}{2}-|\sigma|_{\bar q}^2-\operatorname{Ric}(\ell,\ell).$$
If $\operatorname{Ric}(\ell,\ell)\ge0$ along the generator and $\theta(0)<0$, then a first focal instant occurs by affine parameter
$$\lambda_*=\frac{2}{|\theta(0)|},$$
provided the smooth congruence and generator are defined through $\lambda_*$. Here a focal instant means that the screen Jacobi map loses rank; the conclusion is local along this generator and asserts no curvature singularity.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, as required by the supplied
causal-curve and push-up results. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold, and let $S$ be a smooth spacelike embedded
two-surface. Put $I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p)$,
$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p)$, and
$E^+(S):=J^+(S)\setminus I^+(S)$, using the causal-reachability conventions
of [[def-gr-causal-curves-and-reachability]]. Let
$\gamma:[0,L_1]\to M$ be a future affinely parametrized null geodesic
orthogonal to $S$ at $p=\gamma(0)$, with initial tangent $\ell$ and null
second fundamental form $\chi_\ell$ as in
[[def-gr-fx-null-screen-geometry]]. A **focal instant** $\lambda_0>0$ is an
instant at which a nonzero screen Jacobi field arising from variation of the
initial point in $S$, with initial screen derivative determined by
$q^{-1}\chi_\ell$, has zero screen value.

If $\lambda_0$ is a focal instant, there is $\varepsilon>0$ such that
$$\gamma(\lambda)\in I^+(S)\qquad (\lambda_0<\lambda<\lambda_0+\varepsilon).$$
Consequently, no point on this portion of the generator belongs to
$E^+(S)$. The conclusion is local along the generator and does not assert
geodesic incompleteness or curvature blow-up. In an SI interpretation take
$x^0=ct$ and $\lambda$ in metres; the proof itself is independent of units.
