Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, and Dependent Choice, and
the adopted spinless minimal-coupling form model. Let $m>0$ be mass in kilograms,
$q\ne0$ charge in coulombs, $B\ne0$ the constant signed perpendicular
field component in teslas, and $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. Let
$A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be $A(x,y)=(0,Bx)$ in tesla-metres; then
$B_\perp=\partial_xA_y-\partial_yA_x=B$ is its scalar perpendicular field.
Take wavefunctions in $L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$. Set $V=0$ and define the Hamiltonian by the
closed form of the core expression
$$q_B[u]=\frac1{2m}\left(\|-i\hbar\partial_xu\|_2^2+\|(-i\hbar\partial_y-qBx)u\|_2^2\right),\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C).$$
The resulting Friedrichs Hamiltonian is unitarily equivalent, under partial
Fourier transformation in $y$ followed by
$x=\xi+\hbar k/(qB)$, to the constant family of oscillators
$$h(k)=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_\xi^2+\frac{(qB\xi)^2}{2m},\qquad k\in\mathbb R,$$
with its form-closed realization. Its spectrum is
$$\left\{\frac{\hbar|qB|}{m}\left(n+\frac12\right):n\in\mathbb N_0\right\}.$$
Every listed eigenvalue has infinite multiplicity, and every spectral measure
is purely atomic on this set; there is no continuous spectral measure. This is
a conditional model deduction, not a claim that a material realizes the
ideal infinite-plane Hamiltonian.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, $m,\hbar>0$, and real $q,B$
with $qB\ne0$. Let
$c=\hbar^2/(2m)$, $\omega_c=|qB|/m$, and
$E_n=\hbar\omega_c(n+\tfrac12)$ for $n\in\mathbb N_0$. On
$L^2(\mathbb R^3_{x,y,z};\mathbb C)$ close the nonnegative form
$$q^{(3)}_B[u]=\frac1{2m}\left(\|-i\hbar\partial_xu\|_2^2+\|(-i\hbar\partial_y-qBx)u\|_2^2+\|-i\hbar\partial_zu\|_2^2\right),\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C).$$
Use the wave-number Fourier convention
$$\mathcal F_yg(k_y)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int e^{-ik_yy}g(y)\,dy,\qquad \mathcal F_zg(k_z)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int e^{-ik_zz}g(z)\,dz.$$
and set
$$U_3u(\xi,k_y,k_z)=\mathcal F_z\!\left[\mathcal F_yu\!\left(\xi+\frac{\hbar k_y}{qB},k_y,z\right)\right](k_z).$$
Then $U_3$ extends to a unitary map onto
$L^2(\mathbb R^2_{k_y,k_z};\ell^2(\mathbb N_0))$ by expansion in the
complete transverse oscillator basis $\psi_n(\xi)$. If
$$U_3u(\xi,k_y,k_z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n(k_y,k_z)\psi_n(\xi),$$
the form closure domain and value are exactly
$$D(\overline q^{(3)}_B)=\left\{u:\sum_{n=0}^\infty\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(E_n+ck_z^2\right)|f_n(k_y,k_z)|^2\,dk_y\,dk_z<\infty\right\},$$
$$\overline q^{(3)}_B[u]=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(E_n+ck_z^2\right)|f_n(k_y,k_z)|^2\,dk_y\,dk_z.$$

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, $m,\hbar>0$, and real $q,B$
with $qB\ne0$. Let
$c=\hbar^2/(2m)$, $\omega_c=|qB|/m$, and
$E_n=\hbar\omega_c(n+\tfrac12)$ for $n\in\mathbb N_0$. On
$L^2(\mathbb R^3_{x,y,z};\mathbb C)$ close the nonnegative form
$$q^{(3)}_B[u]=\frac1{2m}\left(\|-i\hbar\partial_xu\|_2^2+\|(-i\hbar\partial_y-qBx)u\|_2^2+\|-i\hbar\partial_zu\|_2^2\right),\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C).$$
Use the wave-number Fourier convention
$$\mathcal F_yg(k_y)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int e^{-ik_yy}g(y)\,dy,\qquad \mathcal F_zg(k_z)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int e^{-ik_zz}g(z)\,dz.$$
and set
$$U_3u(\xi,k_y,k_z)=\mathcal F_z\!\left[\mathcal F_yu\!\left(\xi+\frac{\hbar k_y}{qB},k_y,z\right)\right](k_z).$$
Then $U_3$ extends to a unitary map onto
$L^2(\mathbb R^2_{k_y,k_z};\ell^2(\mathbb N_0))$ by expansion in the
complete transverse oscillator basis $\psi_n(\xi)$. If
$$U_3u(\xi,k_y,k_z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n(k_y,k_z)\psi_n(\xi),$$
the form closure domain and value are exactly
$$D(\overline q^{(3)}_B)=\left\{u:\sum_{n=0}^\infty\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(E_n+ck_z^2\right)|f_n(k_y,k_z)|^2\,dk_y\,dk_z<\infty\right\},$$
$$\overline q^{(3)}_B[u]=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(E_n+ck_z^2\right)|f_n(k_y,k_z)|^2\,dk_y\,dk_z.$$

Use SI units with mass $m>0$ in kilograms, charge $q\in\mathbb R$ in
coulombs, action constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, vector-potential
components $A_j$ in tesla-metres, and scalar potential-energy function $V$ in
joules. For each integer $d\ge1$, let $A\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$
be real and let $V\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ be bounded
below. Adopt the general-dimensional minimal-coupling assignment whose core
form is
$$q_{A,V}[u]=\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^d\|(-i\hbar\partial_j-qA_j)u\|_2^2+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V|u|^2,\qquad u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C).$$
Use its closed form closure and the unique self-adjoint representing
Hamiltonian. For dimensional form norms use the fixed reference energy
$E_0=1\,\mathrm J$: apply the closed-form representation to
$q_{A,V}/E_0$ and multiply the representing operator by $E_0$.

The magnetic-field notation is dimension-specific. In $d=2$, with coordinates
$(x,y)$ and $A=(A_x,A_y)$, define the scalar perpendicular field
$$B_\perp(x,y)=\partial_xA_y(x,y)-\partial_yA_x(x,y),$$
in teslas. Thus $A=(0,Bx)$ gives $B_\perp=B$ for a constant signed scalar
$B$. In $d=3$, for coordinates $(x,y,z)$ and $A=(A_x,A_y,A_z)$, define the
field vector $\mathbf B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ in teslas by
$$\mathbf B=(\partial_yA_z-\partial_zA_y,\ \partial_zA_x-\partial_xA_z,\ \partial_xA_y-\partial_yA_x)=\nabla\times A.$$
No magnetic-field object is assigned by this notation in $d=1$.

For an optional spin-half degree of freedom in three dimensions, define
$$\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S_j=\frac{\hbar}{2}\sigma_j.$$
For a core spinor $u=(u_1,u_2)\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^2)$,
define the spin-independent form
$$q^{(2)}_{A,V}[u]=q_{A,V}[u_1]+q_{A,V}[u_2].$$
For a declared dimensionless real coupling $g$, adopt the effective Pauli core
form
$$q^{\mathrm P}_{A,V,g}[u]=q^{(2)}_{A,V}[u]-\frac{gq}{2m}\int_{\mathbb R^3}u(x)^*(S\cdot\mathbf B(x))u(x)\,dx,$$
where $u^*$ is conjugate transpose and
$(S\cdot\mathbf B)(x)=\sum_{j=1}^3S_jB_j(x)$ for the three-dimensional
field vector just defined.
Include this term only in model instances where the resulting form is
closable and bounded below, and use its closed form closure and representing
Hamiltonian. No universal semiboundedness for arbitrary $A,V,g$ is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, let $Q\subseteq H$ be a dense linear subspace, and let
$q:Q\times Q\to\mathbb C$ be a symmetric sesquilinear form, linear in its
first variable. Write $q[u]=q(u,u)$. Suppose that for some $c\ge0$,
$q[u]\ge-c\|u\|^2$ for every $u\in Q$, and that $Q$ is complete in the form
norm $\|u\|_{q,c}^2=q[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$. Then there is a unique self-adjoint
operator $H_q\ge-cI$ such that
$$D((H_q+cI)^{1/2})=Q,\qquad q(u,v)=\langle H_qu,v\rangle\quad(u\in D(H_q),\ v\in Q).$$
Equivalently, $D(H_q)$ consists exactly of those $u\in Q$ for which there is
$f\in H$ satisfying $q(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle$ for all $v\in Q$, and then
$H_qu=f$. Under the $e^{tA}$ generator convention for associated forms, the
associated operator is $A=-H_q$. If $q_0$ is a densely defined closed symmetric
form with $q_0[u]\ge0$ and $v$ is a symmetric sesquilinear form on $Q(q_0)$
satisfying
$$|v[u,u]|\le a q_0[u]+b\|u\|^2\quad(u\in Q(q_0)),\qquad 0\le a<1,\ b\ge0,$$
then $q_0+v$ is closed and bounded below by $-b$ on the same domain. It has a
unique self-adjoint representing operator there. The form bound is not an
operator-relative bound.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim:
Put $c=\hbar^2/(2m)$,
$M_n(k_y,k_z)=E_n+ck_z^2$, and
$\widehat M_n=M_n/E_{\mathrm{ref}}$. Apply [F1] to the three-dimensional
core form. The normalized closed form has coefficient multiplier
$\widehat M_n$; apply [F2] under the choice hypotheses in [A2]. For a
form-domain vector $F$, its representing operator domain consists exactly
of those $F$ for which there is $G\in L^2$ with
$$\sum_n\int \widehat M_nF_n\overline{H_n}=\sum_n\int G_n\overline{H_n}$$
for every form-domain $H$. If such $G$ exists, fix $n$ and any bounded box
$K\subset\mathbb R^2$. Since $\widehat M_n$ is bounded on $K$, both
$1_K\widehat M_nF_n$ and $1_KG_n$ are in $L^2(K)$. Choose the test vector
with sole component $H_n=1_K(\widehat M_nF_n-G_n)$; it belongs to the form
domain because its index and support are bounded. The identity forces
$$\int_K|\widehat M_nF_n-G_n|^2=0.$$
Exhausting $\mathbb R^2$ by bounded boxes and all $n$ gives
$G_n=\widehat M_nF_n$ almost everywhere, so $\widehat MF\in L^2$.
Conversely, if $\widehat MF\in L^2$, then for every form-domain $H$,
Cauchy–Schwarz gives
$$\sum_n\int \widehat M_nF_n\overline{H_n}=\langle\widehat MF,H\rangle,$$
so [F2] represents the normalized operator by multiplication by
$\widehat M_n$, with domain $\sum_n\int \widehat M_n^2|F_n|^2<\infty$.
Since $E_{\mathrm{ref}}>0$, this is equivalent to
$\sum_n\int M_n^2|F_n|^2<\infty$. The physical Hamiltonian
$H=E_{\mathrm{ref}}\widehat H$ therefore acts by multiplication by $M_n$
on this same domain. This identification follows under [A2].

The essential range of the multiplier $M_n$ is
$[E_0,\infty)$: every $M_n\ge E_n\ge E_0$, while the $n=0$ branch
attains every value in that interval as $k_z$ varies. To verify the spectrum
directly, if $\lambda\notin[E_0,\infty)$ then
$\inf_{t\ge E_0}|t-\lambda|>0$ and
$\sup_{t\ge E_0}t/|t-\lambda|<\infty$. Thus multiplication by
$(M-\lambda)^{-1}$ is bounded and maps into the operator domain, so
$\lambda$ is in the resolvent. If $\lambda\ge E_0$, set
$k_0=\sqrt{(\lambda-E_0)/c}$. For every $\delta>0$, a sufficiently small
interval around $k_0$ (or an interval $0<k_z<\sqrt{\delta/c}$ when
$\lambda=E_0$), together with any bounded positive-measure interval of
$k_y$, gives a set of positive finite measure on which
$|E_0+ck_z^2-\lambda|<\delta$. Normalized indicator functions of these
sets are in the operator domain and have residual norm at most $\delta$;
hence $\lambda$ is in the spectrum. The spectrum is exactly the stated
half-line.

Let $F=(f_n)$ be any coefficient vector. By [F4], each band measure is
the pushforward of $w_n(k_z)\,dk_z$ under $k_z\mapsto E_n+ck_z^2$. Splitting
the integral into $k_z>0$ and $k_z<0$ and applying [F5] gives, for
$E>E_n$, the density
$$\rho_n(E)=\frac{w_n\!\left(\sqrt{(E-E_n)/c}\right)+w_n\!\left(-\sqrt{(E-E_n)/c}\right)}{2\sqrt{c(E-E_n)}}.$$
The threshold $E_n$ has no atom because its preimage is the null set
$\{0\}$. Therefore each band measure is absolutely continuous, and the
countable nonnegative sum of these finite measures remains absolutely
continuous. By [F3] these are all scalar spectral measures of the
represented Hamiltonian. There are no eigenvalues or singular-continuous
spectral measures. The conclusion is conditional on the adopted model assumptions.

citations.quote: The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, integration on smooth simplices followed by the inverse of restriction from continuous to smooth singular cohomology gives a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras
$$J_M:H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R).$$
The source product is wedge of form classes, the target product is the front/back singular cup product, and both stars denote direct sums of the homogeneous groups. Naturality is for smooth maps. No compactness assumption is imposed.

Let $f:M\to N$ be continuous, where $M,N$ are **nonempty connected closed integrally oriented $n$-manifolds** of the same dimension. Closed means compact and boundaryless. Write $[M],[N]$ for their specified fundamental classes from [[def-fundamental-class-of-a-compact-oriented-manifold]]. The **degree** of $f$ is the integer $d=\deg(f)$ determined by
$$f_*[M]=d[N]\quad\text{in }H_n(N;\mathbb Z).$$

Let $M$ be a compact boundaryless $n$-manifold with a specified $R$-orientation $\mu$, where $R$ is a commutative unital ring. Its **fundamental class** is
$$[M]=[M]_M\in H_n(M,M\setminus M;R)=H_n(M;R),$$
using [[lem-compatible-local-orientation-classes-exist-over-compact-subsets]] with the compact support $K=M$. The final equality holds at the chain-complex level: $C_*(\varnothing;R)=0$, so quotienting by it leaves $C_*(M;R)$. The cited lemma proves existence and uniqueness of this class with point restriction $\mu_x$ at every $x\in M$. Thus the notation denotes a class determined by the supplied orientation, not an arbitrary generator chosen afterward.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, integration on smooth simplices followed by the inverse of restriction from continuous to smooth singular cohomology gives a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras
$$J_M:H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R).$$
The source product is wedge of form classes, the target product is the front/back singular cup product, and both stars denote direct sums of the homogeneous groups. Naturality is for smooth maps. No compactness assumption is imposed.

Fix a space $X$, abelian group $G$ and integer $n\ge0$. For a singular cocycle $\varphi\in Z^n(X;G)$ and an integral singular cycle $c\in Z_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, define their **evaluation** to be $\varphi(c)\in G$, using [[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]] and [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. If $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ is its finite formal expansion, this value is $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$.

The Kronecker rule $\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c)$ is independent of both cocycle and cycle representatives and is additive in both variables. For a continuous $f:X\to Y$, $\alpha\in H^n(Y;G)$ and $z\in H_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, it satisfies
$$\langle f^*\alpha,z\rangle=\langle\alpha,f_*z\rangle.$$
For a coefficient homomorphism $u:G\to G'$, it satisfies $\langle u_*\alpha,z\rangle=u\langle\alpha,z\rangle$. The same representative-independence argument gives the $R$-bilinear pairing for $R$-linear cochains on chains over a commutative ring $R$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth boundaryless
$m$-manifold and let $\alpha\in\Omega^m(M)$ be a smooth real or complex top form.
Let $J_M:H^m_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\to H^m_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R)$ be the de Rham
comparison of [[thm-de-rham-theorem]] for real forms, extended
complex-linearly with codomain $H^m_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb C)$ for complex
forms. Use the smooth-orientation normalization: a positively oriented affine
$m$-simplex represents the positive local homology generator at each interior
point. Let $[M]\in H_m(M;\mathbb R)$ be the real fundamental class of
[[def-fundamental-class-of-a-compact-oriented-manifold]], and let
$\langle\,,\rangle$ be the Kronecker evaluation pairing
([[def-kronecker-evaluation-pairing]]). Then

For a topological space $X$ and an abelian group $G$, the singular chain groups
and boundary maps of [[def-singular-boundary-operator]] form the
**singular chain complex**
$$C_\bullet(X;G):=\bigl(\cdots\to C_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\partial_n}C_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots\bigr),$$
because [[thm-the-singular-boundary-squares-to-zero]] gives
$\partial_{n-1}\partial_n=0$.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map of topological spaces. For each $n\geq 0$,
the **induced singular chain map in degree $n$** is the homomorphism
$$f_{\#,n}:C_n(X;\mathbb Z)\to C_n(Y;\mathbb Z)$$
defined on a singular simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$ by
$$f_{\#,n}(\sigma):=f\circ\sigma,$$
and extended $\mathbb Z$-linearly.

For each abelian group $G$, the assignments
$$X\mapsto C_\bullet(X;G),\qquad f\mapsto f_\#$$
and
$$X\mapsto H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G),\qquad f\mapsto H_n(f_\#)$$
define covariant functors from topological spaces to chain complexes and to
abelian groups, respectively. Equivalently,
$$\operatorname{id}_{X,\#}=\operatorname{id}_{C_\bullet(X;G)},\qquad (g\circ f)_\#=g_\#\circ f_\#,$$
and for every $n\geq 0$,
$$H_n((g\circ f)_\#)=H_n(g_\#)\circ H_n(f_\#),\qquad H_n(\operatorname{id}_{X,\#})=\operatorname{id}_{H_n(X;G)}.$$

Let $X$ be any topological space and $G$ an abelian group. Its **singular cochains with coefficients in $G$** are
$$C^n(X;G)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(C_n(X;\mathbb Z),G)\quad(n\ge0),\qquad C^n(X;G)=0\quad(n<0),$$
where the chains are those of [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. Addition and negatives of homomorphisms are pointwise. The **coboundary** is
$$\delta^n:C^n(X;G)\to C^{n+1}(X;G),\qquad \delta^n\varphi=\varphi\circ\partial_{n+1}$$
for $n\ge0$, and is zero for $n<0$. Composition with the homomorphism [[def-singular-boundary-operator|$\partial_{n+1}$]] is additive, so this is a homomorphism. The sign convention is positive: there is no extra degree sign on this composite. On a singular $(n+1)$-simplex it says
$$\delta^n\varphi(\sigma)=\sum_{i=0}^{n+1}(-1)^i\varphi(\sigma\circ\delta_i),$$
where $\delta_i$ denotes the affine face map, distinct from the superscripted coboundary. In particular $\delta^0\varphi$ on an oriented path is its endpoint value minus its initial value.

By [[def-singular-simplex-and-singular-chain-group-with-coefficients]], the integer chains are finite sums on the specified simplex set $S_n(X)$. Thus a cochain is equivalently an arbitrary function $S_n(X)\to G$: the extension sends $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ to $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$. The sum is finite and the formal coefficients are unique. The cochain need not have finite support.

For a commutative unital ring $R$ and an $R$-module $G$, there is a canonical identification
$$C^n(X;G)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(C_n(X;R),G).$$
Indeed the given chain convention is $C_n(X;R)=C_n(X;\mathbb Z)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}R$. A homomorphism $\varphi$ on integer chains defines an $R$-linear map by $c\otimes r\mapsto r\varphi(c)$; the defining additive and integer-balanced tensor relations are preserved. Conversely evaluate an $R$-linear map on $c\otimes1$. These operations are inverse since $c\otimes r=r(c\otimes1)$, and they intertwine the two coboundaries because the coefficient boundary is $\partial\otimes1$. The construction also covers the zero ring with its unital zero module.

The resulting graded group and coboundary are called the **singular cochain complex**. The square-zero identity follows by precomposition with $\partial^2=0$ in the chain complex and is spelled out in the next lemma. If $X$ is empty there are no singular simplices, so every cochain group is zero; if $G=0$ the same is true. The extension and tensor formulas are uniquely specified and require no AC.

Fix a space $X$, abelian group $G$ and integer $n\ge0$. For a singular cocycle $\varphi\in Z^n(X;G)$ and an integral singular cycle $c\in Z_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, define their **evaluation** to be $\varphi(c)\in G$, using [[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]] and [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. If $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ is its finite formal expansion, this value is $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$.

The **Kronecker pairing** on quotient classes is the rule
$$\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c),\qquad H^n(X;G)\times H_n(X;\mathbb Z)\to G.$$
Its descent through both quotients, biadditivity and naturality are justified by the following lemma [[lem-the-kronecker-pairing-is-independent-of-cocycle-and-cycle-representatives]], before any use of the quotient pairing. It is not an assertion that evaluation gives an isomorphism to the full dual of homology.

For negative $n$, the two groups are zero and the pairing is the zero map. Empty $X$ and zero $G$ also give zero evaluation. When $G$ is an $R$-module, the cohomology variable is $R$-linear and the integral homology variable is additive; an $R$-bilinear pairing instead uses chains and homology over $R$ with $R$-linear cochains. No representative-selection function is included in the definition.

A continuous map $f:X\to Y$ induces $f^*:H^n(Y;G)\to H^n(X;G)$ for every integer $n$ and abelian group $G$, by $f^*[\varphi]=[\varphi f_\#]$. These maps satisfy $(1_X)^*=1$ and $(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*$. A coefficient homomorphism $u:G\to G'$ induces $u_*:H^n(X;G)\to H^n(X;G')$, covariantly functorial in coefficients and commuting with $f^*$.

derivations.claim: If $\varphi'=\varphi+\delta\psi$ is a second representative of the same real cohomology class and $c'=c+\partial b$ a second representative of the same real homology class, then $\varphi'(c')=\varphi(c)+\varphi(\partial b)+(\delta\psi)(c)+(\delta\psi)(\partial b)=\varphi(c)$: the three additional terms vanish respectively by $\delta\varphi=0$, $\partial c=0$, and $\partial^2=0$. Thus the real evaluation in [F7] is independent of representatives. For every continuous $f:X\to Y$, the chain-level formulas $f^*\varphi=\varphi\circ f_\#$ and $f_*c=f_\#c$ give $(f^*\varphi)(c)=\varphi(f_\#c)$, so $\langle f^*[\varphi],[c]\rangle_{\mathbb R}=\langle[\varphi],f_*[c]\rangle_{\mathbb R}$. Linearity of $\varphi$ and $c$ makes the pairing real-bilinear.

In spherical coordinates $x=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$, $z=\cos\theta$, the unnormalized displayed two-form is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. Integrating for $0\le\theta\le\pi$ and $0\le\phi\le2\pi$ gives $4\pi$, so $\omega_{S^2}$ is a smooth closed form with integral one; its displayed ambient expression shows it extends smoothly across the coordinate poles.

Let $J$ be the natural comparison in [F3]. By [F5] and the real evaluation defined in [F7], $\int_{\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}}n^*\omega_{S^2}=\langle J([n^*\omega_{S^2}]),[\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}]_{\mathbb R}\rangle_{\mathbb R}$. Naturality of $J$ and the real-chain pairing proved in step 1.1 gives $\int_{\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}}n^*\omega_{S^2}=\langle J([\omega_{S^2}]),n_*[\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}]_{\mathbb R}\rangle_{\mathbb R}$.

By [F1], $n_*[\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}]_{\mathbb Z}=\deg(n)[S^2]_{\mathbb Z}$. The coefficient map $\iota:C_\bullet(X;\mathbb Z)\to C_\bullet(X;\mathbb R)$ sends each finite sum $\sum_j a_j\sigma_j$ to $\sum_j a_j\sigma_j$ with the same coefficients viewed in $\mathbb R$. It commutes with boundaries because [F6] defines the singular boundary as an integer linear combination of faces and $\iota$ is additive; it commutes with $n_\#$ because [F6] postcomposes each simplex without changing its coefficient. Hence it induces a coefficient-change map on homology and carries each integral fundamental class to its real fundamental class: it sends the positive local orientation generator $1$ to $1$, so uniqueness of the class with those local restrictions in [F2] identifies the image. Applying $\iota$ to the degree equation gives $n_*[\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}]_{\mathbb R}=\deg(n)[S^2]_{\mathbb R}$. By the real bilinearity in [F7] and steps 3.1, $\int_{\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}}n^*\omega_{S^2}=\deg(n)\langle J([\omega_{S^2}]),[S^2]_{\mathbb R}\rangle_{\mathbb R}=\deg(n)\int_{S^2}\omega_{S^2}=\deg(n)$ by [F5] and step 2.1.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The map $T\mapsto U(t)=e^{itT}$, computed by the
Borel functional calculus of $T$
([[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]]), is a bijection from the set of
self-adjoint operators on $H$ onto the set of strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary groups on $H$. Its inverse assigns to $U$ its generator
$G$ and the self-adjoint operator $T=-iG$; here $D(T)=D(G)$ is exactly the set
of vectors at which $t\mapsto U(t)x$ is differentiable at $0$, and
$\frac1t(U(t)x-x)\to iTx$ for $x\in D(T)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$, and set
$U(t):=e^{itT}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.
Then $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group,
$U(t)D(T)=D(T)$ and $TU(t)=U(t)T$ on $D(T)$, and the derivative
$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(U(t)x-x)$ exists exactly for $x\in D(T)$, where it equals
$iTx$. Thus the generator of $U$ is $G=iT$, with $D(G)=D(T)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $s$ in the compact segment joining $t_0$ to $t$, put $W(\tau)=e^{i\tau T}$ and $U(s)=W((s-t_0)/\hbar)$, and define $w(s)=U(s)v(s)$. For $h$ with $s+h$ in the interval, the group law gives $\frac{w(s+h)-w(s)}h=U(s+h)\frac{v(s+h)-v(s)}h+U(s)\frac{W(h/\hbar)-I}{h}v(s)$. By [F1], $U$ is strongly continuous and unitary, the first term tends to $U(s)v'(s)$, and since $v(s)\in D(T)$ the second tends to $\frac{i}{\hbar}U(s)Tv(s)$ by the derivative of $W$ at zero and the scalar chain rule. Thus $w$ is differentiable and $w'(s)=U(s)v'(s)+\frac{i}{\hbar}U(s)Tv(s)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}U(s)r(s)$, after substituting $i\hbar v'=Tv+r$. The derivative is continuous because $v'$, $Tv$, and hence $r$ are continuous and $U$ is strongly continuous.

If $t\ge t_0$, apply [F3] on $[t_0,t]$; if $t<t_0$, apply it on $[t,t_0]$ and negate the resulting identity. In either case $w(t)-w(t_0)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{t_0}^{t}U(s)r(s)\,ds$, using step 1.1. Then [F4] gives $\|w(t)-w(t_0)\|\le\frac1\hbar\int_{\min(t,t_0)}^{\max(t,t_0)}\|U(s)r(s)\|\,ds=\frac1\hbar\int_{\min(t,t_0)}^{\max(t,t_0)}\|r(s)\|\,ds$; the equality uses unitarity of $U(s)$. Since $w(t_0)=v(t_0)$ and $w(t)=U_T(t,t_0)^*v(t)$, unitarity also gives $\|w(t)-w(t_0)\|=\|v(t)-U_T(t,t_0)v(t_0)\|$. This is the required estimate, including $t=t_0$ and either time orientation.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ have metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and future direction given by increasing $x^0$. Use units $c=1$, so a mass parameter has inverse-length units. Define $x\in J^+(y)$ by $x^0-y^0\ge|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|$ and $x\in J^-(y)$ by $y^0-x^0\ge|\mathbf y-\mathbf x|$; for $A\subseteq\mathbb M$, put $J^\pm(A)=\bigcup_{y\in A}J^\pm(y)$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi$; it is off shell because no field equation is imposed. The allowed local interactions are compactly supported finite polynomial functionals of $\phi$ and finitely many coordinate derivatives, integrated against $d^4x$. The support of a functional $F$ is the closed set of points each of whose neighborhoods contains the support of a compactly supported variation that changes $F$ for some configuration.

For $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, require $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and preservation of the chosen future cone; $SO^+(1,3)$ denotes this identity component. The proper orthochronous Poincare group consists of $\gamma=(a,\Lambda)$ with $a\in\mathbb M$ and $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$. It acts by $(\gamma\cdot\phi)(x)=\phi(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$ and $(\gamma\cdot F)(\phi)=F(\gamma^{-1}\cdot\phi)$.

For a distribution on a coordinate chart, its wavefront set consists of the nonzero cotangent directions where every compact localization fails to have a rapidly decreasing Fourier transform in every conic neighborhood. Covectors are future or past causal when their metric-dual vectors are causal with the indicated time orientation; a nonzero causal covector has a nonzero time component. Write $\Delta=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb M\}$ and $N^*\Delta=\{(x,\xi;x,-\xi):\xi\ne0\}$. Write $(x,\xi)\sim(y,\zeta)$ when both covectors are nonzero null and cotangent to the same null straight line, with parallel transport carrying $\xi$ to $\zeta$. Precisely, for $x\ne y$ there must be a future-directed nonconstant affinely parametrized null straight line $\gamma$ and parameters $s,t$ in either order with $x=\gamma(s)$, $y=\gamma(t)$ and a real $\lambda\ne0$ such that $\xi=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(s),\cdot)$ and $\zeta=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(t),\cdot)$. When $x=y$, require $\xi=\zeta$ and allow every nonzero null covector. This relation is unsigned: the future first-covector condition below selects $\lambda>0$, while the Feynman past branch selects $\lambda<0$. A fixed free scalar input consists of $m\ge0$, a two-point distribution $W$ satisfying
$$P_xW=P_yW=0,\qquad P=-\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b+m^2,$$
and the positive-frequency null wavefront condition
$$\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+:=\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):(x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}.$$
For a two-point distribution $U$, set $U^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=U(y,x)$ and let $U^*$ be complex conjugation. Assume $W$ is invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, satisfies $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for a fixed distribution $E$ supported where $x-y$ is causal, and satisfies $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$.

The prescribed scalar time-ordered contraction input is a symmetric distribution $H_F\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb M^2)$ invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, equal to $W(x,y)$ on the open set $x^0>y^0$ and to $W(y,x)$ on $y^0>x^0$. The two prescriptions agree on spacelike-separated open supports because $E$ is supported on causal pairs. Translation invariance gives $H_F(x,y)=h_F(x-y)$ and $W(x,y)=w(x-y)$. For a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^4$, set $T_\rho(\varphi)=\rho^{-4}T(\varphi(\cdot/\rho))$ and define $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)$ as the infimum of real $\omega$ for which $\rho^\omega T_\rho\to0$ on each fixed test as $\rho\downarrow0$. Require $\operatorname{sd}_0(h_F),\operatorname{sd}_0(w)\le2$ and
$$\operatorname{WF}(H_F)\subseteq\Gamma_F:=N^*\Delta\cup\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):x\ne y,\ (x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null if }x\in J^+(y),\ \xi\text{ past null if }x\in J^-(y)\}.$$
This is fixed conditional data: it does not claim existence of $W$ or $H_F$, and it does not define any singular restriction or product of $H_F$ on a diagonal.

For $r\ge1$, $F^{(r)}(\phi)$ denotes the distribution kernel on $\mathbb M^r$ of the mixed variation in $r$ compactly supported smooth directions, and set $F^{(0)}(\phi)=F(\phi)$. Define $\deg F$ as the largest positive $r$ with $F^{(r)}\ne0$, or $0$ if all positive-order derivative kernels vanish; in particular $\deg0=0$. The class $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$ consists of finite polynomial functionals with compactly supported derivative kernels such that every nonzero wavefront tuple of each derivative kernel avoids both the cone of tuples whose entries are all future causal and the cone of tuples whose entries are all past causal; zero entries in either cone are allowed. For $F,G$ in this class, define
$$F\star_WG=\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\deg F,\deg G)}\frac{\hbar^r}{r!}\left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi),W^{\otimes r}\right\rangle,$$
using distribution products and pushforwards under the stated wavefront transversality conditions, with the $r=0$ pairing interpreted as the pointwise product $F(\phi)G(\phi)$. Here $\hbar$ is a formal indeterminate, and Countable Choice is assumed for the supplier theorem defining these contractions.

A scalar time-ordered system is a sequence of symmetric multilinear maps
$$T_n:\big(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\big)^n\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket,\qquad T_0=1,\quad T_1=\operatorname{id}.$$
For $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ put $S_I=\bigcup_{i\in I}\operatorname{supp}F_i$ and $F_I=(F_i)_{i\in I}$. Causal factorization requires
$$T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)=T_{|I|}(F_I)\star_W T_{|I^c|}(F_{I^c})$$
for every nonempty proper $I$ such that $S_I\cap J^-(S_{I^c})=\varnothing$; an empty block is the unit.

Field independence means that each numerical graph distribution is independent of the background field $\phi$; all $\phi$-dependence enters through the vertex kernels $F_i^{(r)}(\phi)$. In the graph expansion of $T_n$, vertices are labeled by $1,\ldots,n$ and an edge between distinct vertices contracts one derivative slot at each endpoint by $H_F$. A graph is a finite loopless multigraph, so parallel edges are allowed; if $r_{ij}$ edges join vertices $i$ and $j$, the Wick coefficient for that choice includes $\hbar^{\sum_{i<j}r_{ij}}/\prod_{i<j}r_{ij}!$. Finite-order local jet derivatives may act on incident edge kernels. Each coefficient is a finite sum of such contractions, since every input has finite polynomial degree. No graph term uses a singular product at a diagonal before extension.

For $n\ge2$, use relative coordinates $z_i=x_i-x_n$ ($1\le i<n$), so the total diagonal corresponds to $0\in\mathbb R^{4(n-1)}$. The relative scaling degree $\delta_\Gamma$ of a numerical graph distribution is defined by the same positive-dilation rule above in this relative dimension. The scaling condition is imposed compatibly with integration by parts in the local functionals. First write every local density in its unique balanced-jet representative, in which the derivative variables at a degree-$r$ vertex are the relative combinations $q_a=p_a-r^{-1}\sum_bp_b$. At the extension stage, numerical coefficients on independent balanced labels admit extensions across the total diagonal preserving their actual scaling degree; the final normalization conditions below are imposed within the engineering upper bounds. General jet labels are recovered by total coordinate differentiation of the already extended full coefficients and by linearity; this includes differentiation of the remaining field jets. For a primitive differentiated graph the required upper scaling bound is the engineering degree
$$B_\Gamma=2|E(\Gamma)|+\sum_e|\alpha_e|.$$
For a graph containing proper subgraphs, use a finite upper bound obtained by causal block induction from the edge degrees and the finite derivative orders of the chosen lower-order local counterterms; total derivatives add their orders to that bound. Any two extensions of a fixed punctured coefficient with upper bound $B_\Gamma$ differ by derivatives $\partial^\beta\delta_0$ of order $|\beta|\le\lfloor B_\Gamma-4(n-1)\rfloor$ when $B_\Gamma\ge4(n-1)$, and agree when $B_\Gamma<4(n-1)$. The allowed counterterms must also satisfy the stated linearity and derivative identities. For the analytic degree-preserving extension family of an independent balanced coefficient, its actual degree replaces $B_\Gamma$ in this ambiguity bound. A differentiated coefficient is not required to retain the exact scaling degree of a punctured linear combination that vanishes: total differentiation may force a contact term at the diagonal.

Covariance requires $T_n(\gamma\cdot F_1,\ldots,\gamma\cdot F_n)=\gamma\cdot T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)$ for each proper orthochronous Poincare transformation. Fix the Lorentz Lie-algebra convention $[J_i,J_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, $[J_i,K_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}K_j$, and $[K_i,K_j]=-\epsilon_{ijk}J_i$. For a formal coupling $g$, define coefficientwise
$$\mathcal S_g(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(ig/\hbar)^n}{n!}T_n(V,\ldots,V).$$
The anti-time-ordered series is $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V):=\mathcal S_g(V)^*$, where the involution conjugates scalar coefficients, fixes real $g,\hbar$, and reverses the order of factors; $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$ gives $(F\star_WG)^*=G^*\star_WF^*$. Formal unitarity requires $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V)\star_W\mathcal S_g(V)=1$ for every real $V=V^*$. At each $g$-order, coefficients are finite Laurent polynomials in $\hbar$ before cancellation and are compared algebraically; there is no analytic convergence, positivity of formal coefficients, adiabatic limit, or gauge/Ward identity in this contract.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and use the continuous complex-linear test-function pairing of [[def-distribution]]. For $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $\rho>0$, define its dilation at the origin by

$$\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle:=\rho^{-n}\langle t,\varphi(\cdot/\rho)\rangle,\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(U).$$

Positive dilations preserve $U$, so the displayed pairing is defined for every test function in $\mathcal D(U)$. If $t$ is the regular distribution induced by a locally integrable function $g$, change of variables gives $\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\int_U g(\rho x)\varphi(x)\,dx$.

Convergence $s_\rho\to0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ as $\rho\downarrow0$ means $\langle s_\rho,\varphi\rangle\to0$ for every fixed $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$. The **scaling degree at the origin** is

$$\operatorname{sd}_0(t):=\inf\{\omega\in\mathbb R:\rho^\omega t_\rho\to0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(U)\}.$$

The infimum of the empty set is $+\infty$; if every real $\omega$ belongs to the set, the infimum is $-\infty$. A finite scaling degree means a real value $\delta\in\mathbb R$. For a distribution $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ use the same dilation formula on tests in $\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$. An **extension** of $t$ is a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^n$ whose restriction to $U$ equals $t$. The degree of divergence associated with a finite scaling degree $\delta$ in dimension $n$ is $\delta-n$. Exact homogeneity of scaling degree $\delta$ means $\rho^\delta T_\rho=T$ for every $\rho>0$.

For this fixed $t$, define its **local extension family** by

$$\mathcal E(t):=\{T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n):T|_U=t\}.$$

Here $T|_U=t$ means $\langle T,\widetilde\varphi\rangle=\langle t,\varphi\rangle$ for every $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$, where $\widetilde\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ is its smooth extension by zero. When $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)\in\mathbb R$, the **scaling-degree-preserving local extension family** is

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t):=\{T\in\mathcal E(t):\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta\}.$$

Existence of members and the affine structure of these families require separate results; the set definitions alone assert neither.

The definitions use Euclidean dilations about the specified point only. They do not assert that a given distribution arises from a product of fields or that an extension is physically selected.

Let $u\in\mathcal D'(M)$, where $M$ is a smooth manifold. For a smooth map $f:N\to M$, define its nonzero conormal set by
$$ N_f=\{(f(x),\eta)\in T^*M\setminus0: df_x^T\eta=0\}. $$
If $\operatorname{WF}(u)\cap N_f=\varnothing$, there is a distributional pullback $f^*u\in\mathcal D'(N)$ and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(f^*u)\subseteq \{(x,df_x^T\eta):(f(x),\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\}. $$
For $u,v\in\mathcal D'(M)$, if there is no nonzero covector $\eta$ with both $(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)$ and $(x,-\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)$ at the same $x$, their product is defined by $uv=\Delta^*(u\otimes v)$, where $\Delta(x)=(x,x)$. It agrees with pointwise multiplication when $u,v$ are smooth and satisfies
$$ \operatorname{WF}(uv)\subseteq \{(x,\eta+\zeta):(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup0_M,\ (x,\zeta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)\cup0_M,\ \eta+\zeta\ne0\}. $$
Here $0_M$ is the zero section. If $\pi:X\times Y\to X$ is a coordinate projection, $\nu$ is a smooth positive density on $Y$, and $t\in\mathcal E'(X\times Y)$, define $\pi_{*,\nu}t$ by
$$ \langle \pi_{*,\nu}t,\omega\rangle =\left\langle t,\chi(\pi^*\omega\otimes\nu)\right\rangle, $$
where $\omega$ is a compactly supported test density on $X$ and $\chi$ is a compact cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}t$. This pushforward is independent of $\chi$, compactly supported, and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(\pi_{*,\nu}t)\subseteq \{(x,\eta):\text{ for some }y,\ (x,y;\eta,0)\in\operatorname{WF}(t)\}. $$
The pullback condition is a local transversality requirement; this theorem does not define an arbitrary restriction of a singular kernel to a diagonal where the condition fails.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $D,r\ge1$ be integers, let $u_1,\ldots,u_r$ be distributions on a neighborhood of $0\in\mathbb R^D$, already defined at $0$, and let $a_j\ge0$ be finite real numbers such that $\operatorname{sd}_0(u_j)\le a_j$. Here scaling tests may include the origin. Put $C_j=\{\xi\ne0:(0,\xi)\in\operatorname{WF}(u_j)\}$. Suppose
$$\xi_j\in C_j\cup\{0\},\quad\sum_{j=1}^r\xi_j=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\xi_1=\cdots=\xi_r=0.$$
Then $\prod_{j=1}^r u_j$ is defined on a sufficiently small neighborhood of $0$ and
$$\operatorname{sd}_0\!\left(\prod_{j=1}^r u_j\right)\le\sum_{j=1}^r a_j.$$
The condition is imposed at the scaling center, including the wavefront covectors of the already extended factors there; transversality only on a punctured set is insufficient for this conclusion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and let $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)$. Then there exists $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ such that $T|_U=t$ and $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta$. The result applies to arbitrary distributions with finite real scaling degree; it assumes no smooth kernel or pointwise product representation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $t\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta$, and let $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ be the set of its extensions in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ having scaling degree exactly $\delta$. This set is nonempty by [[thm-qft-finite-scaling-degree-extension]]. If $\delta<n$, then $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ has exactly one member. If $\delta\ge n$, let $k$ be the unique nonnegative integer with $k\le\delta-n<k+1$ (the floor of $\delta-n$). Then, for any $T_0\in\mathcal E_\delta(t)$,

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t)=T_0+\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{\partial^\alpha\delta_0:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$

Here a **point-local counterterm** means a distribution whose support, as defined in [[def-support-of-a-distribution]], is contained in $\{0\}$. Thus the same-degree freedom is finite dimensional, with precisely the displayed delta derivatives as its basis; at the threshold $\delta=n$, only a multiple of $\delta_0$ is allowed.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

derivations.claim: Differentiation adds at most its order to a scaling upper bound: $\langle(\partial^\alpha T)_\rho,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\rho^{-|\alpha|}\langle T_\rho,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle$. A surjective linear pullback does not increase that bound: in coordinates $(y,z)$ with $y=Lx$, $L^*T=T(y)\otimes1(z)$, and integration of a test in $z$ cancels the extra dilation Jacobian. The same observation shows that a translation-invariant kernel, written as a relative distribution tensored with a constant center coordinate, has the same full-coordinate and relative scaling bounds. Its wavefront covectors satisfy $\sum_i\xi_i=0$: with a product localization in center and relative coordinates the center Fourier transform decreases rapidly, and the convolution localization argument of [F3] gives the statement for arbitrary localizations. Thus every cross edge $\partial^{\alpha_e}W(x_i,x_j)$ has upper scaling bound $2+|\alpha_e|$, while every lower-order block kernel has covectors whose sum within its block is zero.

Fix a nontrivial partition $I\mid J$ of the vertices. The extended subgraph kernels $t_I$ and $t_J$ are distributions on their entire separate coordinate blocks, including their own total diagonals. Lift the two kernels to the full vertex-coordinate space by tensoring with the constant distribution in the other block. Step 1.1 preserves their finite nonnegative upper scaling bounds $b_I,b_J$. Their covector tuples occupy disjoint blocks, so their product is their tensor product and [F4] bounds its degree by $b_I+b_J$. A one-vertex block contributes the constant kernel and bound zero. Multiply this tensor product by all cross-edge kernels oriented as $\partial^{\alpha_e}W(x_i,x_j)$ with $i\in I,j\in J$. At a full-diagonal point every nonzero wavefront contribution from a cross edge places a future null covector at $i$ and its negative at $j$. If the sum of all factor covectors were zero, summing its entries over $I$ would give a sum of future null covectors equal to zero, because the internal block covectors sum to zero by step 1.1. The future causal cone is pointed, so every cross-edge covector must vanish. The two remaining block tuples occupy disjoint coordinate blocks, and hence must separately vanish. This proves joint no-cancellation at the full diagonal. It also proves it at other points, since the wavefront condition on $W$ has the same orientation everywhere.

By [F3] and step 2.1 the causal block expression
$$B_I=t_I\otimes t_J\prod_{e=(i,j),\ i\in I,\ j\in J}\partial^{\alpha_e}W(x_i,x_j)$$
is a distribution even at the full diagonal. Apply [F4] there and step 1.1 to obtain the finite upper bound
$$\operatorname{sd}_0(B_I)\le b_I+b_J+\sum_{e\text{ crossing }I\mid J}(2+|\alpha_e|).$$
All factors are already defined at the center where [F4] is used. This argument requires no product of coincident $H_F$ factors and no directional property of an arbitrary unextended punctured-stratum product. Translation invariance makes the full-coordinate estimate exactly the relative-coordinate estimate.

The causal split sets $C_I=\{x_i\notin J^-(x_j):i\in I,j\notin I\}$ cover the complement of the total diagonal. Indeed, choose a timelike linear time function taking unequal values on two distinct entries of a configuration, then split the finitely many values at a level attained by none of them. These open sets are invariant under translations and positive relative dilations. Their intersections with the relative unit sphere form a finite open cover of that compact sphere. Using [F6] in its coordinate patches, choose a finite smooth partition $f_I$ there, subordinate to the cover, and extend it homogeneously by $f_I(\rho z)=f_I(z)$ to punctured relative space. On $C_I$, [F1] and lower-order causal factorization identify the graph coefficient with $B_I$. The lower-order expressions agree on overlaps: refining two causal splits into their intersections expresses both as the same block product, and the two incomparable blocks are spacelike, where $W=W^{\mathsf T}$. Hence the graph distribution is $t_\Gamma=\sum_I f_I B_I$ off zero. For a fixed punctured test $\varphi$, each $f_I\varphi$ is a fixed smooth compactly supported punctured test; homogeneity gives $(f_I B_I)_\rho(\varphi)=(B_I)_\rho(f_I\varphi)$. The finite sum therefore has the maximum of the finite bounds in step 3.1.

For a primitive graph, the definitions above mean every proper induced vertex subgraph lies below its divergence threshold. Induct on vertex number with the engineering upper bound $b_I=\sum_{e\text{ internal to }I}(2+|\alpha_e|)$ for a block $I$, and likewise for $J$. For independent balanced subgraph coefficients choose same-degree extensions by [F5]; their total-derivative descendants and any allowed local normalizations retain the contract's engineering upper bounds. Thus the lower-order block kernels, including any permitted finite delta-derivative terms, have these nonnegative upper bounds, starting from the zero bound at one vertex. Step 3.1 then counts every edge exactly once and step 4.1 gives $\operatorname{sd}_0(t_\Gamma)\le2|E(\Gamma)|+\sum_e|\alpha_e|$. If a proper vertex subgraph has a chosen local counterterm, [F5] makes it a finite sum of finite-order delta derivatives. Each has finite relative scaling degree equal to its relative dimension plus its derivative order. Its translation-invariant lift still has block momentum sum zero by step 1.1, so steps 2.1–4.1 apply with a finite nonnegative upper bound for that chosen block. There are only finitely many vertex subsets and finitely many counterterm jets at this fixed graph order. Taking their finite maximum proves the stated general finite upper bound.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ have metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and future direction given by increasing $x^0$. Use units $c=1$, so a mass parameter has inverse-length units. Define $x\in J^+(y)$ by $x^0-y^0\ge|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|$ and $x\in J^-(y)$ by $y^0-x^0\ge|\mathbf y-\mathbf x|$; for $A\subseteq\mathbb M$, put $J^\pm(A)=\bigcup_{y\in A}J^\pm(y)$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi$; it is off shell because no field equation is imposed. The allowed local interactions are compactly supported finite polynomial functionals of $\phi$ and finitely many coordinate derivatives, integrated against $d^4x$. The support of a functional $F$ is the closed set of points each of whose neighborhoods contains the support of a compactly supported variation that changes $F$ for some configuration.

For $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, require $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and preservation of the chosen future cone; $SO^+(1,3)$ denotes this identity component. The proper orthochronous Poincare group consists of $\gamma=(a,\Lambda)$ with $a\in\mathbb M$ and $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$. It acts by $(\gamma\cdot\phi)(x)=\phi(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$ and $(\gamma\cdot F)(\phi)=F(\gamma^{-1}\cdot\phi)$.

For a distribution on a coordinate chart, its wavefront set consists of the nonzero cotangent directions where every compact localization fails to have a rapidly decreasing Fourier transform in every conic neighborhood. Covectors are future or past causal when their metric-dual vectors are causal with the indicated time orientation; a nonzero causal covector has a nonzero time component. Write $\Delta=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb M\}$ and $N^*\Delta=\{(x,\xi;x,-\xi):\xi\ne0\}$. Write $(x,\xi)\sim(y,\zeta)$ when both covectors are nonzero null and cotangent to the same null straight line, with parallel transport carrying $\xi$ to $\zeta$. Precisely, for $x\ne y$ there must be a future-directed nonconstant affinely parametrized null straight line $\gamma$ and parameters $s,t$ in either order with $x=\gamma(s)$, $y=\gamma(t)$ and a real $\lambda\ne0$ such that $\xi=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(s),\cdot)$ and $\zeta=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(t),\cdot)$. When $x=y$, require $\xi=\zeta$ and allow every nonzero null covector. This relation is unsigned: the future first-covector condition below selects $\lambda>0$, while the Feynman past branch selects $\lambda<0$. A fixed free scalar input consists of $m\ge0$, a two-point distribution $W$ satisfying
$$P_xW=P_yW=0,\qquad P=-\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b+m^2,$$
and the positive-frequency null wavefront condition
$$\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+:=\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):(x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}.$$
For a two-point distribution $U$, set $U^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=U(y,x)$ and let $U^*$ be complex conjugation. Assume $W$ is invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, satisfies $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for a fixed distribution $E$ supported where $x-y$ is causal, and satisfies $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$.

The prescribed scalar time-ordered contraction input is a symmetric distribution $H_F\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb M^2)$ invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, equal to $W(x,y)$ on the open set $x^0>y^0$ and to $W(y,x)$ on $y^0>x^0$. The two prescriptions agree on spacelike-separated open supports because $E$ is supported on causal pairs. Translation invariance gives $H_F(x,y)=h_F(x-y)$ and $W(x,y)=w(x-y)$. For a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^4$, set $T_\rho(\varphi)=\rho^{-4}T(\varphi(\cdot/\rho))$ and define $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)$ as the infimum of real $\omega$ for which $\rho^\omega T_\rho\to0$ on each fixed test as $\rho\downarrow0$. Require $\operatorname{sd}_0(h_F),\operatorname{sd}_0(w)\le2$ and
$$\operatorname{WF}(H_F)\subseteq\Gamma_F:=N^*\Delta\cup\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):x\ne y,\ (x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null if }x\in J^+(y),\ \xi\text{ past null if }x\in J^-(y)\}.$$
This is fixed conditional data: it does not claim existence of $W$ or $H_F$, and it does not define any singular restriction or product of $H_F$ on a diagonal.

For $r\ge1$, $F^{(r)}(\phi)$ denotes the distribution kernel on $\mathbb M^r$ of the mixed variation in $r$ compactly supported smooth directions, and set $F^{(0)}(\phi)=F(\phi)$. Define $\deg F$ as the largest positive $r$ with $F^{(r)}\ne0$, or $0$ if all positive-order derivative kernels vanish; in particular $\deg0=0$. The class $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$ consists of finite polynomial functionals with compactly supported derivative kernels such that every nonzero wavefront tuple of each derivative kernel avoids both the cone of tuples whose entries are all future causal and the cone of tuples whose entries are all past causal; zero entries in either cone are allowed. For $F,G$ in this class, define
$$F\star_WG=\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\deg F,\deg G)}\frac{\hbar^r}{r!}\left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi),W^{\otimes r}\right\rangle,$$
using distribution products and pushforwards under the stated wavefront transversality conditions, with the $r=0$ pairing interpreted as the pointwise product $F(\phi)G(\phi)$. Here $\hbar$ is a formal indeterminate, and Countable Choice is assumed for the supplier theorem defining these contractions.

A scalar time-ordered system is a sequence of symmetric multilinear maps
$$T_n:\big(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\big)^n\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket,\qquad T_0=1,\quad T_1=\operatorname{id}.$$
For $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ put $S_I=\bigcup_{i\in I}\operatorname{supp}F_i$ and $F_I=(F_i)_{i\in I}$. Causal factorization requires
$$T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)=T_{|I|}(F_I)\star_W T_{|I^c|}(F_{I^c})$$
for every nonempty proper $I$ such that $S_I\cap J^-(S_{I^c})=\varnothing$; an empty block is the unit.

Field independence means that each numerical graph distribution is independent of the background field $\phi$; all $\phi$-dependence enters through the vertex kernels $F_i^{(r)}(\phi)$. In the graph expansion of $T_n$, vertices are labeled by $1,\ldots,n$ and an edge between distinct vertices contracts one derivative slot at each endpoint by $H_F$. A graph is a finite loopless multigraph, so parallel edges are allowed; if $r_{ij}$ edges join vertices $i$ and $j$, the Wick coefficient for that choice includes $\hbar^{\sum_{i<j}r_{ij}}/\prod_{i<j}r_{ij}!$. Finite-order local jet derivatives may act on incident edge kernels. Each coefficient is a finite sum of such contractions, since every input has finite polynomial degree. No graph term uses a singular product at a diagonal before extension.

For $n\ge2$, use relative coordinates $z_i=x_i-x_n$ ($1\le i<n$), so the total diagonal corresponds to $0\in\mathbb R^{4(n-1)}$. The relative scaling degree $\delta_\Gamma$ of a numerical graph distribution is defined by the same positive-dilation rule above in this relative dimension. The scaling condition is imposed compatibly with integration by parts in the local functionals. General jet labels are recovered by total coordinate differentiation of the already extended full coefficients and by linearity; this includes differentiation of the remaining field jets. For a primitive differentiated graph the required upper scaling bound is the engineering degree
$$B_\Gamma=2|E(\Gamma)|+\sum_e|\alpha_e|.$$
For a graph containing proper subgraphs, use a finite upper bound obtained by causal block induction from the edge degrees and the finite derivative orders of the chosen lower-order local counterterms; total derivatives add their orders to that bound. Any two extensions of a fixed punctured coefficient with upper bound $B_\Gamma$ differ by derivatives $\partial^\beta\delta_0$ of order $|\beta|\le\lfloor B_\Gamma-4(n-1)\rfloor$ when $B_\Gamma\ge4(n-1)$, and agree when $B_\Gamma<4(n-1)$. The allowed counterterms must also satisfy the stated linearity and derivative identities. For the analytic degree-preserving extension family of an independent balanced coefficient, its actual degree replaces $B_\Gamma$ in this ambiguity bound. A differentiated coefficient is not required to retain the exact scaling degree of a punctured linear combination that vanishes: total differentiation may force a contact term at the diagonal.

Covariance requires $T_n(\gamma\cdot F_1,\ldots,\gamma\cdot F_n)=\gamma\cdot T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)$ for each proper orthochronous Poincare transformation. Fix the Lorentz Lie-algebra convention $[J_i,J_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, $[J_i,K_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}K_j$, and $[K_i,K_j]=-\epsilon_{ijk}J_i$. For a formal coupling $g$, define coefficientwise
$$\mathcal S_g(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(ig/\hbar)^n}{n!}T_n(V,\ldots,V).$$
The anti-time-ordered series is $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V):=\mathcal S_g(V)^*$, where the involution conjugates scalar coefficients, fixes real $g,\hbar$, and reverses the order of factors; $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$ gives $(F\star_WG)^*=G^*\star_WF^*$. Formal unitarity requires $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V)\star_W\mathcal S_g(V)=1$ for every real $V=V^*$. At each $g$-order, coefficients are finite Laurent polynomials in $\hbar$ before cancellation and are compared algebraically; there is no analytic convergence, positivity of formal coefficients, adiabatic limit, or gauge/Ward identity in this contract.

Assume Countable Choice. For two scalar time-ordered systems $T$ and $T'$ satisfying the local scalar contract for the same free data and with $T_0=T'_0=1$, $T_1=T'_1=\operatorname{id}$, define their normalized formal S-maps by
$$\mathcal S(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}T_n(V,\ldots,V),\qquad \mathcal S'(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}T'_n(V,\ldots,V).$$
There is a unique formal map $Z(V)=V+O(V^2)$ from local polynomial functionals to local polynomial functionals such that $Z(0)=0$, $dZ_0=\operatorname{id}$, $Z$ preserves supports and scalar Poincare covariance, and
$$\mathcal S'(V)=\mathcal S(Z(V))$$
coefficientwise. Such maps compose, and each has a recursively defined formal inverse; hence they form a group under composition.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ have metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and future direction given by increasing $x^0$. Use units $c=1$, so a mass parameter has inverse-length units. Define $x\in J^+(y)$ by $x^0-y^0\ge|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|$ and $x\in J^-(y)$ by $y^0-x^0\ge|\mathbf y-\mathbf x|$; for $A\subseteq\mathbb M$, put $J^\pm(A)=\bigcup_{y\in A}J^\pm(y)$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi$; it is off shell because no field equation is imposed. The allowed local interactions are compactly supported finite polynomial functionals of $\phi$ and finitely many coordinate derivatives, integrated against $d^4x$. derivations.claim: Direct substitution gives $C_\rho C_\tau\phi(x)=(\rho\tau)^{-1}\phi((\rho\tau)^{-1}x)=C_{\rho\tau}\phi(x)$. Repeated chain rule gives $\partial^\alpha(C_\rho\phi)(x)=\rho^{-1-|\alpha|}(\partial^\alpha\phi)(\rho^{-1}x)$, so field substitution preserves finite polynomial jets; positive dilations also send compact coefficient supports to compact sets. Thus the induced functional pullback preserves the local polynomial class and has inverse $C_{\rho^{-1}}^*$. The mass relabelling composes as $\tau^{-1}\rho^{-1}m=(\rho\tau)^{-1}m$, including $m=0$, so the functional action obeys $\sigma_{\rho\tau}=\sigma_\rho\sigma_\tau$ and $\sigma_{\rho^{-1}}$ is its inverse. The induced conjugations on map families obey the same composition law, because the pullbacks compose as $C_\rho^*C_\tau^*=C_{\rho\tau}^*$ and the mass labels reindex in that same order. For $T_a\phi(x)=\phi(x-a)$, direct substitution gives $C_\rho T_a C_\rho^{-1}=T_{\rho a}$; scalar dilations commute with each Lorentz transformation. By [F3] this action normalizes the proper orthochronous Poincare group, and by [F4] conjugation preserves covariance of the time-ordered system.

The displayed componentwise definition gives symmetric multilinear maps $T'^{(m)}_{n,\rho}$, and summing their diagonal values with coefficients $1/n!$ gives $C_\rho^*\circ\mathcal S_{\rho^{-1}m}\circ(C_\rho^*)^{-1}$ coefficientwise. At each mass component the sequences $(T_n^{(m)})_{n\ge0}$ and $(T'^{(m)}_{n,\rho})_{n\ge0}$ have the same free data and satisfy the normalization hypotheses of [F2] by the scale-admissibility condition in the Definition. Under [A1], applying [F2] gives a unique formal local map $Z_\rho(V)=V+O(V^2)$ preserving support and covariance and satisfying the displayed equation. This defines $Z_\rho$ only under these hypotheses.

For $\rho=1$, step 1.1 gives $\sigma_1=\operatorname{id}$, so the defining equation is $\mathcal S=\mathcal S\circ Z_1$. The identity map also satisfies the finite-renormalization conditions, and uniqueness in [F2] gives $Z_1=\operatorname{id}$.

Then $f\in\mathcal D$, while $(\mathbf k\times f)\cdot e_3=\chi(\mathbf k)(k_1^2+k_2^2)$ is nonzero near $e_1$. Put $A=[\mathbf a]_\times$, so $A^T=-A$. The norm-convergent power series for the matrix exponential gives continuity in $t$, $R_{\mathbf a}(s+t)=R_{\mathbf a}(s)R_{\mathbf a}(t)$, and $R_{\mathbf a}(t)^T=R_{\mathbf a}(-t)$; hence $R_{\mathbf a}(t)$ is orthogonal. Its determinant is continuous, takes values in $\{+1,-1\}$, and equals $1$ at $t=0$, so it is $1$ for all $t$ and $R_{\mathbf a}(t)\in SO(3)$. Therefore $t\mapsto U(R_{\mathbf a}(t))$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group by steps 1.1, 2.1, and 2.2. Applying Stone's theorem [F3] gives its unique self-adjoint generator $T_{\mathbf a}$ with $U(R_{\mathbf a}(t))=e^{itT_{\mathbf a}}$. Set $J_{\mathbf a}=-\hbar T_{\mathbf a}$; it is self-adjoint and satisfies $U(R_{\mathbf a}(t))=e^{-itJ_{\mathbf a}/\hbar}$. The derivative characterization in [F3] and step 3.1 give $J_{\mathbf a}=L_{\mathbf a}+S_{\mathbf a}^{\mathrm{op}}$ on $\mathcal D$. This uses Stone's self-adjoint generator and makes no essential-self-adjointness claim about the restricted differential expression.
