Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Killing form $B$, let $n\ge2$, and let $V_1,\ldots,V_n$ be finite-dimensional complex vector spaces. A representation here is a complex-linear Lie algebra homomorphism $ho_i:\mathfrak g	o\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_i)$, so $[ho_i(x),ho_i(y)]=ho_i([x,y])$. Let $F_n(\mathbb C)=\{(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\mathbb C^n:z_i
e z_j	ext{ for }i
e j\}$ be the ordered configuration space and put $V:=V_1\otimes\cdots\otimes V_n$ in the indicated factor order. For any pair of $B$-dual bases $(x_a),(x^a)$ define $\Omega_{ij}:=\sum_aho_i(x_a)^{(i)}ho_j(x^a)^{(j)}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, where each superscript means that the operator acts on that tensor factor and as the identity on all other factors. For $i<j$ put $\eta_{ij}:=(dz_i-dz_j)/(z_i-z_j)$, a globally defined complex-valued one-form on $F_n(\mathbb C)$. For $\kappa\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, the **Casimir Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov connection** on the trivial vector bundle $F_n(\mathbb C)	imes V	o F_n(\mathbb C)$ is

$$
abla^{\mathrm{KZ}}_\kappa:=d-\kappa^{-1}\sum_{i<j}\Omega_{ij}\eta_{ij}.$$

Here a connection on this trivial bundle is a complex-linear operator on smooth $V$-valued sections satisfying $
abla(fs)=df\otimes s+f
abla s$ for every smooth scalar function $f$ and section $s$. The associated quadratic Casimir is $C_B:=\sum_a x_ax^a$ in the universal enveloping algebra; with the Killing-form convention above it is central, and $\Omega_{ij}$ is its tensor-level Casimir counterpart.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra, let $B$ be its Killing form, and let $(x_a)$ and $(x^a)$ be $B$-dual bases. The tensor $\Omega:=\sum_a x_a\otimes x^a\in\mathfrak g\otimes\mathfrak g$ corresponds to the identity map under $\Phi_B(u\otimes v)(y):=uB(v,y)$, and is invariant under the diagonal adjoint action:

$$([x,\cdot]\otimes 1+1\otimes[x,\cdot])\Omega=\sum_a [x,x_a]\otimes x^a+x_a\otimes[x,x^a]=0\qquad(x\in\mathfrak g).$$

A connection on a finite-rank smooth vector bundle $E\to M$ is flat if and
only if every point of $M$ has a neighborhood carrying a local frame
$(e_1,\ldots,e_r)$ of parallel sections, meaning $\nabla_Xe_a=0$ for every
local vector field $X$ and every $a$.

For a piecewise smooth curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ and $v\in E_{\gamma(a)}$, let $V_v$ be the unique continuous piecewise parallel section with $V_v(a)=v$, supplied by [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-parallel-sections]]. Its **parallel transport** is
$$P_\gamma:E_{\gamma(a)}\to E_{\gamma(b)},\qquad P_\gamma(v)=V_v(b).$$
More generally, $P_{\gamma;s,t}$ sends initial data at $s$ to its value at $t$, allowing either order of the parameters. The same theorem gives independence from frames and subdivisions. On a singleton, $P_\gamma$ is the identity of its fibre. An empty curve has no endpoint fibres and is not assigned such a map. Zero initial data maps to zero; the transport depends on the supplied connection as well as the curve. Linearity and invertibility are proved next.

Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be smooth on an interval, with smooth one-sided data at included endpoints. For every $t_0\in I$ and $v_0\in E_{\gamma(t_0)}$ there is exactly one parallel section $V$ on all of $I$ with $V(t_0)=v_0$. The same holds for a piecewise smooth curve on a compact interval, with continuity at its finitely many corners. A singleton carries its prescribed vector. No AC is required for a supplied connection and curve.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, so that $n=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ is the set of its
predecessors ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and let $X$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]). Write

$$X^n:=\prod_{k<n}X$$

for the $n$-fold product, carrying the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]),
and display its points as $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$: the **label** $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
names the coordinate of index $i-1$ in the sense of that definition. The
**ordered configuration space** of $n$ points in $X$ is the subspace

$$F_n(X):=\{\,(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in X^n\;:\;x_i\neq x_j\ \text{whenever}\ i\neq j\,\}$$

with the subspace topology inherited from $X^n$
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Equivalently

$$F_n(X)=X^n\setminus\bigcup_{i\neq j}\{(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in X^n:x_i=x_j\},$$

since a tuple lies in $F_n(X)$ exactly when its entries are pairwise distinct:
the **collision diagonals** $x_i=x_j$, $i\neq j$, are removed from the product.
Points of $F_n(X)$ are called **ordered configurations** of $n$ points in $X$.

**The label set.** The labels $1,\dots,n$ are part of the data, and throughout
this page they are identified with the set $n=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ by the
bijection $\kappa(i):=i-1$. It is through $\kappa$ that the symmetric group
$S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(n)$ acts on $F_n(X)$, in
[[prop-the-symmetric-group-acts-freely-on-ordered-configurations]].

**Elementary cases.** For $n=0$ the product $X^0$ is a one-point space
([[def-product-topology]]), and the defining condition is vacuous, so

$$F_0(X)=\{\,\text{the empty tuple}\,\}$$

for every $X$, including $X=\varnothing$. For $n=1$ there is no pair $i\neq j$,
so single-coordinate evaluation $(x_1)\mapsto x_1$ is a canonical
homeomorphism $F_1(X)\cong X$. For $n\geq2$ and any $X$ one has

$$F_n(X)\neq\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\ \text{has at least } n \text{ distinct points}.$$

if $X$ has at least $n$ points, an injection $\{1,\dots,n\}\to X$ is exactly a
tuple of pairwise distinct points of $X$, and conversely such a tuple displays
$n$ distinct points. In particular $F_n(X)=\varnothing$ when $X$ is empty and
$n\geq1$.

**Based configurations.** A **base configuration** in $F_n(X)$ is a point
$q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ of $F_n(X)$. Such a $q$ is fixed once and for all only when
$F_n(X)$ is nonempty; when $n\ge1$, $F_n(X)\ne\varnothing$, and $X$ is
infinite, $F_n(X)$ is infinite: from any one configuration, keep coordinates
$2,\dots,n$ fixed and vary the first coordinate among the infinitely many
points of $X\setminus\{q_2,\dots,q_n\}$. The choice of $q$ is part of the data
of every construction below. All base configurations on this page are chosen in the ordered space
$F_n(X)$; the corresponding basepoint of the unordered quotient is its orbit
([[def-unordered-configuration-space]]).

**Separation of distinct coordinates.** If $X$ is Hausdorff
([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $q\in F_n(X)$, then the finitely many points
$q_1,\dots,q_n$ are pairwise distinct, and for each pair $i\neq j$ Hausdorffness
supplies disjoint open sets separating $q_i$ from $q_j$; a finite intersection
over the finitely many pairs $j\neq i$ therefore gives, for every $i$, an open
neighbourhood $U_i$ of $q_i$ with $U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $i\neq j$.
This is used in
[[lem-disjoint-coordinate-neighborhoods-evenly-cover-unordered-configurations]].

Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and a **base configuration** $q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$, an
ordered $n$-tuple of pairwise distinct points of the open unit disc
$\operatorname{int}D^2=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<1\}$, so that
$$q\in F_n(\operatorname{int}D^2)\subseteq F_n(D^2),\qquad D^2=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le1\}$$
in the notation of [[lem-interior-and-closed-disk-configuration-spaces-are-homotopy-equivalent]]
and [[def-ordered-configuration-space]]. The **pure configuration braid
group** on $n$ strands is the fundamental group
([[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]])

$$PB_n:=\pi_1\big(F_n(D^2),q\big),$$

the group of based-loop classes at $q$ in the ordered configuration space of the
closed disc, with the first-then-second loop product.

**The open-disc model.** The inclusion
$F_n(\operatorname{int}D^2)\to F_n(D^2)$ induces an isomorphism
$$\pi_1\big(F_n(\operatorname{int}D^2),q\big)\longrightarrow\pi_1\big(F_n(D^2),q\big)$$
of fundamental groups at the same base configuration $q$
([[def-induced-homomorphism-on-fundamental-groups]]); this is claim 3 of
[[lem-interior-and-closed-disk-configuration-spaces-are-homotopy-equivalent]].
The isomorphism is canonical — it is induced by the inclusion and involves no
choice — so on this page and its consumers $PB_n$ may be computed from either
the closed-disc or the open-disc ordered configuration space. The closed-disc
model is the one that matches the geometrically drawn braids, and the open-disc
model is the one to which the forgetful fibrations for boundaryless manifolds
apply; both give the same group by the displayed isomorphism.

**The basepoint.** The configuration $q$ is part of the data defining $PB_n$, and
all groups on this page use the same $q$. Different choices of base
configuration give isomorphic groups: $F_n(D^2)$ is path-connected for every
$n$ (claim 2 of
[[thm-ordered-configurations-cover-unordered-configurations-regularly]]), and a
path between base configurations conjugates loop classes and induces an
isomorphism ([[lem-path-conjugation-isomorphism-of-fundamental-groups]]). No
particular such isomorphism is fixed here. For $n=0$ the space $F_0(D^2)$ is a
point, so $PB_0$ is the one-element group; for $n=1$ single-coordinate
evaluation gives $F_1(D^2)\cong D^2$ and $PB_1$ is trivial.

**Scope.** This is the configuration-space definition of the pure braid group,
stated before any comparison with geometric strands or with the Artin
presentation: no presentation of $PB_n$ is asserted here. The description by
geometric braids and the Artin presentation, and the configuration braid short
exact sequence relating $PB_n$ to the unordered configuration braid group,
belong to the later items on braids, which consume this definition.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $X$ be a topological space
([[def-ordered-configuration-space]], [[def-topological-space]]). The label
permutation action

$$S_n\times F_n(X)\longrightarrow F_n(X),\qquad(\sigma,x)\longmapsto\sigma\cdot x,\qquad(\sigma\cdot x)_i=x_{\sigma^{-1}(i-1)+1},$$

is a continuous free left action
([[prop-the-symmetric-group-acts-freely-on-ordered-configurations]]). Its set of
orbits $S_n\cdot x=\{\sigma\cdot x:\sigma\in S_n\}$
([[def-orbit-and-stabilizer]]) is the **unordered configuration space** of $n$
points in $X$, written

$$C_n(X):=F_n(X)/S_n=\{S_n\cdot x:x\in F_n(X)\},$$

and it carries the **quotient topology** of the canonical projection

$$p_n:F_n(X)\longrightarrow C_n(X),\qquad p_n(x):=S_n\cdot x,$$

in the sense of [[def-quotient-topology]]: a subset $V\subseteq C_n(X)$ is open
exactly when $p_n^{-1}(V)$ is open in $F_n(X)$. This projection is a quotient
map, hence continuous and surjective, and points of $C_n(X)$ are written
$[x]:=p_n(x)$.

**Basepoint.** For a base configuration $q\in F_n(X)$ in the sense of
[[def-ordered-configuration-space]], the **basepoint** of $C_n(X)$ is the orbit

$$[q]=p_n(q)=S_n\cdot q,$$

and $C_n(X)$ is nonempty exactly when $F_n(X)$ is, in which case a basepoint can
be fixed. The unordered space is based by the orbit of the ordered base
configuration, and this is the basepoint used in every later construction on
this page.

**Elementary cases.** $C_0(X)$ is the quotient of the one-point space $F_0(X)$
by the trivial group $S_0$, hence is a one-point space. Since $S_1$ is trivial,
$p_1:F_1(X)\to C_1(X)$ is a bijective quotient map and hence a
homeomorphism: for every open $U\subseteq F_1(X)$, the equality
$p_1^{-1}(p_1(U))=U$ makes $p_1(U)$ open by the quotient topology.
Thus $C_1(X)$ is canonically homeomorphic to $X$ by $[(x)]\mapsto x$,
using the single-coordinate homeomorphism $F_1(X)\to X$.
These are canonical identifications, not literal equalities of the orbit set
with the original set.

**Elements are $n$-element subsets, as a set.** Because the coordinates of a
configuration are pairwise distinct, two ordered configurations $x,y\in F_n(X)$
lie in the same orbit exactly when their underlying sets of coordinates agree:
if $y=\sigma\cdot x$ then the coordinates of $y$ are those of $x$ in a different
order, and conversely, if $\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}=\{y_1,\dots,y_n\}$, then for every
label $i$ there is exactly one label $\sigma(i)$ with $y_i=x_{\sigma(i)}$, and
$i\mapsto\sigma(i)$ is a bijection of $\{1,\dots,n\}$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); composing with the identification
$\kappa(i)=i-1$ of labels with $n$, the permutation
$\tau=\kappa\circ\sigma^{-1}\circ\kappa^{-1}\in S_n$ takes $x$ to $y$:
$(\tau\cdot x)_i=x_{\tau^{-1}(i-1)+1}=x_{\sigma(i)}=y_i$. Hence

$$C_n(X)\longrightarrow\{\,S\subseteq X:S \text{ has exactly } n \text{ elements}\,\},\qquad [x]\longmapsto\{x_1,\dots,x_n\},$$

is a bijection of sets, the inverse sending an $n$-element subset $S$ to the
orbit of any enumeration of $S$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]). This identifies
the *elements* of $C_n(X)$ with $n$-element subsets of $X$; the topology on
$C_n(X)$ is the quotient topology displayed above, and no topology on a set of
subsets is asserted here. In particular the quotient topology is not defined
through any metric or hyperspace structure.

Let $M$ be a nonempty connected Hausdorff topological $d$-manifold with boundary, possibly empty boundary, in the sense of [[def-topological-manifold-with-boundary]], of dimension $d\ge2$, and let $n\in\mathbb N$. Write $p:F_n(M)\to C_n(M)$ for the quotient map from the ordered to the unordered configuration space ([[def-ordered-configuration-space]], [[def-unordered-configuration-space]]). Then:

1. $p$ is a covering map in the sense of [[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]; every fibre of $p$ has exactly $n!$ elements, so $p$ is an $n!$-sheeted covering, and each point of $C_n(M)$ has an evenly covered neighbourhood of the form supplied by [[lem-disjoint-coordinate-neighborhoods-evenly-cover-unordered-configurations]].
2. $F_n(M)$ is path-connected, and so is $C_n(M)$; in particular $F_n(M)$ is connected and is a connected covering space of $C_n(M)$.
3. The deck group $\operatorname{Deck}(p)$ ([[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]) is isomorphic to $S_n$: the map $\sigma\mapsto\tau_\sigma$, $\tau_\sigma(x):=\sigma\cdot x$, is an isomorphism of groups from $S_n$ onto $\operatorname{Deck}(p)$, where $S_n$ acts on $F_n(M)$ by permuting the labels $1,\dots,n$ ([[prop-the-symmetric-group-acts-freely-on-ordered-configurations]]).
4. $p$ is a regular covering in the sense of [[def-regular-covering]]: its deck group acts transitively on every fibre.

For $n=0$ the spaces $F_0(M)$ and $C_0(M)$ are one-point spaces and $p$ is their unique homeomorphism, so the assertions hold with $0!=1$. No choice principle, paracompactness or second countability beyond the manifold definition is used.

Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and the same base configuration $q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ of
pairwise distinct points of $\operatorname{int}D^2$ that is used in
[[def-pure-braid-group-from-ordered-configurations]], with $D^2$ the closed unit
disc. Write $p:F_n(D^2)\to C_n(D^2)$ for the quotient of the ordered by the
unordered configuration space, so that $p(q)=[q]$ is the orbit of $q$
([[def-unordered-configuration-space]]). The **configuration braid group** on
$n$ strands is the fundamental group
([[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]])

$$B_n^{\mathrm{conf}}:=\pi_1\big(C_n(D^2),[q]\big),$$

the group of based-loop classes at the orbit $[q]$ in the unordered
configuration space of the closed disc, with the first-then-second loop product.

**The open-disc model.** The inclusion-induced map
$\iota^C:C_n(\operatorname{int}D^2)\to C_n(D^2)$ of
[[lem-interior-and-closed-disk-configuration-spaces-are-homotopy-equivalent]]
induces an isomorphism
$$\pi_1\big(C_n(\operatorname{int}D^2),[q]\big)\longrightarrow\pi_1\big(C_n(D^2),[q]\big)$$
at the same basepoint (claim 3 of that lemma,
[[def-induced-homomorphism-on-fundamental-groups]]), so $B_n^{\mathrm{conf}}$
may be computed from either disc model exactly as $PB_n$ may. Both groups in
this definition and in
[[def-pure-braid-group-from-ordered-configurations]] are taken at the
basepoints $[q]$ and $q$ coming from the same tuple $q$, which is what makes the
comparison map of the configuration braid short exact sequence, proved in a
later item on this page, a map of based fundamental groups.

**The basepoint.** Since $F_n(D^2)\to C_n(D^2)$ is surjective every basepoint of
$C_n(D^2)$ is an orbit, and since $C_n(D^2)$ is path-connected (claim 2 of
[[thm-ordered-configurations-cover-unordered-configurations-regularly]]) the
groups at different orbits are isomorphic by conjugation along a path
([[lem-path-conjugation-isomorphism-of-fundamental-groups]]); no particular
isomorphism is fixed. For $n=0$ the space $C_0(D^2)$ is a point and
$B_0^{\mathrm{conf}}$ is the one-element group.

**The superscript.** The decoration $\mathrm{conf}$ records that the group is
defined here through configuration spaces, and it is retained until the later
geometric identification of $B_n^{\mathrm{conf}}$ with the braid group given by
strand diagrams and with its Artin presentation. No such identification and no
presentation is asserted on this page; neither is any identification of
$B_n^{\mathrm{conf}}$ with a group of self-homeomorphisms of the disc.

derivations.claim: If $\{i,j\}$ and $\{k,l\}$ are disjoint pairs, then $\Omega_{ij}$ and $\Omega_{kl}$ act on disjoint tensor factors. Each factorwise operator commutes with every operator on the other factors, so $[\Omega_{ij},\Omega_{kl}]=0$.

For three distinct indices $i,j,k$, write $\Omega=\sum_a x_a\otimes x^a$. Apply [F2] with $x=x_b$, place its two tensor factors in slots $i,j$, apply $\rho_i\otimes\rho_j$, multiply on slot $k$ by $\rho_k(x^b)$, and sum over $b$. The first resulting sum is $- [\Omega_{ij},\Omega_{ik}]$ and the second is $-[\Omega_{ij},\Omega_{jk}]$, because $[x_b,x_a]=-[x_a,x_b]$ and $[x_b,x^a]=-[x^a,x_b]$. Hence $[\Omega_{ij},\Omega_{ik}+\Omega_{jk}]=0$.

Set $u=z_i-z_j$ and $v=z_j-z_k$, so $z_i-z_k=u+v$. Then $\eta_{ij}=du/u$, $\eta_{jk}=dv/v$, and $\eta_{ik}=(du+dv)/(u+v)$. Direct expansion gives $\eta_{ij}\wedge\eta_{jk}+\eta_{jk}\wedge\eta_{ik}+\eta_{ik}\wedge\eta_{ij}=\left(1/(uv)-1/(v(u+v))-1/(u(u+v))\right)du\wedge dv=0$, since the numerator after taking a common denominator is $(u+v)-u-v=0$.

Put $B_0:=\sum_{i<j}\Omega_{ij}\eta_{ij}$, so $
abla=d-\kappa^{-1}B_0$. Each $\eta_{ij}$ is closed because $d(dw/w)=0$ on $w
e0$, hence $dB_0=0$, and the curvature is $R^
abla=\kappa^{-2}B_0\wedge B_0$. Expanding the wedge product groups terms by disjoint pairs and by triples. The disjoint terms vanish by step 1.1. For $i<j<k$, the triple contribution is $C_{ijk}(\eta_{ij}\wedge\eta_{ik}-\eta_{ij}\wedge\eta_{jk}+\eta_{ik}\wedge\eta_{jk})$, where $C_{ijk}:=[\Omega_{ij},\Omega_{ik}]$: step 1.2 gives the other two commutators as $-C_{ijk}$ and $C_{ijk}$. This form is the negative of the zero Arnold sum in step 1.3, so every triple contribution vanishes and $R^
abla=0$.

By [F3], every point has a neighborhood with a parallel frame. A parallel section has constant coordinates in that frame. On an overlap, if one parallel frame is the other times a smooth matrix $G(x)$, the connection equation gives $dG=0$, so $G$ is constant on each connected component of the overlap. These charts therefore define a locally constant sheaf of horizontal sections; define its transport along a continuous path by subdividing the path into chart intervals and retaining the same frame coordinates. For a piecewise smooth path this agrees with differential parallel transport by [F4] and uniqueness in [F5].

Suppose $V_i=V_0$ and $\rho_i=\rho_0$ for every $i$. The coordinate-permutation action from [F7] lifts to the same permutation of tensor factors. Since $\eta_{ij}$ is symmetric in $i,j$, and the factor permutation sends $\Omega_{ij}$ to the correspondingly relabeled $\Omega$, it preserves the connection. The action is free on $F_n(\mathbb C)$ by [F7]. The usual $\mathbb C$ is a connected Hausdorff real 2-manifold, so [F10] makes the quotient map a regular covering.

Given $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in F_n(\mathbb C)$, choose pairwise disjoint open discs $D_i\subset\mathbb C$ about $z_i$ and put $\widetilde U:=D_1\times\cdots\times D_n$. This is an open connected subset of $F_n(\mathbb C)$, and its $S_n$-translates are pairwise disjoint because the $D_i$ are disjoint. By [F10] these sheets evenly cover their open image $U$ in the quotient; write $p(z)=[z]$ for the orbit quotient, so $p|_{\widetilde U}:\widetilde U\to U$ is a homeomorphism. These product charts give the quotient its smooth-manifold structure: on overlaps the change of ordered representative is locally one fixed coordinate permutation, hence smooth. The map $(p(z),v)\mapsto[(z,v)]$, for the unique $z\in\widetilde U$ over $p(z)$, is a local trivialization of $(F_n(\mathbb C)\times V_0^{\otimes n})/S_n$ over $U$. On each connected component of an overlap, changing the chosen sheet acts on the fiber by one fixed $\tau_\sigma$, a linear isomorphism, so these are smooth vector-bundle transition maps. In these local trivializations the connection is obtained by restricting the KZ connection to the chosen sheet. If a different sheet is chosen, the connection agrees under the transition $\tau_\sigma$ because the KZ connection is equivariant. Thus the quotient is a vector bundle and its connection descends, with fiber identified with $V_0^{\otimes n}$ at $[q]$ by the representative $q$.

For an endpoint-fixed homotopy of paths, pull back the parallel-frame neighborhoods to the compact square. A finite subcover has a positive Lebesgue number: choose finitely many smaller metric balls covering the square whose doubled balls lie in cover members, and take the minimum radius $\delta$ of those smaller balls. Choose a rectangular grid whose cell diameters are less than $\delta$; every cell then maps into one parallel-frame neighborhood. Transport around each cell is the identity because its four edges use one constant frame. Multiplying the cell identities cancels every interior edge with its reverse, so the boundary paths have identical local-system transport. By concatenating the unique parallel sections on successive path segments, [F5] gives $P_{\alpha*\beta}=P_\beta P_\alpha$; reversing a parallel section gives $P_{\bar\alpha}=P_\alpha^{-1}$. The same composition and inverse rules hold for local-system transport by its subdivision definition.

Let $T_\gamma$ denote the local-system transport for a continuous path. Step 4.1 makes it depend only on the path-homotopy class. Under [F6], the first-then-second product satisfies $T_{\alpha*\beta}=T_\beta T_\alpha$, so $\rho([\gamma]):=T_\gamma^{-1}$ is a left representation because $\rho([\alpha][\beta])=(T_\beta T_\alpha)^{-1}=T_\alpha^{-1}T_\beta^{-1}$. On piecewise smooth loops $T_\gamma=P_\gamma$ by step 3.1. The map $h(z)=z/(1+|z|)$ has inverse $h^{-1}(w)=w/(1-|w|)$ from $D^\circ$ to $\mathbb C$; its coordinatewise product is a homeomorphism of ordered configuration spaces and takes $q$ to $\widetilde q$. It induces a based isomorphism on fundamental groups, and the inclusion $D^\circ\hookrightarrow D^2$ induces the based isomorphism in [F8]. Hence the ordered monodromy representation is based at $\widetilde q$ when identified with $PB_n=\pi_1(F_n(D^2),\widetilde q)$.

The descended connection is flat because its pullback is the flat connection of step 2.1. Applying the local-system monodromy construction of steps 3.1 and 5.1 on the quotient gives its left monodromy representation of $\pi_1(C_n(\mathbb C),[q])$. The coordinatewise homeomorphism $h$ is $S_n$-equivariant, so it descends to a homeomorphism of unordered configuration spaces and takes $[q]$ to $[\widetilde q]$. The inclusion-induced isomorphism at $[\widetilde q]$ in [F11] then identifies this based fundamental group with $B_n^{\mathrm{conf}}=\pi_1(C_n(D^2),[\widetilde q])$. No identification with any quantum-group ribbon representation follows from this construction.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes in
this definition are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$; the filtration is
neither assumed complete nor right-continuous. The Axiom of Choice is declared
because the conditional-expectation classes used in clause 3 are supplied by
the Radon--Nikodym interface of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]],
which assumes it; the countable-choice obligations inherited from that
interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

1. **Adapted.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when $X_t$
   is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$. This is exactly the notion
   of [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

2. **Stopped process.** For a stopping time $\tau$ for $(\mathcal F_t)$
   [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] the **stopped process** is
   $$X^{\tau}_t(\omega):=X_{t\wedge\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\qquad t\ge0,$$
   with the convention $t\wedge\infty:=t$, so no value $X_\infty$ is ever
   required and $X^\tau_0=X_0$ identically. This formula defines a pathwise
   family; adaptedness of $X$ alone does not assert measurability or
   adaptedness of its stopped values. If in addition $\tau\le c$ for a
   deterministic constant $c$, then $X^\tau_t=X_{t\wedge\tau}$, and only the
   values of $X$ on $[0,c]$ enter. Stopping at a stopping time is not the same
   as replacing a process by a modification; it is a pathwise operation.

3. **Martingale.** $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **martingale** (an all-pairs
   continuous-time martingale) relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted,
   $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$, and for all $0\le s\le t$
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
   The equality is an equality of the almost-everywhere classes of
   [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; equivalently, every version
   of the conditional expectation on the left equals $M_s$ off one null set.
   At $s=t$ the identity reduces to the known-variable case. The word
   "continuous-time" refers to the index set only and does not assert path
   continuity.

4. **Local martingale.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **local martingale** relative
   to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted, $E|X_0|<\infty$, and there exist stopping times
   $(\tau_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots$ and
   $\tau_n\uparrow\infty$ almost surely such that for every $n\ge0$ the stopped process
   $$X^{\tau_n}-X_0=(X_{t\wedge\tau_n}-X_0)_{t\ge0}$$
   is a martingale in the sense of clause 3. The sequence $(\tau_n)$ is called
   a **localizing sequence**. Equivalently, every $X^{\tau_n}$ is a
   martingale: adaptedness makes the integrable variable $X_0$ measurable with
   respect to every $\mathcal F_t$, so the constant process with value $X_0$
   is a martingale and may be added to, or subtracted from, each stopped
   process. The centering merely makes every localized process start at $0$;
   apart from the required integrability of $X_0$, no claim is made that $X$
   is integrable at a positive deterministic time, and no claim is made that
   $X$ has continuous paths.

5. **Path and integrability attributes.** A process has **continuous paths**
   when $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega$
   in an event of probability one; the usual almost-sure path conventions of
   [[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]] apply. A
   martingale $M$ is **square-integrable** when $EM_t^2<\infty$ for every
   $t\ge0$, and **$L^2$-bounded** when $\sup_{t\ge0}EM_t^2<\infty$. These are
   properties of the single process under consideration, not of its versions:
   a modification of a martingale need not be adapted, so every later statement
   names the adapted versions it uses.

The following remarks specify what follows directly from this vocabulary.

1. **A martingale is a local martingale.** If $M$ is a martingale, the constant
   sequence $\tau_n:=n$, $n\ge0$, localizes it: the stopped process $M^{n}-M_0$ is again
   a martingale by the martingale identity applied at the deterministic times
   $s\wedge n\le t\wedge n$. The converse fails; a local martingale need not be
   a martingale, and no such implication is used in this development.
2. **Localization after a separately justified stopping operation.** Suppose
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X$, $\sigma$ is a stopping time, $X^\sigma$ is
   adapted, and each $(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$ is a martingale. Then
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X^\sigma$. Indeed it still increases to infinity,
   $(X^\sigma)_0=X_0$, and the pathwise identity
   $$(X^\sigma)^{\tau_n}-(X^\sigma)_0=X^{\sigma\wedge\tau_n}-X_0=(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$$
   verifies exactly clause 4. The stopped-piece martingale assertion and
   adaptedness are hypotheses here, not consequences of the unrestricted
   all-pairs definition. They must be established in each application.
   The sequence $(\sigma\wedge\tau_n)$ is not a substitute for $(\tau_n)$:
   its almost-sure limit is $\sigma$, which need not be infinity.

No path continuity, no right continuity of the filtration, and no completeness
of the underlying probability space is imposed by this definition. Choice
enters only through the conditional-expectation interface named above,
whose countable-choice obligations are declared as dependencies of this item.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: The result is immediate when $T=0$. Suppose $T>0$, fix $n\ge0$, and let $t_k=kT/2^n$ for $0\le k\le2^n$. Put $S_n=\max_{0\le k\le2^n}|M_{t_k}|$, which is square-integrable because it is bounded by the finite sum $\sum_k|M_{t_k}|$. For $r>0$, let $\tau$ be the first grid index $k$ with $|M_{t_k}|\ge r$, or leave it undefined if no grid value reaches $r$. Each event $\{\tau=k\}$ belongs to $\mathcal F_{t_k}$. By [F1] and [F2], $|M_{t_k}|=|\mathbb E[M_T\mid\mathcal F_{t_k}]|\le\mathbb E[|M_T|\mid\mathcal F_{t_k}]$ almost surely. Multiplying by $\mathbf1_{\{\tau=k\}}$ and taking expectations gives $\mathbb E[|M_T|\mathbf1_{\{\tau=k\}}]\ge r\mathbb P(\tau=k)$. Summing over the finite grid yields $$ r\,\mathbb P(S_n\ge r)\le\mathbb E[|M_T|\mathbf1_{\{S_n\ge r\}}]. $$

Apply [F4] to $S_n^2$, use $\mathbb P(S_n>r)\le\mathbb P(S_n\ge r)$ and integrate the bound from step 1.1. [F5] for the nonnegative indicator $\mathbf1_{\{S_n\ge r\}}$ gives $$ \mathbb E S_n^2=\int_0^\infty2r\,\mathbb P(S_n>r)\,dr\le2\,\mathbb E[|M_T|S_n]. $$ By [F3], the right side is at most $2(\mathbb E|M_T|^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E S_n^2)^{1/2}$. If $\mathbb E S_n^2=0$ the desired finite-grid bound is immediate; otherwise divide by its square root and square to obtain $\mathbb E S_n^2\le4\mathbb E|M_T|^2$.

The dyadic grids are nested, so $S_n\uparrow S_*:=\sup_{t\in D_T}|M_t|=S_T$. For every $\omega\in\Omega_0$ and each $t<T$, there are dyadic grid times decreasing to $t$, and right-continuity makes their process values converge to $M_t(\omega)$; time $T$ is in every grid. Hence $S_*$ equals the pathwise supremum on $[0,T]$ almost surely. Apply [F6] to $S_n^2$ and take limits in the finite-grid estimate from step 2.1 to obtain the stated inequality.

Fix $d\geq1$. A pair potential is an even Borel function $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. For a finite list of positions $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, set $U_0=U_1=0$ and
$$U_N(X)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(x_i-x_j).$$
The value $+\infty$ is allowed and represents a forbidden configuration; $-\infty$ is not allowed.

The potential is **stable** if some finite $B\geq0$ satisfies $U_N(X)\geq-BN$ for every $N$ and every $X$. Fix a cell side $\ell>0$ and the half-open cubic tiling $C_k=\ell(k+[0,1)^d)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and let $n_k(X)$ count the positions of $X$ in $C_k$. The potential is **cell-superstable** if there are constants $A_*>0$ and $B_*\geq0$ such that
$$U_N(X)\geq A_*\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}n_k(X)^2-B_*N$$
for every finite configuration; the sum is finite for finite $X$.

For disjoint finite cell-index sets $I,J$, let $W_{I,J}(X)$ be the sum of pair terms with one point in a cell indexed by $I$ and the other in a cell indexed by $J$. The potential is **lower regular** for this tiling if a nonnegative envelope $\Psi:\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}\to[0,\infty)$ exists with $\sum_{k\ne0}\Psi(k)<\infty$ and
$$W_{I,J}(X)\geq-\sum_{k\in I}\sum_{l\in J}\Psi(k-l)n_k(X)n_l(X)$$
for all such $I,J,X$. The ordered-pair convention in this formula is fixed as written.

A **decreasing-integrable tail bound** means that for some $R_0\geq0$ there is a nonnegative nonincreasing function $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R_0$ and $\int_{R_0}^{\infty}\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty$. This explicit envelope condition is stronger than bare Lebesgue integrability of an arbitrary signed tail. Stability, cell-superstability, lower regularity, and a tail bound are separate properties; none is inferred from finite range alone.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. All displayed integrals use Lebesgue measure. Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq2$ and write $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. A simple graph on $[n]$ is $([n],E)$ with $E$ a set of unordered two-element subsets of $[n]$; a path is a finite vertex list with distinct vertices and consecutive pairs in $E$; connected means every two vertices are joined by a path; a cycle is a vertex list $(v_0,\ldots,v_k)$ with $k\geq3$, $v_k=v_0$, $v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}$ distinct, and consecutive pairs in $E$; a tree is a connected graph with no cycle; a forest is a graph with no cycle. Finite sums and products over graph, edge, vertex, and subset sets below are enumeration-independent; the empty sum is $0$ and the empty product is $1$. Fix $d\in\mathbb N$ with $d\geq1$, let $v:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ be an even Borel pair potential with no $-\infty$ values, and suppose it is stable with constant $B\in\mathbb R$, $B\geq0$. Fix $\beta\in\mathbb R$ with $\beta>0$, set $e^{-c(+\infty)}:=0$ for every $c>0$, define the Mayer function $f_\beta(x):=e^{-\beta v(x)}-1$, and suppose

$$C_\beta:=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|f_\beta(x)|\,dx<\infty.$$

Let $\mathcal C_n$ be the connected simple graphs on $[n]$ and let $\mathcal T_n$ be the trees on $[n]$. These families are finite because $[n]$ has finitely many unordered two-element subsets and each graph is determined by a subset of those edges. A spanning tree of a finite graph is a tree with the same vertex set and a subset of its edges. A leaf is a vertex incident to exactly one edge. Put

$$U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\sum_{G\in\mathcal C_n}\ \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_\beta(x_i-x_j).$$

For every configuration $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in(\mathbb R^d)^n$,

$$|U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)|\leq e^{2\beta Bn}\sum_{T\in\mathcal T_n}\ \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}|f_\beta(x_i-x_j)|,$$

where $\mathcal T_n$ is the set of labelled trees on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. In particular,

$$\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^{n-1}}|U_n(0,x_2,\ldots,x_n)|\,dx_2\cdots dx_n\leq e^{2\beta Bn}n^{n-2}C_\beta^{\,n-1}.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ be measurable with $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere. Suppose $g\ge0$ is measurable and $\int g\,d\mu<\infty$, and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Let $f_0(x)$ be the finite complex pointwise limit of $(f_n(x))$ where it exists, and $0$ elsewhere. Then $f_0$ is measurable, equals $f$ almost everywhere, is integrable, and $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f_0\,d\mu$ and $\int|f_n-f_0|\,d\mu\to0$. If the specified $f$ is measurable, these same conclusions hold with $f$ in place of $f_0$. In particular this is automatic when $\mu$ is complete. On a noncomplete measure space an arbitrary almost-everywhere representative need not be measurable, so no integral of such a nonmeasurable $f$ is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex
numbers** by the quotient ring
$$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set
$$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$
Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map
$\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the
field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which
$\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of
[[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Let $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ have radius $R$. If $|z-a|<R$, then $f$ is complex differentiable at $z$ and
$$f'(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}n c_n(z-a)^{n-1}.$$
Consequently $f$ is holomorphic on its open disc of convergence ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from A total pointwise product for extended-real-valued functions, and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
The positive and negative parts of a function. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of Borel measurable and Lebesgue measurable functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space (Measure spaces). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ (The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
(The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space) is Lebesgue
measurable (Lebesgue measurable sets, the family $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and the restricted set function $\lambda_n$). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

For every real $r$, write $\lambda_r$ for its canonical image in $\mathbb C$. Then
$$
|\lambda_r|_{\mathbb C}=|r|_{\mathbb R}.
$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ (The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion when the
values are real and of Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$ when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ (Injection, surjection, bijection), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
A finite sum is unchanged by a permutation of its index range: $\sum_{k<n} a_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every bijection $\pi : n \to n$ to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
(The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of Laws of finite sums and products in $\mathbb{N}$, and $\iota\big(\sum_{k<n} a_k\big) = \sum_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of Laws of finite sums and finite products in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field).

derivations.claim: For every $N$-point configuration, the energy $E_N=\sum_{i<j}v(x_i-x_j)$ is an extended-real Borel function: coordinate differences are continuous and hence Borel [F13], composition with $v$ preserves Borel measurability [F11], and finite sums preserve it wherever defined. The map $u\mapsto e^{-\beta u}$ on the extended real line, assigned $0$ at $+\infty$ and $+\infty$ at $-\infty$, is Borel because it is continuous on $\mathbb R$ [F12] and the endpoints are Borel [F14]. Thus the Boltzmann integrand is Borel on $\mathbb R^{dN}$. For $N\geq2$, repeated application of the two-factor product identity [F15] identifies the finite product Borel sigma-algebra; the Borel-to-Lebesgue inclusion [F16] then makes the integrand product-measurable. For $N=0$ or $1$ the same measurability is immediate from the empty or one-factor product. The same extended exponential map and the Borel potential show that $f_\beta$ is Borel. Stability [F1] gives $E_N\geq-BN$, so the Boltzmann integrand is real, nonnegative and at most $e^{\beta BN}$, with a forbidden $+\infty$ configuration contributing $0$. Since $|\Lambda_L|=(2L)^d<\infty$ [F17], multiplicativity of complex modulus and its agreement with real absolute value [F21] bound the modulus of the $N$th term of $\Xi_L(z)$ by $(|z|e^{\beta B}|\Lambda_L|)^N/N!$. The sum of these bounds is finite for every $z$ by [F7], so $\Xi_L$ is entire.

Stability at $N=2$ gives $v(x)\geq-2B$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$; hence $-1\leq f_\beta(x)\leq e^{2\beta B}-1$ by [F12]. Thus for each fixed $N$ every graph term in the finite expansion $\prod_{i<j}(1+f_\beta(x_i-x_j))$ is bounded and measurable on the finite-measure box $\Lambda_L^N$. Expanding the product gives a sum over all simple graphs; each graph decomposes uniquely into connected components as in [F2]. If the component sizes are $m_1,\ldots,m_k$, assigning the $N$ labels to an ordered list of blocks contributes $N!/\prod_jm_j!$, and division by $k!$ removes block order. Integrating a product over disjoint coordinate blocks factorizes by Fubini [F5], since the factors are bounded on finite-measure boxes. Therefore the coefficient of $z^N$ in $\Xi_L$ equals that in the formal exponential of $A_L(z):=\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{z^n}{n!}\int_{\Lambda_L^n}U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n$.

For $n\geq2$, integrate the pointwise tree estimate [F2] over $\Lambda_L^n$. Root each tree at vertex $1$, then remove leaves other than the root. At each removal the leaf integral over $\Lambda_L$ is at most the whole-space integral $C_\beta$ by monotonicity [F19] and translation invariance [F6]; Tonelli [F10] applies to the nonnegative tree products. The final root integral is $|\Lambda_L|$. The labelled-tree count in [F2] is $n^{n-2}$. Finite additivity [F20] sums those tree integrals, giving $\int_{\Lambda_L^n}|U_n|\leq e^{2\beta Bn}|\Lambda_L|n^{n-2}C_\beta^{n-1}$. Thus $U_n$ is integrable on $\Lambda_L^n$. Regard its real values as complex values by the real embedding; [F21] identifies the complex modulus with real absolute value, so the integral triangle inequality [F18] gives $|b_n(L)|\leq e^{2\beta Bn}n^{n-2}C_\beta^{n-1}/n!$. The same bound holds for $|b_n|$ by the pinned estimate [F2].

Fix $n\geq2$ and write $y_1=0$, $y_i=x_i-x_1$ for $i\geq2$. Translation invariance of $U_n$ gives $U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=U_n(0,y_2,\ldots,y_n)$. By Tonelli [F10], translation invariance [F6], and the pinned integrability from [F2], $\int_{\Lambda_L^n}|U_n(x)|dx=\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^{n-1}}|U_n(0,y)|\,|\Lambda_L\cap(\Lambda_L-y_2)\cap\cdots\cap(\Lambda_L-y_n)|dy\leq|\Lambda_L|\int|U_n(0,y)|dy<\infty$, using the finite cube volume [F17]. Thus the integrand is absolutely integrable and Fubini [F5] applies. Translating each remaining coordinate in its section gives $b_n(L)=\frac1{n!}\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^{n-1}}U_n(0,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\theta_L(y)\,dy_2\cdots dy_n$, where $\theta_L(y)=\frac{|\Lambda_L\cap(\Lambda_L-y_2)\cap\cdots\cap(\Lambda_L-y_n)|}{|\Lambda_L|}=\prod_{j=1}^d(1-\frac{\max_i y_{i,j}-\min_i y_{i,j}}{2L})_+$, with $r_+=\max(r,0)$. For each fixed $y$, $0\leq\theta_L(y)\leq1$ and $\theta_L(y)\to1$. The cube-intersection volume formula follows from [F17]; $U_n$ is Borel by [F11, F13, F14, F15, F16], hence measurable. For every sequence $L_m\to\infty$, dominated convergence [F4] with majorant $|U_n(0,\cdot)|$ gives $b_n(L_m)\to b_n$. If the limit as a real variable $L\to\infty$ failed, some $\epsilon>0$ would have $|b_n(L)-b_n|\geq\epsilon$ for arbitrarily large $L$; Countable Choice [A1] selects such an $L_m\geq m$ for each $m$, contradicting the sequential conclusion. Hence $b_n(L)\to b_n$.

For every integer $n\geq2$, the positive series for $e^n$ in [F7] contains the term $n^n/n!$, so $n^{n-2}/n!\leq e^n/n^2$. If $C_\beta>0$, put $q(r)=rC_\beta e^{2\beta B+1}$. For $0<r$ with $q(r)<1$, step 1.3 yields $|b_n(L)|r^n\leq r e^{2\beta B+1}q(r)^{n-1}/n^2$ and $n|b_n(L)|r^{n-1}\leq e^{2\beta B+1}q(r)^{n-1}/n$; the same bounds hold for $b_n$. Both majorant series converge. If $C_\beta=0$, step 1.3 gives $b_n(L)=b_n=0$ for $n\geq2$. Each $U_n$ is real-valued by [F2], so each coefficient $b_n(L),b_n$ is real; [F21] identifies its complex-embedding modulus with its real absolute value and gives $|z^n|=|z|^n$. Hence the coefficient and derivative majorants bound the complex power-series terms on the corresponding closed subdiscs. Thus the pressure series and their formal derivative series converge uniformly on every closed subdisc strictly inside $\mathcal D$; [F9] identifies the derivatives with the termwise derivatives.

The coefficient identity in step 1.2 is the formal identity $\Xi_L=\exp(A_L)$, and $A_L(z)=|\Lambda_L|p_L(z)$ by the definitions of $b_n(L)$. Fix a volume $L>0$ and a radius $r$ strictly inside $\mathcal D$. Step 2.1 gives $\sum_n|b_n(L)|r^n<\infty$, so $\sum_n|[z^n]A_L|r^n=|\Lambda_L|\sum_n|b_n(L)|r^n<\infty$ for this fixed volume. Expanding the complex exponential in [F8], the sum of absolute values of all terms is bounded by $\exp(\sum_n|[z^n]A_L|r^n)$; hence its products and coefficient sums may be regrouped, so the formal identity is an equality of convergent series and $\Xi_L(z)=\exp(|\Lambda_L|p_L(z))$. To pass to the limit on a compact subdisc $|z|\leq r$ inside $\mathcal D$, the pressure and derivative tails are uniformly bounded in $L$ by the convergent majorants of step 2.1. For each fixed $n$, step 1.4 gives coefficient convergence; finite partial sums and their derivatives therefore converge uniformly, and the uniform tail bounds give $p_L\to p$ and $p_L'\to p'$ uniformly there. [F8, F9, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.4, step 2.1] ∎

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized product Haar measure $dx$, with $dx(\mathbb T^d)=1$. Coordinates and time are dimensionless in the diffusive normalization $D=1$. For $r\in(0,1)$ set the mobility function $\chi(r):=r(1-r)$. For any finite interval $[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $\rho:[a,b]\times\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$ be a scalar density and let $j:[a,b]\times\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be a vector current. Require both fields to be smooth up to the time endpoints and periodic in space, and require that for some $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, $\varepsilon\le\rho(t,x)\le1-\varepsilon$ for every $(t,x)$. Call $(\rho,j)$ admissible when it also satisfies the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot j=0$. Define its dimensionless action by

$$\mathcal I_{[a,b]}(\rho,j):=\frac14\int_a^b\int_{\mathbb T^d}\frac{|j(t,x)+\nabla\rho(t,x)|^2}{\rho(t,x)(1-\rho(t,x))}\,dx\,dt.$$

This is the macroscopic fluctuation functional in the stated normalized SSEP coefficient convention. It is a definition of a functional and does not assert a microscopic path-space large-deviation principle or a probability estimate.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let $\rho_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $0\le\rho_0\le1$ almost everywhere, using normalized product Haar measure $dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ define $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i k\cdot x)$ and $\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dx$. For $t>0$ set

$$\rho_t(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat\rho_0(k)e_k(x),$$

and at $t=0$ set $\rho_t=\rho_0$ as an almost-everywhere class. For smooth periodic $G$, define

$$P_tG(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat G(k)e_k(x)\quad(t>0),\qquad P_0G:=G.$$

Then on every strip $[\epsilon,T]\times\mathbb T^d$ with $0<\epsilon<T<\infty$, the series for $\rho_t$ and all its space and time derivatives converge absolutely and uniformly; in particular $\rho_t$ is real and smooth for each $t>0$ and $\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta\rho_t$. For every finite $T$ and every smooth $G$, $P_tG$ is smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$, satisfies $\partial_tP_tG=\Delta P_tG$, has uniformly bounded derivatives of every fixed order there, and $P_tG\to G$ uniformly as $t\downarrow0$. Moreover

$$\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_tG\,dx=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_0P_tG\,dx,$$

so $(\rho_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ is the unique weak heat solution with datum $\rho_0$ in the stated weak formulation. It preserves $0\le\rho_t\le1$ almost everywhere and the mass $\int\rho_t\,dx=\int\rho_0\,dx$.

derivations.claim: Since $\rho$ is smooth and periodic, repeated integration by parts gives $(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)^m\widehat\rho(k)=\widehat{(1-\Delta)^m\rho}(k)$, so $|\widehat\rho(k)|\le C_m(1+|k|^2)^{-m}$ for every integer $m\ge1$. The number of lattice points with $\|k\|_\infty=r$ is at most $(2r+1)^d-(2r-1)^d\le C_dr^{d-1}$. Thus for every multi-index $\alpha$, choosing $m>(d+|\alpha|)/2$ makes $\sum_k(2\pi|k|)^{|\alpha|}|\widehat\rho(k)|$ finite, so the Fourier series and its differentiated series converge uniformly on compact time intervals including $s=0$. For $s\ge1$, the same shell bound and the Fourier formula in [F2] give $\|\partial^\alpha(\rho_s-\bar\rho)\|_\infty\le e^{-4\pi^2s}\sum_{k\ne0}(2\pi|k|)^{|\alpha|}|\widehat\rho(k)|e^{-4\pi^2(|k|^2-1)}\le C_{\alpha,\rho}e^{-4\pi^2s}$. The zero Fourier coefficient is $\widehat\rho(0)=\bar\rho$, proving the asserted smoothness and $C^\infty$ convergence.

The heat profile stays in $[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]$: the affine rescaling $v_0=(\rho-\varepsilon)/(1-2\varepsilon)$ lies in $[0,1]$, and its Fourier heat profile $v_s$ preserves $[0,1]$ by [F2]. The multiplier is linear and fixes constants, so $\rho_s=\varepsilon+(1-2\varepsilon)v_s$; its mean is $\bar\rho$ by the zero-mode calculation in step 1.1.

Define $a(t)=0$ for $t\le0$ and $a(t)=e^{-1/t}$ for $t>0$, and set $\zeta(t)=a(t)/(a(t)+a(1-t))$ on $[0,1]$. For each derivative order, the right derivatives of $a$ at zero are sums of terms $t^{-m}e^{-1/t}$, which tend to zero; hence $a$ is smooth and flat at zero. The denominator is positive on $[0,1]$, $\zeta(0)=0$, $\zeta(1)=1$, and $\zeta$ is flat at both endpoints in the sense that all derivatives of $\zeta$ vanish at zero and all derivatives of $\zeta-1$ vanish at one. Define $\sigma_t^S=\bar\rho+\zeta(t)(\rho_{S+1-t}-\bar\rho)$. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$ and let $\rho_0:\mathbb T^d\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with $0\le\rho_0\le1$ almost everywhere, using normalized product Haar measure $dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ define $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i k\cdot x)$ and $\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dx$. For $t>0$ set

$$\rho_t(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat\rho_0(k)e_k(x),$$

and at $t=0$ set $\rho_t=\rho_0$ as an almost-everywhere class. For smooth periodic $G$, define

$$P_tG(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat G(k)e_k(x)\quad(t>0),\qquad P_0G:=G.$$

Then on every strip $[\epsilon,T]\times\mathbb T^d$ with $0<\epsilon<T<\infty$, the series for $\rho_t$ and all its space and time derivatives converge absolutely and uniformly; in particular $\rho_t$ is real and smooth for each $t>0$ and $\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta\rho_t$. For every finite $T$ and every smooth $G$, $P_tG$ is smooth on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$, satisfies $\partial_tP_tG=\Delta P_tG$, has uniformly bounded derivatives of every fixed order there, and $P_tG\to G$ uniformly as $t\downarrow0$. Moreover

$$\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_tG\,dx=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_0P_tG\,dx,$$

so $(\rho_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ is the unique weak heat solution with datum $\rho_0$ in the stated weak formulation. It preserves $0\le\rho_t\le1$ almost everywhere and the mass $\int\rho_t\,dx=\int\rho_0\,dx$.

Let $X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $k\ge1$, let $w:X\to(0,\infty)$ be a positive reference weight, and let $T:X\to\mathbb R^k$. Use the Euclidean inner product $\theta\cdot T(x):=\sum_{j=1}^k\theta_jT_j(x)$. For $\theta\in\mathbb R^k$, define the partition sum and log-partition function by
$$Z(\theta):=\sum_{x\in X}w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)},\qquad A(\theta):=\log Z(\theta),$$
and define the finite exponential Gibbs family by
$$\pi_\theta(x):=w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)-A(\theta)}\quad(x\in X).$$
All objects here are mathematical; $\theta\cdot T(x)$ is a real number. The representation is called minimal when there is no nonzero $a\in\mathbb R^k$ for which $a\cdot T(x)$ is constant over all $x\in X$.

For a finite set $S\subseteq\mathbb R^k$, its convex hull is the set of sums $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s s$ with $\lambda_s\ge0$ and $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s=1$. Its affine hull is the set of sums of the same form with real coefficients $\lambda_s$ whose sum is $1$. The relative interior of a convex set is its interior in its affine hull with the Euclidean subspace topology. These definitions will be used for the sufficient-statistic support $T(X)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,m)$ be a sigma-finite measure space, let $w\ge0$ be
measurable with $m(\{w>0\})>0$, let $r\ge1$ and let
$X=(X_1,\ldots,X_r):\Omega\to\mathbb R^r$ be measurable and finite, and let
$\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For
each compact $K\subset\Theta$, assume an integrable $G_K$ satisfies
$$w(x)e^{\theta\cdot X(x)}\left(1+\sum_a|X_a(x)|^2\right)\le G_K(x)\quad(\theta\in K).$$
Then $Z(\theta)=\int w e^{\theta\cdot X}\,dm$ is finite, strictly positive
and $C^2$, and the probability density $\rho_\theta=Z(\theta)^{-1}we^{\theta\cdot X}$
defines $dP_\theta=\rho_\theta\,dm$ as in [[def-measure-with-density]].
For any integrable real $A$, write $\langle A\rangle_\theta:=\int A\,dP_\theta$;
for square-integrable real $A,B$, define
$\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(A,B):=\int(A-\langle A\rangle_\theta)(B-\langle B\rangle_\theta)\,dP_\theta$.
These extend the phase-space conventions of
[[def-csm-statistical-state-observable]] to the present measure space.
Then
$$\partial_a\log Z=\langle X_a\rangle_\theta,\qquad \partial_a\partial_b\log Z=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b).$$
In particular, the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

derivations.claim: The envelope verified in [F1] lets [F2] apply with counting measure, so $\nabla A(\theta)=\mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}T$ and $\nabla^2A(\theta)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_\theta}(T)$.

For any $a\in\mathbb R^k$, the quadratic form is
$a^\mathsf T\nabla^2A(\theta)a=\sum_{x\in X}\pi_\theta(x)\bigl(a\cdot T(x)-\mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}[a\cdot T]\bigr)^2$.
Every weight is positive by [F1], so this sum is zero exactly when $a\cdot T(x)$ has the same value at every $x\in X$. Thus the Hessian is positive definite for every $\theta$ exactly when no nonzero $a$ makes $a\cdot T$ constant, which is minimality by [F1].

If $\pi_\theta=\pi_\varphi$ as functions on $X$, positivity allows taking logarithms of their equal positive values. The product law and inverse identity [F5, F6] then give $(\theta-\varphi)\cdot T(x)=A(\theta)-A(\varphi)$ for every $x$. Under minimality this forces $\theta-\varphi=0$. Conversely, if a nonzero $a$ makes $a\cdot T(x)=c$ constant, the exponential addition formula [F7] gives $Z(\theta+ta)=\exp(tc)Z(\theta)$. Since $Z(\theta)>0$ and $\exp(tc)>0$ by [F1, F8], the logarithm laws [F5, F6] give $A(\theta+ta)=A(\theta)+tc$. Substitution in the family formula and another use of [F7] show $\pi_{\theta+ta}=\pi_\theta$ for every real $t$; the parametrization is not injective.

Let $D=\operatorname{span}\{T(x)-T(x_0):x\in X\}$ for a fixed $x_0\in X$. If $D$ is proper, choose a basis $v_1,\dots,v_r$ of $D$, with $r<k$, and define $L:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R^r$ by $L(a)=(a\cdot v_1,\dots,a\cdot v_r)$. Rank-nullity [F3] gives $\dim\ker L\ge k-r>0$, so some nonzero $a$ is orthogonal to every difference and $a\cdot T$ is constant. Conversely, if such a nonzero $a$ exists, every difference lies in the proper hyperplane $a^\perp$, so $D$ is proper. By [F4], $D=\mathbb R^k$ exactly when the affine hull is $\mathbb R^k$. This proves the stated equivalence with full affine dimension and completes the identifiability conditions.

boundaries.evidence: The finite family requires nonempty X; step 1.1 uses a probability law with full support.
The quadratic-form criterion tests only nonzero directions; step 2.1 identifies zero variance exactly for constant projections.
If X is a singleton and k≥1, every statistic projection is constant, the Hessian is zero, and the parameter map is not injective; steps 2.1 and 2.2 cover this degenerate case.
Repeated statistic vectors are allowed; the span-of-differences argument in step 3.1 detects the resulting affine deficiency.

boundaries.reason: No endpoint or boundary-extremum assertion occurs.
Step 4.1 fixes one x0 and uses finite-dimensional linear algebra; the proof selects no family of nonempty sets.

boundaries.evidence: Minimality implies positive-definite covariance in step 2.1; the parameter-map implication is proved in step 2.2 and the affine-hull equivalence in step 3.1.
A constant nonzero projection forces Hessian degeneracy and noninjectivity in steps 2.1 and 2.2; step 3.1 proves the converse affine-hull direction.
