citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. All inner products are linear in their first
argument. If $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, its **conjugate Hilbert space**
$\overline H$ consists of symbols $\overline x$ for $x\in H$, with
$\overline x+\overline y=\overline{x+y}$,
$a\,\overline x=\overline{\overline a\,x}$ for $a\in\mathbb C$, and
$$\langle\overline x,\overline y\rangle_{\overline H} :=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle_H}.$$
The canonical map $c_H:H\to\overline H$, $c_Hx=\overline x$, is a
conjugate-linear surjective isometry.

For complex Hilbert spaces $H_1,H_2$, a linear operator $A$ is a linear map
$A:D(A)\to H_2$ on a linear domain $D(A)\subseteq H_1$. Its graph is
$\Gamma(A)=\{(x,Ax):x\in D(A)\}\subseteq H_1\oplus H_2$, with the direct-sum
Hilbert norm. It is densely defined when $D(A)$ is dense in $H_1$, and closed
when $\Gamma(A)$ is closed.

For a densely defined linear operator $A:D(A)\subseteq H_1\to H_2$, define
$D(A^*)$ to consist of those $y\in H_2$ for which
$x\mapsto\langle Ax,y\rangle_{H_2}$ is bounded on $D(A)$ in the $H_1$ norm.
The bounded functional extends uniquely to $H_1$; its Riesz vector
$A^*y\in H_1$ is specified by
$$\langle Ax,y\rangle_{H_2}=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_{H_1} \qquad(x\in D(A)).$$
This defines the linear adjoint $A^*:D(A^*)\subseteq H_2\to H_1$.

An operator $S:D(S)\subseteq H\to H$ is **antilinear** when
$S(ax+by)=\overline a\,Sx+\overline b\,Sy$. Its associated linear operator
$\widetilde S:D(\widetilde S)\subseteq\overline H\to H$ is
$D(\widetilde S)=c_H(D(S))$ and
$\widetilde S(\overline x)=Sx$. For densely defined antilinear $S$, define
$$S^*:=c_H^{-1}\widetilde S^*,$$
on the domain $D(S^*)=D(\widetilde S^*)$. Thus $S^*$ is antilinear and
$$\langle Sx,y\rangle_H=\langle S^*y,x\rangle_H \qquad(x\in D(S),\ y\in D(S^*)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_1,H_2$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:D(A)\subseteq H_1\to H_2$ be a linear operator with dense domain and closed
graph. Define $A^*$ as in the local Hilbert-space adjoint convention. Then
$T:=A^*A$, on
$D(T)=\{x\in D(A):Ax\in D(A^*)\}$, is positive and self-adjoint. Its positive
square root $P:=T^{1/2}$ has domain $D(P)=D(A)$ and satisfies
$\|Px\|=\|Ax\|$ for every $x\in D(A)$. There is a unique partial isometry
$U:H_1\to H_2$ such that
$$A=UP,\qquad \ker U=\ker A.$$
Its initial space is $\overline{\operatorname{ran}P}=(\ker A)^\perp$ and its
final space is $\overline{\operatorname{ran}A}$. If $A$ is injective and has
dense range, then $U$ is unitary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$R\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a unital star subalgebra. Its strong-operator
closure is $R''$. If $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ is a concrete von Neumann
algebra and $\Omega\in H$, then $\Omega$ is cyclic for $M$ exactly when it is
separating for $M'$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Throughout this page $H$ is a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with
inner product linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

A **(possibly unbounded) linear operator on $H$** is a linear map
$T:D(T)\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]) whose **domain** $D(T)\subseteq H$ is a linear
subspace ([[def-linear-subspace]]). The domain is part of the data: $T=S$ means
$D(T)=D(S)$ and $Tx=Sx$ for all $x\in D(T)$. One writes $T\subseteq S$, and
calls $S$ an **extension** of $T$, when $D(T)\subseteq D(S)$ and $Sx=Tx$ for
every $x\in D(T)$.

The **graph** of $T$ is
$$\Gamma(T):=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}\subseteq H\oplus H .$$
The direct sum $H\oplus H$ is read as the complex vector space of pairs with
coordinatewise operations and the inner product
$\langle (x,y),(u,v)\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle+\langle y,v\rangle$, whose induced
norm is
$$\|(x,y)\|=(\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2)^{1/2};$$
it is complete because $H$ is ([[def-complete-metric-space]]). The **graph norm**
on $D(T)$ is
$$\|x\|_T:=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2},$$
so that $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$
onto $\Gamma(T)$ with the norm restricted from $H\oplus H$.

$T$ is **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of $H\oplus H$. A linear
operator is determined by its graph, and the following elementary translations
are used silently below: $\Gamma(T)$ is a linear subspace of $H\oplus H$;
$\Gamma(T)\cap(\{0\}\oplus H)=\{(0,0)\}$; the image of $\Gamma(T)$ under the
first coordinate projection is $D(T)$; and $T\subseteq S$ if and only if
$\Gamma(T)\subseteq\Gamma(S)$. In particular a closed operator is exactly one
whose graph is a closed subspace of $H\oplus H$.

**Notation.** No boundedness of $T$ is assumed, and $T$ is frequently called
*unbounded* to stress this; a bounded everywhere defined operator on $H$ is the
special case $D(T)=H$ in which $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subspace by continuity.
The letter $I$ denotes the identity operator on $H$ with domain $H$.

**Completeness of $H\oplus H$.** If $(x_n,y_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in
$H\oplus H$, then $\|x_n-x_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ and
$\|y_n-y_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ show that $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are Cauchy
in $H$; let $x,y$ be their limits. Then
$\|(x_n,y_n)-(x,y)\|^2=\|x_n-x\|^2+\|y_n-y\|^2\to0$, so $H\oplus H$ is
complete. Consequently a sequence in $H\oplus H$ converges exactly when its two
coordinate sequences converge in $H$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a linear
operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$ and graph $\Gamma(T)$
([[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]).

$T$ is **densely defined** when $D(T)$ is a dense subset of $H$
([[def-dense-top]]); **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of
$H\oplus H$; and **closable** when $T$ has a closed extension.
Recall that the graph norm is $\|x\|_T=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2}$.

**The graph-norm dictionary.** The following three statements are part of the
definition's content and are proved in the remarks below rather than assumed:

1. $\|\cdot\|_T$ is a norm on $D(T)$, and
   $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ onto
   $\Gamma(T)$;
2. $T$ is closed if and only if $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]);
3. if $T$ is closed, then $D(T)$ is a Hilbert space for the inner product
   $\langle x,y\rangle_T=\langle x,y\rangle+\langle Tx,Ty\rangle$ whose induced
   norm is $\|\cdot\|_T$.

A linear subspace $D_0\subseteq D(T)$ is a **core** for a closed operator $T$
when $D_0$ is dense in $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$, equivalently when
$\overline{\Gamma(T|_{D_0})}=\Gamma(T)$, where the closure is taken in
$H\oplus H$ and $T|_{D_0}$ denotes the restriction of $T$ to $D_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_1,H_2$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:D(A)\subseteq H_1\to H_2$ be a linear operator with dense domain and closed
graph. Define $A^*$ as in the local Hilbert-space adjoint convention. Then
$T:=A^*A$, on
$D(T)=\{x\in D(A):Ax\in D(A^*)\}$, is positive and self-adjoint. Its positive
square root $P:=T^{1/2}$ has domain $D(P)=D(A)$ and satisfies
$\|Px\|=\|Ax\|$ for every $x\in D(A)$. There is a unique partial isometry
$U:H_1\to H_2$ such that
$$A=UP,\qquad \ker U=\ker A.$$
Its initial space is $\overline{\operatorname{ran}P}=(\ker A)^\perp$ and its
final space is $\overline{\operatorname{ran}A}$. If $A$ is injective and has
dense range, then $U$ is unitary.

derivations.claim: Put $C=c_H$ and $T=\overline S$. The definition of graph closure above makes $A:=\widetilde T$ a closed densely defined complex-linear operator $\overline H\to H$. By [F2], write $A=U B$, where $B=(A^*A)^{1/2}$ is positive self-adjoint with $D(B)=D(A)$ and $U$ is a partial isometry with initial space $\overline{\operatorname{ran}B}=(\ker A)^\perp$, final space $\overline{\operatorname{ran}A}$, and kernel $\ker A$. Set $J:=UC$ and $P:=C^{-1}BC$, with domain $D(P)=C^{-1}D(B)$. The composition $P$ is linear. If $E$ is the spectral measure of $B$, then $F(\Lambda):=C^{-1}E(\Lambda)C$ is a spectral measure of orthogonal projections on $H$, and its spectral integral is $P$; hence $P$ is positive self-adjoint. More explicitly, $D(T^*T)=\{x:Cx\in D(A),\ ACx\in D(A^*)\}=C^{-1}D(A^*A)$, and the adjoint convention [F1] gives $T^*T=C^{-1}A^*AC$ there. Also $D(P^2)=C^{-1}D(B^2)$ and $P^2=C^{-1}B^2C=C^{-1}A^*AC=T^*T$ on that domain; uniqueness of the positive self-adjoint square root gives $P=(T^*T)^{1/2}$. For $x\in D(T)$, $JPx=UCC^{-1}BCx=UBCx=ACx=Tx$, so $T=JP$. The operator $J$ is antilinear, vanishes on $\ker T$, and is isometric on $(\ker T)^\perp$, since $C$ maps $\ker T$ onto $\ker A$ and preserves orthogonality. Its final space is $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$. If $T$ is injective and has dense range, then $A$ is injective with dense range, so $U$ is unitary by [F2] and $J=UC$ is antiunitary.

For $x,y\in M$, if $x\Omega=y\Omega$, then $(x-y)\Omega=0$; separatingness of $\Omega$ for $M$ forces $x=y$. Thus the rule $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ is well defined. It is antilinear because $(a x+b y)^*=\overline a\,x^* +\overline b\,y^*$, and its domain is dense because $\Omega$ is cyclic for $M$.

Let $u_n\in D(\widetilde S_0)$ satisfy $u_n\to0$ in $\overline H$ and $\widetilde S_0u_n\to\eta$ in $H$. Write $u_n=C(x_n\Omega)$ with $x_n\in M$; then $x_n\Omega\to0$ and $x_n^*\Omega=S_0(x_n\Omega)=\widetilde S_0u_n\to\eta$. For every $y'\in M'$, the linear-first adjoint identity and commutation give $$\langle\eta,y'\Omega\rangle =\lim_n\langle x_n^*\Omega,y'\Omega\rangle =\lim_n\langle y'^*\Omega,x_n\Omega\rangle=0.$$ Since $\Omega$ is separating for $M$, [F3] makes it cyclic for $M'$, so $M'\Omega$ is dense and $\eta=0$. Thus the graph closure of the linear operator $\widetilde S_0$ has zero vertical fiber: because $\overline H\oplus H$ is a metric space, every point of that closure is the limit of a sequence of graph points, and the argument just given excludes a nonzero limit over $0$. This closed linear subspace is therefore the graph of a closed linear extension of $\widetilde S_0$. By [F4], $\widetilde S_0$ is closable, and the local convention above proves that $S_0$ is closable with graph closure defined there.

Step 1.1 proves the polar decomposition for the closure of every densely-defined closable antilinear operator, and steps 1.2–2.1 prove the Tomita operator clause with its stated cyclic-separating hypotheses. The Choice assumption is inherited through the spectral theorem used in [F2].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in its first argument. An operator $\rho\in\mathcal B(H)$ is a **density operator** when it is positive, trace class, and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Here trace class means compact with summable singular values, and $\operatorname{Tr}$ is the basis-independent trace of a trace-class operator.

The **normal density state represented by $\rho$** is the functional on bounded operators
$
\omega_\rho(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A),\qquad A\in\mathcal B(H).
$
In this page, “normal density state” means this specified trace-pairing representation; no equivalence with other definitions of normal functionals is assumed. The trace pairing is used only for bounded $A$. Unbounded observables are treated through their spectral probability measures in [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a unital $*$-subalgebra closed in the weak operator topology. Then $M''=M$, and $M$ is also closed in the strong operator topology. Consequently the concrete von Neumann algebras of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]] are exactly the unital $*$-subalgebras that are closed in either of these topologies. For an arbitrary set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ one has $W^*(\mathcal S)''=W^*(\mathcal S)$.

Here a complex C$^*$-algebra is a complex Banach algebra with associative bilinear multiplication, submultiplicative norm, and a conjugate-linear involution satisfying $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$; **unital** means that it has a nonzero identity $I$ ([[def-c-star-algebra]]). A $*$-automorphism is a bijective complex-linear map preserving multiplication and involution. Let $t\mapsto\alpha_t$ be a strongly continuous one-parameter group of such automorphisms, so $\alpha_0$ is the identity and $\alpha_s\alpha_t=\alpha_{s+t}$. It is **strongly continuous** when $t\mapsto\alpha_t(A)$ is norm-continuous for each fixed $A\in\mathcal A$. A **state** is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal A\to\mathbb C$ with $\omega(I)=1$ and $\omega(A^*A)\ge0$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$; this is the state convention of [[def-qsm-infinite-algebraic-state]].

Fix absolute temperature $T>0$ in kelvins and Boltzmann's constant $k_B>0$ in J K$^{-1}$; the inverse-temperature parameter is $\beta:=(k_BT)^{-1}>0$, measured in J$^{-1}$. Let the reduced Planck constant $\hbar>0$ have units J s. Write $b:=\beta\hbar$, measured in seconds, and

$$S_b:=\{z\in\mathbb C:0\le\operatorname{Im}z\le b\},\qquad S_b^\circ:=\{z\in\mathbb C:0<\operatorname{Im}z<b\}.$$

A state $\omega$ is a **$\beta$-KMS state for $\alpha$ in physical time** when for every $A,B\in\mathcal A$ there is a bounded function $F_{A,B}:S_b\to\mathbb C$ (that is, $\sup_{z\in S_b}|F_{A,B}(z)|<\infty$) that is continuous on $S_b$, complex-differentiable at every point of $S_b^\circ$, and satisfies

$$F_{A,B}(t)=\omega\!\left(A\alpha_t(B)\right),\qquad F_{A,B}(t+ib)=\omega\!\left(\alpha_t(B)A\right)\quad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

For the assigned quantum spin model, $\mathcal A$ is the norm-completed quasi-local algebra of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]] and $\alpha$ is the thermodynamic dynamics of [[thm-qsm-finite-range-spin-dynamics]], under that theorem's stated hypotheses. The strip width is $\beta\hbar$ in physical seconds; setting $\hbar=1$ is a separate natural-unit convention. This is a mathematical equilibrium criterion for the specified algebra and dynamics. It does not assert that a model describes a material, that a system has dynamically relaxed, or that all stationary states are KMS.

derivations.claim: Let $M=\{L_A:A\in M_n(\mathbb C)\}$ on $\mathcal H_{\rm HS}$, where $L_A X=AX$. The Hilbert-Schmidt adjoint satisfies $L_A^*=L_{A^*}$, so $M$ is a unital star subalgebra. The ambient operator space $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_{\rm HS})$ is finite dimensional; hence $M$ is weak-operator closed. By [F2], $M$ is a concrete von Neumann algebra. Since $\rho^{1/2}$ is invertible, every $X\in\mathcal H_{\rm HS}$ equals $L_{X\rho^{-1/2}}\Omega$, so $\Omega$ is cyclic. If $L_A\Omega=0$, then $A\rho^{1/2}=0$ and invertibility gives $A=0$, so $\Omega$ is separating. Finally, $$\langle L_A\Omega,\Omega\rangle_{\rm HS}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^{1/2}A\rho^{1/2})=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A),$$ using finite trace cyclicity.

For $A,B\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ define $$F_{A,B}(z)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\rho A e^{izH/\hbar}Be^{-izH/\hbar}\right).$$ Finite matrix exponentials are entire, so $F_{A,B}$ is entire. If $0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq\beta\hbar$, the real-time factors are unitary and the two imaginary-time factors have norms at most $e^{\beta\|H\|}$ each. Since $\|\rho\|_1=1$, $|F_{A,B}(z)|\leq\|A\|\|B\|e^{2\beta\|H\|}$ uniformly on that strip. The group $\alpha_s$ is norm-continuous because its matrix entries are continuous.

Choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $\rho$, with eigenvalues $p_j>0$, and write $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$. Then $E_{ij}\Omega=\sqrt{p_j}E_{ij}$ and $E_{ij}^*\Omega=\sqrt{p_i}E_{ji}$, whence $S(E_{ij})=\sqrt{p_i/p_j}\,E_{ji}$. The maps $JX=X^*$ and $\Delta X=\rho X\rho^{-1}$ satisfy $J\Delta^{1/2}E_{ij}=\sqrt{p_i/p_j}\,E_{ji}$ and $\Delta E_{ij}=(p_i/p_j)E_{ij}$. Thus $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$ on a basis, so uniqueness of the polar decomposition gives the stated modular data.

For $X\in\mathcal H_{\rm HS}$, $$\Delta^{it}L_A\Delta^{-it}X=\rho^{it}A\rho^{-it}X,$$ because $\Delta^{-it}X=\rho^{-it}X\rho^{it}$ and the final right factor $\rho^{it}$ cancels $\rho^{-it}$. Hence $\sigma_t(A)=\rho^{it}A\rho^{-it}$.

For $\rho=e^{-\beta H}/Z$, functional calculus gives $\rho^{it}=Z^{-it}e^{-i\beta tH}$; the scalar factor cancels in conjugation. Substituting $t=-s/(\beta\hbar)$ into step 3.1 yields $\sigma_{-s/(\beta\hbar)}(A)=e^{isH/\hbar}Ae^{-isH/\hbar}=\alpha_s(A)$. Here $\beta\hbar$ has units seconds, so the modular parameter is dimensionless.

At $z=t+i\beta\hbar$, write $U=e^{itH/\hbar}$. Since $U$ commutes with $e^{\pm\beta H}$, $$F_{A,B}(t+i\beta\hbar)=Z^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(e^{-\beta H}A e^{-\beta H}\alpha_t(B)e^{\beta H}\right) =Z^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(Ae^{-\beta H}\alpha_t(B)\right) =\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\rho\alpha_t(B)A\right).$$ The middle equality cycles $e^{\beta H}$ past the trace, and the last cycles $A$ past the trace. The lower boundary is $F_{A,B}(t)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A\alpha_t(B))$. Thus [F3] gives the physical-time $\beta$-KMS condition with width $\beta\hbar$.

For a vertex $v$ and face $f$, put $A_v=X(\partial_1^T v)$ and $B_f=Z(\partial_2 f)$, where $v$ and $f$ also denote the corresponding basis vectors. Thus $A_v$ is the product of $X$ over incident edges with odd incidence, and $B_f$ is the product of $Z$ over boundary edges with odd incidence. The identity $\partial_1\partial_2=0$ makes every $A_v$ commute with every $B_f$; each is a self-adjoint involution.
A nonempty compact connected orientable boundaryless topological surface $S$ has a unique genus $g\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$ and Euler characteristic $\chi(S)=2-2g$.

derivations.claim: Since $\partial_1\partial_2=0$, the supports of $A_v$ and $B_f$ overlap in even parity, so they commute. Each is a self-adjoint involution; hence $(I-A_v)/2$ and $(I-B_f)/2$ are commuting orthogonal projections. Multiplication by the positive coefficients makes each summand positive semidefinite.

The product of all vertex operators is $I$, because each edge has two endpoint incidences counted modulo two. The product of all face operators is $I$, because the closed surface has two incident face sides at each edge. Therefore any simultaneous joint eigenvalue assignment has an even number of violated vertex constraints and an even number of violated face constraints.

The image of $\partial_1$ is the even-parity subspace of $\mathbb F_2^V$: every edge boundary has even parity, while for a fixed vertex $v_0$, a path to each $v\ne v_0$ has boundary $v+v_0$, and these vectors span that subspace. Thus $\operatorname{rank}\partial_1=|V|-1$. A vertex coefficient vector lies in $\ker\partial_1^T$ exactly when it is orthogonal to this even-parity subspace; this orthogonal complement consists of the constant vectors and has dimension one. Rank-nullity gives $\operatorname{rank}\partial_1^T=|V|-1$, the number of independent vertex stabilizers. A face 2-chain is in $\ker\partial_2$ exactly when its coefficients agree across adjacent faces; dual-graph connectedness makes this kernel the one-dimensional constant subspace, so $\operatorname{rank}\partial_2=|F|-1$, the number of independent face stabilizers. Hence the combined stabilizer group has rank $r=|V|+|F|-2$.

Choose independent generators $S_1,\ldots,S_r$ from those commuting involutions and set $\Pi=2^{-r}\prod_{j=1}^r(I+S_j)$. This is an orthogonal projection. Independence of the vertex and face support vectors implies that its $2^r$ Pauli terms are distinct and only the all-identity term is the identity matrix. Every other Pauli term has trace zero because at least one tensor factor is $X$, $Z$, or $XZ$, each of which has trace zero. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}\Pi=2^{-r}2^{|E|}>0$, so the common $+1$ eigenspace is nonzero and has dimension $2^{|E|-r}$. The positive Hamiltonian vanishes exactly on that eigenspace, proving frustration freeness and identifying the ground space.

Put $m=\min(\{J_v\}\cup\{K_f\})$. In a joint eigenvector outside the ground space, at least one constraint is violated; by the two product identities of step 1.2, at least two constraints of that same type are violated. Each contributes at least $m$, so every excited eigenvalue is at least $2m$ above the ground energy zero. If the orthogonal complement of the ground space is zero, the stated $+\infty$ convention applies.
The dimension found in step 2.1 is $2^{|E|-|V|-|F|+2}$. By [F2], under [A1], $|V|-|E|+|F|=2-2g$, so $|E|-|V|-|F|+2=2g$. Therefore the ground-space dimension is $2^{2g}$.

On the uniform square torus, applying $Z$ on one edge to any ground vector flips exactly the two distinct endpoint vertex eigenvalues and no face eigenvalue, giving an excited vector of energy $2J$. Applying $X$ on one edge flips exactly the two adjacent face eigenvalues and no vertex eigenvalue, giving an excited vector of energy $2K$. The lower bound of step 2.2 is $2\min(J,K)$, and one of these two constructions attains it. Thus the exact first-excitation cost is $2\min(J,K)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as inherited through the cited Hall supplier. Let
$V=\mathbb C^2$ with ordered orthonormal basis $|\uparrow\rangle,|\downarrow\rangle$.
On $V$ define
$$ E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad F=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad H=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}. $$
They satisfy $[H,E]=2E$, $[H,F]=-2F$, and $[E,F]=H$, and therefore define
the standard two-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$.
Write $S^+=E$, $S^-=F$, and $S^z=H/2$.

For each integer $N\geq1$, the spin space is
$\mathcal H_N=V^{\otimes N}$ with its tensor-product inner product. If $A$ is
an endomorphism of $V$, let $A_j$ act as $A$ on factor $j$ and as the identity
on the other factors. Define the diagonal generators
$$ S_N^+=\sum_{j=1}^N E_j,\qquad S_N^-=\sum_{j=1}^N F_j,\qquad S_N^z=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^N H_j. $$
For $m\in\{-N/2,-N/2+1,\ldots,N/2\}$, its weight space is
$\mathcal H_{N,m}=\ker(S_N^z-mI)$. These are dimensionless matrices in the
algebraic spin convention.

For each integer $r\geq0$, define $V(r)$ to be the vector space
$\mathbb C[x,y]_r$ of homogeneous polynomials of degree $r$, with
$\mathfrak{sl}_2$ action
$$ E=x\partial_y,\qquad F=y\partial_x,\qquad H=x\partial_x-y\partial_y. $$
The ordered monomials $x^{r-k}y^k$ for $0\leq k\leq r$ form its basis.
Under $x\mapsto|\uparrow\rangle$ and $y\mapsto|\downarrow\rangle$,
$V(1)$ is the representation on $V$ above. A tensor power $V(1)^{\otimes N}$
uses the diagonal action defined by the sums $S_N^+,S_N^-,2S_N^z$.

Let $q_H>1$ be a prime power, fix a finite field $\mathbb F_{q_H}$, and put
$\nu=\sqrt{q_H}>1$ and $K=\mathbb Q(\nu)$. The representation category
$\mathcal A=\mathrm{Vect}^{\mathrm{fd}}_{\mathbb F_{q_H}}$ of the one-vertex,
no-arrow quiver has one simple isomorphism class, represented by
$S=\mathbb F_{q_H}$. For objects $M,N$, write
$\chi_0(M,N)=\dim_{\mathbb F_{q_H}}\operatorname{Hom}(M,N)-
\dim_{\mathbb F_{q_H}}\operatorname{YExt}^1(M,N)$. In the Hall convention of
[[def-euler-twisted-hall-algebra]], the Hall space is
$H_{\mathcal A,\nu}=\bigoplus_{[M]}K[M]$, with basis $[M]$ indexed by
isomorphism classes and product
$$[M]\star[N]=\nu^{\chi_0(M,N)}\sum_{[L]}g^L_{M,N}[L],$$
where $g^L_{M,N}$ counts subspaces $N'\subseteq L$ with $N'\cong N$ and
$L/N'\cong M$, or equivalently short exact sequences
$0\to N\to L\to M\to0$. Thus the twist is part of the multiplication.
For $M\cong\mathbb F_{q_H}^{m}$ and $N\cong\mathbb F_{q_H}^{n}$,
$\dim\operatorname{Hom}(M,N)=mn$ and every short exact sequence splits, so
$\operatorname{YExt}^1(M,N)=0$ and $\chi_0(M,N)=mn$.

By [[def-extended-hall-algebra-and-composition-subalgebra]], the composition
subalgebra is the subalgebra of this Hall algebra generated by the classes of
simple objects; its torus extension is the distinct extended composition
subalgebra. Denote the former by $\mathcal C$ here, so
$\mathcal C=K\langle[S]\rangle\subseteq H_{\mathcal A,\nu}$. The rank-one
positive quantum half is $U_\nu^+(\mathfrak{sl}_2)=K[E]$, the polynomial
algebra on one generator. The Ringel map $E\mapsto[S]$ embeds this positive
half with image $\mathcal C$; since the one-vertex graph is finite Dynkin type
$A_1$, the finite-Dynkin criterion identifies $\mathcal C$ with the full Hall
algebra in this case. The simple object is unique up to isomorphism, not as a
chosen representative. The Axiom of Choice is inherited through the cited
Ringel supplier.

Fix an integer $N\ge3$. Let $V=\mathbb C^2$ with ordered basis
$e_\uparrow,e_\downarrow$, let $V_N=V^{\otimes N}$ in left-to-right site
order, and let $V_a=V$ be an auxiliary copy. For $u\in\mathbb C$, define
$R_{aj}(u)=uI_{aj}+iP_{aj}$ on $V_a\otimes V_N$, where $P_{aj}$ swaps the
auxiliary factor and site $j$. Define
$$T_a(u)=R_{aN}(u)\cdots R_{a1}(u),\qquad t(u)=\operatorname{tr}_a T_a(u),$$
where products mean composition with the rightmost factor acting first, and
$\operatorname{tr}_a$ is the ordinary finite-dimensional trace over $V_a$.
For distinct sites $j,k$, $P_{jk}$ swaps those two tensor factors. Define the
oriented cyclic shift by
$$U(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N)=v_N\otimes v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{N-1}.$$
The spectral parameter $u$ is dimensionless. All operators in this definition
are finite-dimensional complex-linear endomorphisms.

Use the periodic convention $P_{N,N+1}:=P_{N,1}$. The rational transfer
matrix satisfies
$$i\,t'(0)t(0)^{-1}=\sum_{j=1}^N P_{j,j+1}.$$
Consequently, for real $J,c$, the finite matrix
$$H_N:=J\sum_{j=1}^N P_{j,j+1}+cI$$
is Hermitian and commutes with every $t(u)$. If $H_N$ is interpreted as a
physical energy in the stated QSM convention, $J$ and $c$ are in joules.
For the Pauli matrices
$$X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},$$
the adjacent swap on $V\otimes V$ is
$$P=\frac{I+X\otimes X+Y\otimes Y+Z\otimes Z}{2}.$$

Let $d\ge1$, let $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ act on $\mathbb C^d$ with its standard complex inner product, and let $z\in\mathbb C$. Define the finite-dimensional matrix exponential by
$$e^{zA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^kA^k}{k!},\qquad A^0=I_d.$$
Every matrix $B=(b_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ is bounded on $\mathbb C^d$: since $|x_j|\le\|x\|$ for the standard Euclidean norm, $\|Bx\|^2\le\sum_{i=1}^d(\sum_{j=1}^d|b_{ij}|)^2\|x\|^2$. Thus its operator norm is defined by the unit-ball supremum in [[def-operator-norm]]. For $B,C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $\|x\|\le1$, that definition and the bound $\|By\|\le\|B\|\|y\|$ give $\|BCx\|\le\|B\|\|Cx\|\le\|B\|\|C\|$; taking the supremum over the unit ball proves $\|BC\|\le\|B\|\|C\|$. Since $d\ge1$, the standard unit ball contains a unit vector and $\|I_d\|=1$. Hence $\|A^0\|=1$, while induction using submultiplicativity gives $\|A^k\|\le\|A\|^k$ for every $k\ge1$. The terms are therefore dominated by the convergent scalar exponential series $\sum_{k\ge0}(|z|\|A\|)^k/k!$; the displayed series converges absolutely in operator norm. The scalar exponential uses the convention $\exp z=\sum_{k\ge0}z^k/k!$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

derivations.claim:
For any endomorphism $A$ of $V=\mathbb C^2$, the two-factor flip obeys
$P(A\otimes I)P=I\otimes A$ and $P(I\otimes A)P=A\otimes I$. Hence
$P(A\otimes I+I\otimes A)=(A\otimes I+I\otimes A)P$. The same identity on
factors $i,j$, while $P_{ij}$ commutes with every $A_k$ for $k\ne i,j$,
proves the three displayed commutators for $A=E,F,H/2$. This is a direct
matrix identity under the inherited assumption [A1] and the spin definition
[F1].

For $N\geq3$, every term in $H_N$ from [F3] is a real scalar multiple
of a swap $P_{ij}$, including the periodic bond $P_{N,1}$, and the identity
term commutes with every endomorphism. Step 1.1 therefore gives
$[H_N,S_N^+]=[H_N,S_N^-]=[H_N,S_N^z]=0$. Each swap is a unitary involution
on the standard tensor-product inner product, hence $P_{ij}^*=P_{ij}$;
the real linear combination $H_N$ is Hermitian.

On $V_a\otimes\mathcal H_N$, the flip $P_{aj}$ commutes with
$A_a+\sum_{k=1}^N A_k$ for each $A\in\{E,F,H/2\}$: the two-factor flip
identity from step 1.1 applies to $A_a+A_j$, and $P_{aj}$ commutes with
$A_k$ for $k\ne j$. Thus $R_{aj}(u)=uI+iP_{aj}$ commutes with this total
generator. A product of operators commuting with a fixed operator also
commutes with it, since $[XY,G]=X[Y,G]+[X,G]Y$. Hence $T_a(u)$ commutes
with $A_a+\sum_kA_k$.

The partial trace defined in the Statement is cyclic for an endomorphism acting only on
$V_a$. In an auxiliary basis, write $X=(X_{rs})$ in chain-operator blocks
and $A=(A_{rs})$ in scalar entries. Then
$\operatorname{tr}_a((A_a\otimes I)X)=\sum_{r,s}A_{rs}X_{sr}$ and
$\operatorname{tr}_a(X(A_a\otimes I))=\sum_{r,s}X_{rs}A_{sr}$; relabelling
$r,s$ in the second sum and commuting scalar coefficients shows equality.
Taking $\operatorname{tr}_a$ of
$[A_a+\sum_kA_k,T_a(u)]=0$ therefore gives
$[\sum_kA_k,\operatorname{tr}_aT_a(u)]=0$: the chain generators act only on
the untraced tensor factors, so their commutator passes through
$\operatorname{tr}_a$. With $t(u)$ as in [F2], this is each asserted
transfer-matrix commutator.

By [F1], $S_N^z$ is diagonal in the tensor basis with eigenvalues
$-N/2,-N/2+1,\ldots,N/2$, so its weight spaces form an orthogonal direct
sum of $\mathcal H_N$. Since $[H_N,S_N^z]=0$ by step 2.1, each
$\mathcal H_{N,m}$ is invariant under $H_N$ and under every power $H_N^r$.
The series defining $\exp(-\beta H_N)$ converges in operator norm by [F4].
Its partial sums preserve every $\mathcal H_{N,m}$, and their
limits do as well because these subspaces are closed. The exponential is
therefore block diagonal for the orthogonal decomposition
$\mathcal H_N=\bigoplus_m\mathcal H_{N,m}$. In a basis formed by concatenating
orthonormal bases of the blocks, its matrix is block diagonal, so its trace
is the sum of the traces of the restrictions. Basis independence [F5] gives
the stated identity.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice as inherited through the cited Hall supplier. Let
$V=\mathbb C^2$ with ordered orthonormal basis $|\uparrow\rangle,|\downarrow\rangle$.
On $V$ define
$$ E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad F=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad H=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}. $$
They satisfy $[H,E]=2E$, $[H,F]=-2F$, and $[E,F]=H$, and therefore define
the standard two-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$.
Write $S^+=E$, $S^-=F$, and $S^z=H/2$.

For each integer $N\geq1$, the spin space is
$\mathcal H_N=V^{\otimes N}$ with its tensor-product inner product. If $A$ is
an endomorphism of $V$, let $A_j$ act as $A$ on factor $j$ and as the identity
on the other factors. Define the diagonal generators
$$ S_N^+=\sum_{j=1}^N E_j,\qquad S_N^-=\sum_{j=1}^N F_j,\qquad S_N^z=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^N H_j. $$
For $m\in\{-N/2,-N/2+1,\ldots,N/2\}$, its weight space is
$\mathcal H_{N,m}=\ker(S_N^z-mI)$. These are dimensionless matrices in the
algebraic spin convention.

For each integer $r\geq0$, define $V(r)$ to be the vector space
$\mathbb C[x,y]_r$ of homogeneous polynomials of degree $r$, with
$\mathfrak{sl}_2$ action
$$ E=x\partial_y,\qquad F=y\partial_x,\qquad H=x\partial_x-y\partial_y. $$
The ordered monomials $x^{r-k}y^k$ for $0\leq k\leq r$ form its basis.
Under $x\mapsto|\uparrow\rangle$ and $y\mapsto|\downarrow\rangle$,
$V(1)$ is the representation on $V$ above. A tensor power $V(1)^{\otimes N}$
uses the diagonal action defined by the sums $S_N^+,S_N^-,2S_N^z$.

Let $q_H>1$ be a prime power and fix a finite field $\mathbb F_{q_H}$ of that
cardinality. Put $\nu=\sqrt{q_H}>1$ and $K=\mathbb Q(\nu)$. The representation category of
the one-vertex, no-arrow quiver over $\mathbb F_{q_H}$ is the category of
finite-dimensional $\mathbb F_{q_H}$-vector spaces, with unique simple object
$S=\mathbb F_{q_H}$. Its Hall composition algebra is the subalgebra generated
by the class $[S]$ in the twisted Hall algebra with the normalization of the
Ringel supplier. The rank-one positive quantum half is
$U_\nu^+(\mathfrak{sl}_2)=K[E]$. The canonical Ringel map $E\mapsto[S]$
identifies this positive half with the composition algebra; the finite-Dynkin
criterion identifies it with the full Hall algebra in this one-vertex case.

Assume Countable Choice and the finite-matrix C$^*$-identity hypothesis used by [[thm-qsm-dt-algebraic-kubo]]. Use its finite-range spin algebra $\mathcal A$, strongly continuous automorphism group $\alpha_t$, and invariant state $\phi$ obtained from consistent local densities. Let $V=V^*\in\mathcal A$ satisfy $\phi(V)=0$, and define
$$X_T=\int_0^T\alpha_t(V)\,dt,\qquad G(t)=\operatorname{Re}\phi(V\alpha_t(V)).$$
If $G\in L^1([0,\infty))$, then
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\phi(X_T^2)}{2T}=D:=\int_0^\infty G(t)\,dt\ge0.$$
For a finite list of centered self-adjoint observables $V_1,\ldots,V_m$, if each symmetrized covariance $G_{ab}(t)=\tfrac12(\operatorname{Re}\phi(V_a\alpha_t(V_b))+\operatorname{Re}\phi(V_b\alpha_t(V_a)))$ is absolutely integrable on $[0,\infty)$, then $D_{ab}=\int_0^\infty G_{ab}(t)dt$ is a real positive semidefinite matrix. For a velocity observable measured in m s$^{-1}$, $D$ has units m$^2$ s$^{-1}$; for general $V$, its units are $[V]^2$ s. The result is a variance of a time-integrated observable, not a joint classical trajectory or a universal transport law.

Fix either a finite open chain with sites $\{1,\ldots,L\}$, $L\ge2$, or a periodic chain with sites $\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$, $L\ge3$, and denote its site set by $\Lambda_L$. Let $\mathcal H_L$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space. For each site $j$, let $q_j=q_j^*$ be a bounded charge observable, with physical unit $\mathsf Q$. For each oriented nearest-neighbor bond $(j,j+1)$, let $h_{j,j+1}=h_{j,j+1}^*$ be an energy operator in joules. Require $[h_{k,k+1},q_j]=0$ whenever $j\notin\{k,k+1\}$, and require local charge conservation $[h_{j,j+1},q_j+q_{j+1}]=0$. On an open chain set $H_L=\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}h_{j,j+1}$; on a ring set $H_L=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z}h_{j,j+1}$ with periodic indices. For an open chain define the absent boundary currents $j_{0,1}=j_{L,L+1}=0$. Use $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. These finite local data may be realized on a tensor-product spin space or on a finite fixed-particle site space, provided the stated commutation conditions hold.

The oriented bond current from $j$ to $j+1$ is
$$j_{j,j+1}:=\frac{i}{\hbar}[h_{j,j+1},q_{j+1}].$$
It has unit $\mathsf Q\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The total current is the sum over existing bonds, $J_L:=\sum_{(j,j+1)}j_{j,j+1}$, and its Heisenberg evolution for $t\in\mathbb R$ is $J_L(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_Le^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. For finite inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$, define $\rho_{\beta,L}:=e^{-\beta H_L}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_L})$ and $\omega_{\beta,L}(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{\beta,L}A)$. Write $J_L^\circ:=J_L-\omega_{\beta,L}(J_L)I$ and $J_L^\circ(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_L^\circ e^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. Define the real, connected, symmetrized correlation per site by
$$C_L(t):=\frac{1}{L}\operatorname{Re}\,\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ\right)=\frac{1}{2L}\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ+J_L^\circ J_L^\circ(t)\right).$$
The correlation has unit $\mathsf Q^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ per site.

This definition assigns no transport coefficient by itself. Any proposed finite-volume or thermodynamic transport quantity must additionally state its time cutoff, frequency regulator (for example $e^{-\eta t}$ with $\eta>0$ in seconds$^{-1}$), spatial normalization, and the exact order in which $L\to\infty$, the time cutoff tends to infinity, and any regulator is removed. Existence of those limits is not part of this definition.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable
at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
(Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$.

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

**Continuity of $f$ is a hypothesis and cannot be weakened to integrability.**
With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

derivations.claim: In the classical alternative fix $T>0$ and use Lebesgue measure on $[0,T]$ for the Bochner integral. For each $n\ge1$, let $J_n:[0,T]\to L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ take the value $J(kT/n)$ on $[kT/n,(k+1)T/n)$ for $0\le k<n$ and the value $J(T)$ at $T$. Each $J_n$ is a measurable simple function. Uniform continuity of $J$ on $[0,T]$ gives $\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|J_n(t)-J(t)\|_2\to0$, and hence $\int_0^T\|J_n(t)-J(t)\|_2\,dt\to0$. Thus $J$ is strongly measurable (an almost-everywhere limit of measurable simple functions), and $\int_0^T\|J(t)\|_2\,dt<\infty$ because $J$ is bounded. By the definition of the Bochner integral as the $L^1$-norm limit of integrals of simple functions, $J$ is Bochner integrable. The Bochner integrals of $J_n$ are the left-endpoint Riemann sums for $J$; they converge both to the Bochner integral by the $L^1$ approximation and to the norm-Riemann integral by [F6]. Hence these integrals agree. The expectation functional $\Lambda(Y):=\mathbb E[Y]=\langle Y,1\rangle_{L^2}$ is bounded since $|\Lambda(Y)|=|\langle Y,1\rangle_{L^2}|\le\|Y\|_2\|1\|_2=\|Y\|_2$. Applying the bounded-linear-map clause of [F6] gives $\mathbb E[X_T]=\int_0^T\mathbb E[J(t)]\,dt=0$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X_T)=\mathbb E[X_T^2]$.

The spatially normalized current convention is fixed by [F1]. In the quantum alternative, [A1] and [F2] apply to the exact $\alpha_t$, invariant state $\phi$, and centered self-adjoint $V$ in the Statement, so the supplier gives the variance identity and limit. The evenness asserted in the Statement follows from $C(-t)=\operatorname{Re}\phi(V\alpha_{-t}(V))=\operatorname{Re}\phi(\alpha_t(V)V)=\operatorname{Re}\overline{\phi(V\alpha_t(V))}=C(t)$, using invariance and self-adjointness. In the classical alternative, continuity of the inner product makes $(s,t)\mapsto\mathbb E[J(s)J(t)]=C(t-s)$ continuous on $[0,T]^2$. Riemann sums for $X_T$ converge in $L^2$, so continuity of the inner product makes the expectations of their squared norms converge to $\mathbb E[X_T^2]$; each squared-sum expectation is a product Riemann sum for this continuous kernel. Thus [F3] gives $\mathbb E[X_T^2]=\int_0^T\int_0^T C(t-s)\,ds\,dt$, which equals $\operatorname{Var}(X_T)$ by step 1.1. The integrand is symmetric because $C$ is even. The diagonal has zero area: it lies in strips of width $\delta$ and area at most $2T\delta+\delta^2$, tending to zero, so a bounded continuous integrand contributes zero there. Off the diagonal the two triangular restrictions are continuous; on a grid meeting the diagonal their upper-lower gap is bounded by the kernel oscillation away from the diagonal plus twice its supremum times the diagonal-strip area. Hence the product of the triangular indicator with the kernel is Riemann integrable. Each section has at most one jump and is therefore Riemann integrable. For the upper triangle, $g(t):=\int_0^t C(t-s)\,ds$ satisfies $|g(t)-g(t\prime)|\le T\omega_C(|t-t\prime|)+\|C\|_\infty|t-t\prime|$, where $\omega_C(\delta):=\sup_{|u-v|\le\delta}|C(u)-C(v)|\to0$; hence its outer integral is continuous. The lower triangle has the same estimate with reversed limits. Splitting the square into its two triangles and applying [F3] to each gives $2\int_0^T\int_0^t C(t-s)\,ds\,dt$.

For the classical alternative, apply [F4] to $\varphi(s)=t-s$ on $[0,t]$. It gives $\int_t^0 C(u)\,du=-\int_0^t C(t-s)\,ds$; reversing the oriented endpoints yields $\int_0^t C(t-s)\,ds=F(t)$, where $F(t):=\int_0^t C(u)\,du$. By [F7], $F'=C$; the product rule gives $(tF(t))'=F(t)+tC(t)$, a continuous derivative. Applying [F5] to $tF(t)$ and using $F(T)=\int_0^T C(u)\,du$ yields $\int_0^T F(t)\,dt=\int_0^T(T-u)C(u)\,du$. Thus step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{Var}(X_T)/(2T)=\int_0^T(1-u/T)C(u)\,du$.

In the classical alternative, put $K:=\int_0^\infty|C(u)|\,du<\infty$. For $T>R>0$, the difference between step 3.1 and the improper integral is bounded by
$$\left|\int_0^T(1-u/T)C(u)\,du-\int_0^\infty C(u)\,du\right|\le\frac{R}{T}K+2\int_R^\infty|C(u)|\,du.$$
First choose $R$ so the tail is arbitrarily small, then let $T\to\infty$; this proves the classical limit. The quantum limit is supplied by [F2].

In the classical alternative every finite-time variance is nonnegative, so its limit is nonnegative; in the quantum alternative nonnegativity is part of [F2]. The limit therefore has the stated sign in either case.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix either a finite open chain with sites $\{1,\ldots,L\}$, $L\ge2$, or a periodic chain with sites $\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$, $L\ge3$, and denote its site set by $\Lambda_L$. Let $\mathcal H_L$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space. For each site $j$, let $q_j=q_j^*$ be a bounded charge observable, with physical unit $\mathsf Q$. For each oriented nearest-neighbor bond $(j,j+1)$, let $h_{j,j+1}=h_{j,j+1}^*$ be an energy operator in joules. Require $[h_{k,k+1},q_j]=0$ whenever $j\notin\{k,k+1\}$, and require local charge conservation $[h_{j,j+1},q_j+q_{j+1}]=0$. On an open chain set $H_L=\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}h_{j,j+1}$; on a ring set $H_L=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z}h_{j,j+1}$ with periodic indices. For an open chain define the absent boundary currents $j_{0,1}=j_{L,L+1}=0$. Use $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. These finite local data may be realized on a tensor-product spin space or on a finite fixed-particle site space, provided the stated commutation conditions hold.

The oriented bond current from $j$ to $j+1$ is
$$j_{j,j+1}:=\frac{i}{\hbar}[h_{j,j+1},q_{j+1}].$$
It has unit $\mathsf Q\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The total current is the sum over existing bonds, $J_L:=\sum_{(j,j+1)}j_{j,j+1}$, and its Heisenberg evolution for $t\in\mathbb R$ is $J_L(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_Le^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. For finite inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$, define $\rho_{\beta,L}:=e^{-\beta H_L}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_L})$ and $\omega_{\beta,L}(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{\beta,L}A)$. Write $J_L^\circ:=J_L-\omega_{\beta,L}(J_L)I$ and $J_L^\circ(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_L^\circ e^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. Define the real, connected, symmetrized correlation per site by
$$C_L(t):=\frac{1}{L}\operatorname{Re}\,\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ\right)=\frac{1}{2L}\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ+J_L^\circ J_L^\circ(t)\right).$$
The correlation has unit $\mathsf Q^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ per site.

This definition assigns no transport coefficient by itself. Any proposed finite-volume or thermodynamic transport quantity must additionally state its time cutoff, frequency regulator (for example $e^{-\eta t}$ with $\eta>0$ in seconds$^{-1}$), spatial normalization, and the exact order in which $L\to\infty$, the time cutoff tends to infinity, and any regulator is removed. Existence of those limits is not part of this definition.

Assume Countable Choice and the finite-matrix C$^*$-identity hypothesis used by [[thm-qsm-dt-algebraic-kubo]]. Use its finite-range spin algebra $\mathcal A$, strongly continuous automorphism group $\alpha_t$, and invariant state $\phi$ obtained from consistent local densities. Let $V=V^*\in\mathcal A$ satisfy $\phi(V)=0$, and define
$$X_T=\int_0^T\alpha_t(V)\,dt,\qquad G(t)=\operatorname{Re}\phi(V\alpha_t(V)).$$
If $G\in L^1([0,\infty))$, then
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\phi(X_T^2)}{2T}=D:=\int_0^\infty G(t)\,dt\ge0.$$
For a finite list of centered self-adjoint observables $V_1,\ldots,V_m$, if each symmetrized covariance $G_{ab}(t)=\tfrac12(\operatorname{Re}\phi(V_a\alpha_t(V_b))+\operatorname{Re}\phi(V_b\alpha_t(V_a)))$ is absolutely integrable on $[0,\infty)$, then $D_{ab}=\int_0^\infty G_{ab}(t)dt$ is a real positive semidefinite matrix. For a velocity observable measured in m s$^{-1}$, $D$ has units m$^2$ s$^{-1}$; for general $V$, its units are $[V]^2$ s. The result is a variance of a time-integrated observable, not a joint classical trajectory or a universal transport law.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable
at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
(Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$.

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

**Continuity of $f$ is a hypothesis and cannot be weakened to integrability.**
With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ be a real vector space ([[def-vector-space]]) with a norm $\|\cdot\|$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]) whose metric $d(x,y):=\|x-y\|$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]). Let $a<b$ be reals ([[def-interval]]) and let $g:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). For endpoints $c,d\in[a,b]$, set $\int_c^c g:=0_X$ and, when $c>d$, set $\int_c^d g:=-\int_d^c g$; for $c<d$ use the Riemann-sum construction below on the restriction to $[c,d]$. Then:

1. **Integral.** For every sequence of tagged partitions of $[a,b]$ whose mesh tends to $0$, the Riemann sums $\sum_i(t_{i+1}-t_i)\,g(s_i)$ converge in $X$; the limit, written $\int_a^b g$, is independent of the sequence, and
$$\Bigl\|\int_a^b g\Bigr\|\;\le\;(b-a)\sup_{t\in[a,b]}\|g(t)\| .$$
2. **Fundamental theorem.** The curve $G:[a,b]\to X$, $G(t):=\int_a^t g$, is well defined, satisfies $\|G(t)-G(s)\|\le(t-s)\sup_{[s,t]}\|g\|$ for $a\le s\le t\le b$, and is differentiable with $G'=g$ on $[a,b]$ in the one-sided sense at the endpoints.
3. **Linearity.** For continuous $g,h:[a,b]\to X$ and reals $\alpha,\beta$: $\int_a^b(\alpha g+\beta h)=\alpha\int_a^b g+\beta\int_a^b h$; and for $a\le c\le b$, $\int_a^b g=\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g$.
4. **Bounded linear images.** If $Y$ is a normed real vector space and $T:X\to Y$ is linear with $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for some $C<+\infty$ and all $x$, then $T\circ g$ is continuous and $T\bigl(\int_a^b g\bigr)=\int_a^b (T\circ g)$; in particular, for every real-linear functional $\Lambda:X\to\mathbb R$ with $|\Lambda x|\le C\|x\|$, $\Lambda\bigl(\int_a^b g\bigr)=\int_a^b\Lambda\circ g$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
(The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$), let $F$ be its integral function
(The integral function $F(x) := \int_a^x f$ of an integrable $f$), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

citations.quote:
A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

A **piecewise $C^1$ curve** in $M$ is a continuous map $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with a finite subdivision such that, in local charts on each closed piece, its coordinate representative is $C^1$ on the interior and its derivative extends continuously to both endpoints. The endpoint values of this extension are the corresponding one-sided derivatives.

Use the chartwise regularity convention of [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]] and the finite path operations of [[def-piecewise-c1-path-operations-and-oriented-reparametrizations]]. Refining a piece into finitely many chart pieces is allowed. No nonzero-velocity hypothesis is imposed: constant segments and pauses are admissible. A singleton parameter interval is interpreted as a constant curve.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
(Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $f$ is bounded (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
(Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$,
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$ earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Any two admissible finite subdivisions have a finite common refinement. Repeatedly applying [F5] shows that subdividing a piece leaves the sum unchanged; hence the defined period is a unique real number independent of the chosen subdivision.

In the length coordinate $\tau$, the map $x(\tau):=\ell(\tau/\chi)$ satisfies $x(\tau)=x_H+\lambda U_\kappa(\tau)$, since $\lambda U_\kappa(\tau)=-\chi A e^{-\kappa\tau}$. By [F1], $U_\kappa$ is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism from $\mathbb R$ onto $(-\infty,0)$; the positive affine map $y\mapsto x_H+\lambda y$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from $(-\infty,0)$ onto $(-\infty,x_H)$. Since $u\mapsto\tau=\chi u$ is also a positive linear diffeomorphism, $\ell$ is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism from $\mathbb R$ onto $(-\infty,\ell_H)$, with smooth inverse $u_\ell(x)=\chi^{-1}U_\kappa^{-1}((x-x_H)/\lambda)$. Differentiating the supplied coordinate formula gives $\ell'(u)=\chi\lambda e^{-\kappa\chi u}=\chi Ak e^{-ku}$ and hence $U'(u)=Ak e^{-ku}>0$. If $\operatorname{supp}g\subseteq[a,b]$, then $\operatorname{supp}f_g\subseteq[\ell(a),\ell(b)]\subset(-\infty,\ell_H)$, so the zero extension is smooth and compactly supported. Thus $J(f_g)$ is defined by [F1]–[F2].

The map $(u,v)\mapsto(\ell(u),\ell(v))$ is a smooth diffeomorphism, so [F4] transports the two-variable test pairing with Jacobian $\ell'(u)\ell'(v)$. Since $\ell=\chi U$, the regularized identity $\chi^2[-(4\pi)^{-1}(\chi s-i\epsilon)^{-2}]=-(4\pi)^{-1}(s-i\epsilon/\chi)^{-2}$ shows that the positive unit scale cancels in the boundary distribution, giving the stated seconds-coordinate kernel. Positivity is the supplied Fock norm identity $W(g,g)=\|h_{f_g}\|_2^2\ge0$ from [F1].

On the finite-particle domain, the left vacuum annihilates every creation term and the right vacuum is annihilated by every annihilation operator. Commuting the annihilation part of the leftmost $J(f_{g_1})$ through the later fields, [F3] replaces each commutator by its scalar two-point contraction; the term with the annihilator reaching the right vacuum vanishes. Hence
$$M_n(g_1,\ldots,g_n)=\sum_{j=2}^n M_2(g_1,g_j)\,M_{n-2}(g_2,\ldots,\widehat{g_j},\ldots,g_n).$$
The base cases are $M_0=1$ and $M_1=0$. Induction gives zero for odd $n$ and the stated sum over pair partitions for even $n$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $I$ be a finite nonempty index set. For each $\alpha\in I$, let $H_\alpha$ and $K_\alpha$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, and give

$$H_A:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}(H_\alpha\otimes K_\alpha)$$

the orthogonal direct-sum inner product: distinct summands are orthogonal and the inner product within a summand is the Hilbert tensor-product inner product. On elementary tensors that inner product is $\langle x\otimes y,x'\otimes y'\rangle=\langle x,x'\rangle\langle y,y'\rangle$. A map $T\otimes U$ acts by $(T\otimes U)(x\otimes y)=Tx\otimes Uy$, and a direct-sum map acts blockwise with zero off-diagonal blocks.

A complex-linear endomorphism is a linear map from a vector space to itself. A density matrix on a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space is a self-adjoint endomorphism with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one; it is faithful when all eigenvalues are strictly positive. These are the conventions used for the finite density matrices in the earlier modular-balance result. The summand indexed by $\alpha$ is called the $\alpha$ sector. For each $\alpha$, fix a faithful density matrix $\chi_\alpha$ on $K_\alpha$. Let $\mathbf p=(p_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}$ satisfy $p_\alpha>0$ and $\sum_{\alpha\in I}p_\alpha=1$, and let $\rho_\alpha$ be density matrices on $H_\alpha$. Define the encoded endomorphism

$$\mathcal E_\chi(\mathbf p,\rho):=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}p_\alpha\,\rho_\alpha\otimes\chi_\alpha.$$

When this encoded endomorphism is a density matrix, call it the encoded reduced state. The logical data are $\mathbf p$ and $\{\rho_\alpha\}$; the ancillary matrices $\{\chi_\alpha\}$ are held fixed. For a second strictly positive probability vector $\mathbf q$ and faithful density matrices $\sigma_\alpha$ on the same $H_\alpha$, write $\sigma_A:=\mathcal E_\chi(\mathbf q,\sigma)$ for the encoded reference endomorphism.

This is a finite-dimensional algebraic model. The definition makes no gravitational interpretation and does not identify a matrix entropy term with a geometric area.
